div.p: THE EXAMINER, RATIJ NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &e. M. PASTEGE'S SHEEP VacciNATrotas.—Statistics brought up to October 1 show that the inoculations of splenic fever, according to Pasteur's method, were performed on 160 flocks comprising 68,000 sheep, of which 33,576 were vac- cinated, and 21,938 animals were left uninoculated, so as to judge of the results of difference of treatment. Before vac- cination, says the British Medical Journal, the losses caused by splenic fever amounted, on the whole of the flocks, to 2,986 animals. Daring vaccination, and until its effects were perfected, 260 sheep out of the whole number of 33,596 perished. During the same period, the mortality rose to 366 out of the group of 21,938 which were not vac- cinated. When the effects of vaccination were complete in the first group, the mortality fromolenic fever fell to five. This rate has persisted up jo the present time; and the next statistical account will gave, it is expected, the same satisfactory results as regards the groups of animals vac- cinated and left unvaccinated. Lavia's Csgasr SEPARATOR.-Dr. Voelcker found by experiments conducted in the Agricultural Hall that the proportion of fat left in the skimmilk from Laval's separator was only .31, whereas the proportion in the skim milk after ordinary skimming was 1.25 per cent. Mr. Tisdall, of Hol- land Park Dairy, who employs regularly two of Laval's separators, finds the proportion of fat to be only .25, and he is in the habit of sending up skim milk from his dairy near Epsom to go through the separator. On calling at his place last week we found one of the separators operating on milk which had been skimmed three times, and there had been quite a large bucket full of thin cream abstracted, sufficient it was said to make 10lbs. of butter, the quantity from which this was taken being twenty-four barn gallons. Laval's separator will operate on thirty gallons per hour, and the batter can be churned quite as quickly after its employment. The cream can be separated immediately after milking, and churning be proceeded with at once, so that the slopping tedious work of milk setting is entirely dispensed with, and the butter is not only made perfectly sweet, but the skim milk is rendered fit for human food. The poor people even in the west of London consider it a boon to take it away from Mr.Tisdall's yard at id. per pint. It would pay any dairy farmer to have a separator, in Mr. Tisdall' s opinion, who has to deal with as much as 100 gal- lons of milk a day, but if he had a steam engine already. it would be worth while to buy the separator itself for a much smaller quantity. THE VALUE OF TESTING A Cow's Mrs Flaw.— Nothing can possibly prove the importance of dairy farmers keeping accurate records of the yield of their cows than the tabulated return of Mr. Tisdall, which is published in the Volume of the British Dairy Farmers' Association recently published. Mr. Tisdall is in the habit of testing the milk yields of all his cows regularly, and, as he explained in his speech at the Farmers' Club on the 7th inst., the task of doing so involves no very laborious or tedious labour. For all practical purposes, if the test be applied about fence a fortnight it is found sufficient; and as he said, with force of truth, on the occasion referred to, it is hard if a man, de- sirous of conducting his business in a 'proper way, cannot get_up early in the morning occasionally to see after a matter of this kind himself. Mr. Allender in his paper very pointedly alluded to this record of Mr. Tiede% as showing what enormous yields are afforded by some of the best cows, inasmuch as twenty-five of the heaviest milkers in the list show a total produce for the year averaging no less than 885 gallons each, while ten cows averaged no less 1,100 gallons. But Mr. Tisdall's list contains records of sixty cows, and if five of the lowest-Prodacine. ones be taken, their respective; yields would still average 659 gallons each. Thus the entire slAty are good milchers oat of a herd of about a hundred, so that we may make the reasonable con- clusion that even our best herds afford very variable re- turns in the respective animals which belong to them. And if such is the case in the green, what must it be in the dry? In other words, if in such a herd as that of bir. Tisdall, where ainnenee in milk yield is deemed a condition for any cow to ha retained, where breeding from the best milking families has been carried on for some years, what immense discrepancies would be found in ordinary herds where a system of haphazard selection prevails, and no great care is taken to breed only from the best milkers. Very probably the ill-success which attends the business of many dairy farmers may be directly referable to the ill-policy of keeping animals which are only moderately endowed with lacteal fertility- and if they were only to apply tests and keep re- cords like Mr. Tisdall, they would very soon find out what serious losses they lay themselves open to by not breeding and selecting the right kinds of cows. Another very im- portant fact which becomes prominently fixed on attention by the tabulated record which Mr. Tisdall has made public is the immense difference in the holding-out properties of cows. The majority of those in the list which gave most milk just after calving did not yield the largest quantities taking the entire period they were in milk. Some cows milk abundantly nearly up to the period of calving, while others give out at the end of the eighth month, and there are one or two cases lathe list where heavy milkers during the first three or four months have been dry at the end of the seventh month. Such facts ought certainly to exert a great influence on the policy of breeding only from families which have the reputation of being possessed not only with tolerably affluent milking properties at the first, but of re- taining the function permanently, or at least as long est they can reasonably be expected to hold out. For this reason it would be' good policy for all dairy farmers to imitate Mr. Tisdall in making periodical tests, and retaining the records of all the milk yields of the members of their herds. And I it would be an invaluable assistance to them abso if the I British Dairy Farmers' Association were to establish a Dairy Herdbook of heavy-class milkers and their progeny. HEEEDITARY LenualecEs.--" Like begets like' is an ex- pression as true of health and vigour of constitution as it is of colour, symmetry, character, and outward form. ,It is to a knowledge of this fact, and the enterprise it has awakened in the stock-breeders of this country, that the super-excel- lence of English horses, oxen, and sheep is attribufable., duet as the progeny of our domestic creatures bear the general impress, temperament, and qualities of the parent, so do they inherit the strength or weakness of the let. tr, the tendency or predisposition Ca actual disease. The inflaence of parentage is as decidedly and completely shown In the good or indifferent performance of the various functions of the body as it is in the exterior physical conformation, and the defects of the one are as readily transmitted from parent to offspring as are those of the other. Weak lungs are capable of being as directly and powerfully inherited as are beht limbs and other bodily distortions, and even in some Instances as the coloursof the animal itself. General con- stitutional weakness, with an aptitude to relapse into dis- ease, is the inheritance of some of our most valuable strains of both horses, oxen, and sheep. The over zealous desire to Introduce or improve some special quality of form, func- tion, or expression, or to modify the general appearance in conformity with the requirements of breeders of stock, has led to the adoption of a sysAm of in-and-in breeding, i.e., the mating of animals of the same family or strain or kin- dred blood. The results obtained have been highly beneficial in promoting rapid growth, early maturity, and fattening properties; but they have likewise in numerous instances proved destructive of constitutional vigour and "general health by multiplying the intensity of family iitirmities. IFrom a health point of view, it is of the highest importance to breeders of farm stock that dams and sires should be judiciously selected. Animals only with sound constitution and good, physical development, born of sound parents, should be used for stock purposes. some of the most in- tractable enduring, and fatal diseases are hereditary and transmissible 'from parent to offspring. The destructive disorders known as tuberculosis and scrofula, which present themselves in the form of consumption or wasting, are among the number. Rheumatism, rickets, and the various diseases .of the legs of horses known as splints, spavins, ringbones, and curbs are all the outcome of inherited weak- nese in by far the majority of cases. Roaring, broken wind, and ophthalmia or inflammation of the eye—diseases which incapacitate and render worthless some of our best equine blood—are born of hereditary influence. Similarly, the powers of endurance possessed by some horses and the tolerance of cold and deprivation exhibited by some other animals, are properties built up in the constitution and handed down from parent to progeny. Certain strains of weightsleitiAssrxratonapypooecatnriogti over long racehorses, for example, are notorious for carrying heavy distances, and performing feats of en- durance which other equally stout-looking and highly- trained animals are utterly incapable of. The hereditary tendency to disease may be strongly or slightly inherited. In some families particular weaknesses appear in every member, at one period or another. In others they are only occasional, or may even altogether di;appear from one or a succession of generations—to return again under the influ- ence of indifferent regard for the laws of health. The in- fluence of external circumstances may do much to uphold health and ward off disease where the tendency to ills only feebly inherited, and ewes in some cases permanently stamp out the morbid faculty altogether. In this connection good food, a suitable climate, and the general eArvance of the laws of health, added to judicious crossing with sound stock, are the essential elements of success. Low. " A COLD Eracn.—The coldest place on the eartft is not, as has hitherto been believed by meteorologists, Yakutsk, in Siberia, but Verkoyansk, in the same region, lying in 67A N. lat., on the river Yana. Its lowest mean winter tem- perature is 4813 deg, below zero centigrade. This, then, is the cold pole of the earth in Asia; the corresponding pole in America being to the north-west of the Parry Islands ; and the line joining these two places does not pass through the North Pole itself, which is thus, in all probability, out- side the line of greatest cold. It Is noteworthy that Ver. kovansk, like Yakutsk, is on the mainland, a considerable distance from the Siberian coast, which possesses a compara- tively milder climate. The recent Schwatka Franklin- search expedition, however, found that in the neighbour- hood of the Back River the mean winter temperature is not far behind that of Verkoyansk ; of course the minima of both places reach a much lower figure. It is well known that in the tropics, on the other hand, the greatest heat is not at the Equator, but some distance north and south of it. —Pall Mall Gazette. • ISST4LNTLNEOLITS PIIOTOORLPILS rec Oil BALLOONS.—At a meeting of the Balloon Society, Del r. Woodbury read a paper on the taking of instantaneous photographs from balloons. Although the subject is still in its infancy, the lines for future progress are tolerably clear. The two desiderata are a most sensitive plate with a rapidly-acting shatter and the attainment of the greatest steadiness for the camera. It has been found that frea balloons, with the motion of revolving as they do on their own axis, are not suitable. Captive balloons can, however, be prevented by their attaching cords from revolution. The plan brought forward by Mr. Wood-. bury is that of sending up a balloon with a camera, which has its shutter movements connected with an electric wire running up the cord attached to the balloon. The move- ments include the instantaneous opening of the shutter, fol- lowed by the moving of a fresh plate into the place of that which has taken a photograph. Some four or five plates can thus in succession ba brought into use. By pivot arrangements the motion of the camera is reduced to a swing in one direction only, and, as the balloon can be watched with a field-glass, the exact moment for opening the shutter by means of the electric current can be selected. Photo- graphs can now be taken in the two-thousandth part of a second, and progress in rapidity is being constantly made. As regards the fens, it is found that after 200 yards dis- tance there is but little or no need for change, just as is the case with the distant view through a telescope. It is ex- pected that such a method of photographing will be of value in warfare. Supposing it is expected there are troops on the other side of a hill, a photograph from a balloon at a suitable elevation would make this known, and a series of four or five photographs, taken at intervals of a minute or two, would give the direction of their movement. Although some specimens of photographs shown do not exhibit much sharpness, it is believed they would be good enough for oh - t lining the first rough basis of charts in districts to be sur- veyed for the first time. Now that attention is once directed to the subject, it may be expected that, as has been the case in other inventions, steps towards greater perfection will fellow. Tan Sinitnns itnanainasatvn Gxs-Banlzna.—One of the results of the introduction of electric lighting has been to stimulate invention in the direction at improved gas illumi- nation, and, as a consequence, several practical improve- ments have been introduced in gas-burners, is has been re.. corded by us from time to time. The latest advance in this direction which has been brought under our notice is that made by Mr. F. Siemens, of Dresden, and Dr. C. W. Siemens, of London, who some time since entered upon a long series of experiments with gas as an illuminant. The result has been the development of a perfectly new method of burning gas for illuminating purposes, which is now known as the regenerative system. The distinguishing characteristics of the new burner are—increased illumination, with a corre- sponding economy in the consumption of gas, perfect venti- lation, and complete combustion. The products of combus- tion are continuously returned by a downward current to the interior of the burner itself, and there utilised to heat a S resh supply of gas and air prior to their use at the orifice of the burner. We recently examined some of the regene- rative burners at the offices of the Siemens Gas-light Com- pany, 40, Queen Victoria-street, London, where they were giving excellent results. The burner consists mainly of three concentric metallic chambers, into one of which—the intermediate one—the gas is delivered from the supply-pipe, passing through a serie%of very small vertical tubes'at the tops of which it is ignited and burned. At this point the gas mingles with a current of air which has been heated by passing through the ckamber surrounding the gas chamber, which is also heated. Within the ring of gas-jets is a tube which opens downwards into the third or central chamber. After rising for a short distance,the luminous band of flame, produced by the gas and heated air, curves over the top edge of this inner tube, and is sucked down into the inner cham- ber, which it heats. . The products of combastion pass away through an exit tube, heating on their way the chambers through which the gas and air are passing to the com- mingling point. The intimate mixture of the gas and air is insured by means of deflectors. The success of the system has led to its adoption in Germany, France, and other comfl. tries, while in _England, Mr. T. W. Beate.% the consulting chemist to the Metropolitan Board of Works, after careful investigation, reports that the results are better than any he has known to be obtained with any gas-burner hitherto in- vented.

THE CAPTAIN OF THE CIfERIAN. Broken and wrecked by the pitiless storm. The good ship Cyprian lay ; Her timbers craslaed, as the hurricane Swept helm and mast away; And the sea sprang over'her shivering side Like a tiger on its prey. The captain stood on the vessel's deck That he might tread no more; He had fought the tempest manfully; Had fought, but the fight was o'er One hope, the life-buoy, yet remained. And he might win the shore. Then from souse hiding-place there crept All drenched with salt sea spray, A little ragged, half-starved child. • A wretched stowaway; Who wrung his hands and shrieked aloud In pitiful dismay. Only a little stowaway With terror almost mad: The captain looked on the yawning waves. He looked upon the lad, Be held the life-belt in his hand. The one last hope he had. And far beyond the clamouring sea. Beyond the binding foam. Be saw the firelight gleaming bright Within his English home; He heard the voice of his love—lals wits , It seemed to whisper, " Come;" The vision passed, as passing breath child, HeThaturtnsedtrivteews tarhde,sttehe t el tr eo mdim; l n g Be gave the belt to him. w lake it, my lad," the captain Said, "And I must try to swim." They plunged together in the waves, The stowaway and he, But vain was swimmer's sturdiest stroke. As infant's strength might be; His life-belt bore the'lad to shore, He—perished in the sea. Oh, never nobler deed was done Never, on land or wave, Shall the Cyprian's captain be forgot Bo tender and so brave; Who gave his life so willingly. The stowaway to save! z•-. Leeds Mercury MeAly. "Old!" said the child indignantly. "I'm not old at all. I'm quite new !" ' Profanity never did any man the least good. No man is licher, happier, or wiser for it. Asking the cost of a pre- sent that has been made to you ; " pumping " a servant to bear what has been given by way of parting vall ; loud talking in public ; hard staring at table; insolent disrespect to husband, wife, sister, or brother; showing temper in trifles and making scenes in public; showing an embarrass- ing amount of fondness and making love in public; covert sneers, of which people can see the animus if they do not always understand the drift; persistent egotism, which talks for ever of itself, itself, itself, only itself, and cannot feign the most passing interest in another; detraction of I friends and it may be of relations--a husband telling of his wife's unpleasantness, a wife complaining of her husband's faults; a bold assumption of superiority,and the servile con- fession of infinite unworthiness; all these are signs and evi- dences of vulgarity—vulgarity of a far worse type than that which eats its fish with a steel knife, and says "you was" and "each of the men were." That we require a re- adjustment of local taxation there can be no doubt; but when it does come I trust it wM be one leading to economy not to added extravagance.* It is astonishing how generous public bodies can become, and how wasteful, I might add, when they have the public purse to take at, yet how cheese- paring the self-same men are individually when their own pockets are concerned. -.411•-••
MISCELLANEOUS.

Sheerness Dockyard Okurch was destroyed by fire on Saturday night. Three young children have been poisoned at Poplar through the administration of morphia in mistake for simple ". powders." Damage estimated at £B,OOO was caused by a fire at the East Lancashire Soap Works, near Accrington, early on Sunday morning. Her Majesty held a Council at Windsor on Tuesday. Parliament was prorogued till the 7th of February, when it will meet for the despatch of busines9. Lady Caroline Laskeiles, aunt to the Marquis of Harting- ton, died on Monday, and his Lordship's engagements in Lancashire have therefore been postponed. - A serious.landslip has taken place in upper Rhondda Valley, several houses being in imminent banger. The damage done in the Rhondda Valley amounts to £1,5044. At the agricultural hirings in North and East Yorkshire last week there was a great superfluity of labour, and agri- cultural servants had to accept a reduction in the year's hire of from £2 4s. to £3. The judges of the Queen's Bench have decided that a lodger claiming to be placed on the list ef voters is not bound to appear before the Revising Barrister to support his claim, the declaration annexed thereto being prima facie evidence of qualification. A farmer named Edward Trickett, living at Ash, near Whitchurch, has been fined £2O and costs for sending milk to dealer in Manchester which had been adulterated with water to the extent of 30 per cent. The penalty was the highest allowed by the law. In the collision on Friday night on the North British Railway, near Tayport, three passengers were killed and seven seriously injured. The signalman, Thomas Dippie, has been arrested. He had been in the service of the com- pany for about 30 years. The stoker of the goods train has since died from the injuries he had sustained. A CLERGYMAN'S DAUGHTER MARRYING A GARDENER. —The youngest daughter of a vicar, near Leigh, on Satur- day married a young man who has recently been employed as her father's gardener. He left his situation at the begin- ning of last week,- and the lady followed on Friday, and a telegram on Saturday anounced that the wedding had taken place. Detective Fowler was charged, at Bradford, on Monday, with indecently assaulting a girl named gavanagh. The prosecutrix, who is aged 15, was confined for robbery, and she alleged that Fowler put her in a separate cell on Sunday night, and took liberties with her. She screamed, and he desisted. Females in the adjoining cells deposed to hearing screatns, and the bench sentenced the prisoner to six mouths' imprisonment. MR. BURT, M.P., AND "FAIR TRADE" A collier at Ashton-under-Lyne recently wrote to Mr. T. Burt, M.P., asking his opinion on "fair trade." The hon. member's i reply sas follows :—" I have only time for a word. 'Fair trade' is but another name for protection, and my opinion is that its adoption in any shape or form would be entirely mischievous to the working classes." Mr. Justice Fly gave judgment on Tuesday in the im- portantsuit brought brought by Mr. W. Smith, of Sheffield, against Messrs. Chadwicks, Adamson, and Co., for alleged misrepresentation in the "promotion" of the Blochairn Iron Works Company, Limited. His Lordship held that the defendants had been guilty of " deceit " in the statements they put forth in the prospectus of the Company, and he ordered them fo pay plaintiff £5,000 and the costs. THE WELSH Barium Quits-rim—Referring to a recent burials case which has occurred in North Wales, in yehich the clergyman has declinekto bury a• parishioner without payment, Mr. Osborne Morgan, Q.C., M.P., the Judge Advocate-General, has written stating that if it has been the custom in the parish in question to bestow offerings, then the clergyman has no right to charge fees on any occasion. It did not appear to him that there could be any legitimate distinction drawn by the clergyman between old and new parishioners. The latter have formed a defence fund, and should there be further scandal the point at issue will be legally tested. Sentence was passed on Tuesday by M. Justice Denman on the defendants who bad been convicted of corrupt prac- tices at elections. Messrs. May and Mair, of Macclesfield, were severally sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. Mr. Justice Denman commented with great severity on the "sickening disclosures" which.had been made, and said that I,the defendants had been convicted of practices disgraceful in themselves and damaging to the community. In reference to the Sandwich election, Messrs. Edwards and Olds were each sentenced to six months" imprisonment. Three of the others, who were publicans,,Mackins, Rae, and Spears, and also 'Wood, a farmer, were sentenced to three months' im- prisonment. The sentence upon the two others, who were boatmen, was two months' imprisonment. The Court also directed that all the defendants should be treated as ordinary misdemeanants, and not as first-class misdemeanants. Detachments of the Salvation Army, from Birkenhead, Crewe, Northwich, and other places, headed by a " Captain " George, have begun what they announced in large placards as "The storming of Chester." They, have, secured .the Station Skating Rink, and services are held daily, including the "knee drill." The rink was crowded on Sunday at all the services with men and women who, out of curiosity, had gone to see the "army." The "S." men were on the plat- form, and their religious exercises seem to afford great amusement to the immense audience in front. In the after- noon of Sunday certain individuals upset the money boxes and kicked them about, while the crowd outside showered bricks and stones on the metallic roof, causing a terrific noise, but, nothing daunted, the "soldiers" continued the service,

• ---• Tax Barran EIALF.—Of course, the lady is the better half in most cases; do you not think so? That is, when- ever she is true to herself as a woman. Always remember that womanliness comprises the highest and holiest virtues, and it is only when a woman is false to herself, and tries to assume the qualities and bearing of men, that she loses the blessedness of her own high estate. Everything is beautiful that is and does just what God would have it be and do. So God made women to be patient, gentle, tender, forbearing, holy, meek, and pure, and when they are such they are true women and the better halves of men; but when they are vain and self-seeking, loud and talkative, fast and frivolous, they are no longer the better halves, but very much the worserones.

div.p: STATE OF-IRELO,D.

The nomination for county Derry took place on Wednes- day. The Home Rule candidate, Mr. Dempsey; the Parnell- Conservative candidate, Sir Samuel Wilson, of Hughenden ; and the Solicitor-General for Ireland, Mr. Porter, were severally nominated. Parties of armed men on Monday night attacked the houses of James Reddon and Pat Alen, near Barfield, three miles from Ennis. Several shots were fired in each instance, and Reddon narrowly escaped being struck by a bullet which lodged over the fireplace. On Monday night, a contingent of constabulary, return- ing to Kilfinane from some evictions at Brnff, were attacked by a mob with stones. The police fixed bayonets, and charged the people, dispersing them. The latter, however, returned, and were again charged before they would retire. Some arrests will be made. The Daily News is informed that Mr. A. M. Sullivan has applied for the Chiltern Hundreds. It has been officially intimated to Mr. Sullivan that it is not in the prLwer of the Speaker to issue a new writ in such circumstances whilst , Parliament is in recess. A (further election for Meath will not, therefore, take place ,till after Parliament has met. Evictione on a large scale commenced on the property of Lord Bantry, near Castletown, Berehaven, in the extreme west of county Cork, on Tuesday. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., who has been staying in Glengariffe for thepast week, accompanied the expedition, and entered several of the houses, which are on the poorest description of mountain land. The tenants, who are two years in arrears, offerecT in most cases one year's rent, and in some instances the rum was accepted on account. All the tenants were evicted, but eight were reinstated conditionally for a month. There was no crowd or attempt at resistance. The Freeman's Journal protests against the cry of "the English and landlord Irish press" for more coercion, and says that every man in Ireland knows that the pictures of Ithe country in the columns of the English press are outra- geous and most-mischievous exaggerations. In these cir- cumstances, says our contemporary," a grave duty devolsles open the Chief Secretary from which he should not shrink. He should at once seek or create an opportunity of speaking out plainly on the present crisis. Nothing which the Irish popular press can say, nothing which Irish popular repre- sentatives can say, has now the slightest effect upon English Opinion. An artificial panic is being created ha England in order to enable the landlord class in Ireland to put money in their pockets." A Bradford paper makes the announce- ment that in view of the condition of Irish affairs Mr. Forster will spend the winter in Dublin. AN IRISH CONSERVATIVE AGRICULTURIST'S OPINION OF THE Lem) geattleman has received from a friend 1 near Coleraine the following letter In replr to a question as to what he thought of the Land Bill. The writer is one of the largest tenant farmers in that part of the country, and a first-class prize taker in various branches of agriculture. He is a tenant of Sir Harvey Bruce Conservative M.P. for Coleraina:—" November 24, 1881. My political opinions are aril always have been staunch Conservative. The Land Bill of 1881 has beed accepted by all about here as a great boon both by Conservatives and Liberals alike. I myself accept it as such, but my view of it is this that it only makes legal what good landlords have always been doing for their tenants, while very justly it compels bad landlords to do the same. The tenant farmers about here are flocking into the Land Court. I have not thought of doing so as yet, as I have always been on such good terms with my landlord so far as to be able to have matters settled in a friendly way." _ - The Western Land Commissioners gave judgment on Saturday in a considerable number ef cases of tenants on the estate of Sir C. Knox Gore and Mrs. Slevin. In Sir C. Knox Gore's cases the judicial rents were fixed at a consi- derable rednction upon existing rents, but in the case of one of Mrs. Slevin's tenants the existing rent of £lO was sus- tained as the fair judicial rent, the landlady obtaining her costs, In the full Court at Dublin, on Saturday, a re- markable case from Waterford was heard. A tenant named May applied loran order extending the time for rcdemption with a view to sale, and it transpired that the rent of the bolding was £425, that the sum of £1,052 was due on the 29th of September last, and that the agent had offered to accept £250 in full settlement, and allow the tenant to remain in possession, but May refused, and during the evic- tion he did much damage. After the eviction he intimidated the labourers who had been employed to save the crops, com- pelled them to leave, and was returned for trial for threaten- ing the agent. The landlord now held possession in a state of siege. Mr. Justice O'Hagan remarked that it was a shocking thing to see a man with a holding of this kind going on in such a way, and if any relief was given it must be on condition that a year's rent was paid within three weeks. The tenant was ordered to pay £3 coats.

EX-PAR- LIAMENTARY SPEECHES. -- Sir Wilfred Lawson, M.P., and Mr. Ferguson, M.P., addressed a crowded meeting of their constituents at Carlisle. The meeting derived peculiar interest from Sir Wilfrid's intended withdrawal froni the representation of the city for the purpose of contesting West Cumberland at the next election, along with Mr. David Ainsworth, who was returned in 1880. The hon. Baronet, who was well received, delivered an address ire his characteristic vein, reviewing the history of his connection with the city, and the reforms passed whilst he had represented it. Mr. Goschen was present at a political meeting in connec- lion with the Liberal Association of Rugby, on Tuesday, and an address was presented to him as a distinguished Rugebian and statesman, and in acknowledging the compliment the right hon. gentleman touched at some length upon the land question. He believed that something must be done to free the land from the incumbrances of settlements, dowries, and other charges; that the tenant, without giving him absolute free sale, should be compensated for all his improvements; and personally he should be prepared to support the bill of Sir T. D. Acland on the question. In regard to Ireland he expressed fear that, unless energetic measures were taken, the action of Parliament o a social reforms would be hampered by Irish obstruction. He trusted there would be suffcient patriotism on the part of Conservatives and Liberals to repress it, and so promote conciliatory measures. Delivering his annual address to his constituents at Mor- riston, near Swansea, on Monday, Mr. Dillwyn, M.P., in reply to the comments made upon hie recent speech at Swansea, said that the reason why Irish questions had not been dealt with before FM that although there had been Liberal Governments in power before there had never in fact been such a Liberal Government as now controlled the country. The Governments in past times had been composed of Whigs and Liberals, but the present Parliament was the Parliament of the people. All other Governments that he had seen had been half-hearted. They had been Whigs. He was not a Whig. He was a Radical. (Cheers.) No former Govern- ment had been honest enough and earnest enough in its con- victions to pass such a measure as the Irish Land Bill. He declared his intention to do all he could to promote disestab- ' lishment, and defended free trade, saying that but for it things would be much worse than they are now.

LIGHT rig THE BIM:Mr.—In the kitchen the grand essential really is light. If light be abundant, if it pass into every part, there will almost certainly be cleanliness and purity in every part. If light be absent, if artificial light has to be employed to supplement sunlight, I care little what care be taken, the place will never be thoroughly clean.lbhiav, in fact,esee thisnthe paper btioans beenoft in hisfactquite re- cently, while, progress. have visited a house where the whole of the arrangements are on the most comprehensive scale, where money is con- sidered no object, where the most skilful assistance is sought and obtained, where work is always in progress, where the strictest order and system is carried out. The best that can be done is done, but the best is a poor effort compared with what might be dons; and all the difficulty lies in the bad lighting. There is no direct sunlight, for all is under- ground, and even when the gas is on in full blaze there is dark shadow somewhere. In such a place the nice refine- ments by which the art of cookery is made into a science as well as an art are out of the question. The best chef cannot see in gloom, and accidents are necessary evils, unavoidable and annoying. When there is accident there is delay, when there is delay there is loss of material, and when these two faults are enforced by a bad system there is constant vexa- tion and unnecessary trouble. More than this, the attend- ants are not comfortable. They wear on their faces a settled gloom, which is but a reflex of the place in which L they labour. These same objections apply to the dwelling- house, whether it be public or private, little or great. In a dark kitchen there must of necessity be five enemies to the ; householder--
There must be waste. There must be uncleanliness. There must be bad order. There must be bad cooking. There must be bad health.

I say no more OTtiti—s-iesi.--Vviie—re—the kitchen is well lighted there are, however, other requirements which have to be thought of carefully, although the requirement of light comes first.—. Dr. B. W. Eichardson, ia "Good Words."

How lenvy Mrs. Lyon Hunter's butler !" Miss Meagrim (likewise wallflower) : "Oh, yes! demolishing some time-honoured, oat-worn creed in every sentence! How they would appreciate women like you and me,,Cynthia!" Mr. Professor: "Mrs. Ponsonby de Tom- kyns ? I should think so! The dearest creature that ever lived! Such a thorough woman of the world, you know! Tells such capital stories, and gives such capital dinners !" M. le Professeur : "He, he! and 'ow yell she dress! And she dance like an angel! And vat a sharming figure and vat a pretty foot! Hein, mon ami?"—Punch. Manufacturers have rather a good story to tell just.noiv at the expense of one of her Majesty's insptetors. He went to a town; which shall be nameless, in order to inspect a mill. He was received by the millowner in his private office, a beautiful Turkey-carpeted room, and there was a goodly lunch spread out, which-the inspector, being young, and having a healthy appetite, did fall justice to. The meal finished, the host said to his guest, "Well, if you won't have any more wine, let us go into the cardroom' meaning, of course, the room where the carding is done. "You must excuse me," said the inspector, "but I never play cards before dinner." This is almost as good as the story told of a noble lord who, going over a cotton mill, and being shown some of the raw material—" wool," as it is called—looked at it knowingly and said, "Ah ! wool, I see. Well, now, Mr. —, is this the wool of Australian Or Eng- lish sheep r COLD FEET.—What a common complaint this is! and yet no one seems to know anything about it. You suffer from it for years, and yet you don't go to a doctor, or if you do you derive very little benefit from his advice. Some people suffer from it at night only, whilst others are troubled in the daytime as well. It occurs most frequently in women, but still you often hear men complain of it. We believe that the best remedy is hypophosphite of lime in one or two grain doses twice a day. This is soluble in water, and should be taken in the form of a mixture, nothing else being put with it, with the exception, if you like, of a tea- spoonful of syrup, to make it more palatable, although it is really by no means disagreeable .by itself. Another good remedy is aux vomica—five drops of the tincture in a little water three or four times a day. It is highly recommended, and you may hope for great things from it. Then you must do all you possibly can to improve the state of your general health. It is probable that you are below par some- how or other, although we must admit that it does not fol- low of necessity. If you feel generally out of sorts, and your appetite is poor, quinine will do you good. If you are pale and ansemie, you must put your faith in iron. Parrish's Chemical Food often does good. Cod-liver oil is an excellent remedy for improving the general nutrition; many people feel quite in a glow after each dose. DE QUINCEY'S INDIFFERENCE TO MONEY.—There are many absurd anecdotes of De Quincey's eccentricities, and more particularly of his almost incredible innocence in all pecuniary transactions; as, for instance, a story of Mr. Hill Burton's:—" One night, very late, tie Qaincey, arriving at a friend's door, and having obtained admission with diffi- culty, explained, with all the skill and pathos of his beauti- ful rhetoric that it was absolutely essential that he should be provided' at once with 7s. 6d. On perceiving surprise on his friend's face, he proceeded to explain that he had a document in his possession the transference of which to hie friend's care would probably obviate his hesitation; and then, after rummaging in his pockets, and fetching a mis- cellany of small articles out of them, he produced at last _a crumpled piece of paper which he tendered as security:_ _lt was a £5O note; and his friend's impression was that if he had kept the note in exchange for the 7s. Gd. he would, have heard no more of the transaction, and, indeed, that before coming to his door De Quincey bad been trying tonegotiate the exchange at several shops, and had failed only through abrychDr6Sch AtaUnr d re2lol, th Ringer, gnedr , May extreme scepticism on the part of the shopkeepers." Of course his uncertain, erratic movements led to many curl. : cue incidents, and his wonderful ways and strange doings were the cause of very curious sdventures for his mann- scripts, many of which must have only been preserved from destruction by the merest chance. We now come to a rather delicate subject, the second "F" "Fair Rents." A great political party has recently had much to say about "Fair Trade," but it would be more practical if they would tarn their attention -to "Fair Rents." It is well known that house, shop, and other pro- perty in and about all large towns and populous districts has depreciated in value during the last few years, and that rents have COnae dOWn, Is it poseilile to? Meet Oat Nor rents will keep up in the face of disastrous seasons and foreign competition? Certainly not, and if the English farmer must compete with foreign producers who have no rent whatever to pay, he must have a considerable and per- manent redaction made in his own rent. Temporary reduc- tions will not meet the case, and although many landlords have acted very generously to their tenants, it has usually taken the form of temporary abatement merely. If a farmer loses £5OO in one year, £lOO reduction off his year's rent is considerate as far as it goes, but does not meet the farmer's circumstances during a succession of bad seasons. The Irish farmer has been favoured by Parliament to the extent that he is now able to call in an independent an-' thority, the officials of the Land Court, to fix "a fair rent" for his holding. Mr. Justice O'Hagan, the Judge of the new Court, defines a fair rent as "a rent which may be fairly paid, and yet permit a tenant (not deficient in those qualities of industry and providence which are expected in any walk of life) to live and thrive." If that test were ap- I plied to English farms, the rents of very many of them would haye to be considerably reduced. Though some landlords go in for rack rents, or as much as they can possibly get, the bulk of them profess only to require "fair" rents. Who shall settle what are fait rents? Valuation by so- called "indifferent" valuers is often little more than a farce. A valuer in good practice, or trying to get a connec- tion, will naturally lean to the side of a large landowner, able to give him plenty of work and good pay, than to the 1 aide of a simple tenant. The proper authority to arbitrate between landlord and tenant, and to say what is a "fair" I rent, is a duly constituted Court such as they now have in Ireland. One thing is certain—no landlord ought to have the power to raise a tenant's rent on account of a tenant's own improvements. The Land Bill of the Farmers' Alliance provides that the rent of an incoming tenant (purchasing the interest of an outgoing tenant) shall be decided before the expiration of the outgoing tenant's lease or agreement, that the rent thus fixed shall not be altered for seven years, that the covenants-and conditions of tenancy shall not be more onerous than under the expiring contract. The amount of rent may be agreed upon by the landlord and tenant, or in case of disagreement, either may appeal to a Court (to be established under the proposed Act), and the Court will then decide. If at the end of the tenancy both are willing to renew the contract, but the landlord demands an increase of rent which the tenant is not willing to give, either party may apply to the Court to decide the differences between them, and the Court will not be empowered to sanction an incense of rent unless it is proved that the value of the holding has increased from other causes than the improvements made by the tenant. When notice has been given of the termination of a tenancy, if the landlord intends to demand an increase of rent, or the tenant a de- crease, tither party must give a year's notice to the other of such intention; then, if they cannot agree, the Court will decide whether the value of the holding has increased from ether causes than the improvements made or acquired by the tenant, or decreased from other causes than the acts or defaults of the tenant, and pronounce judgment accordingly. We want the principle laid down by Archdeacon Paley one hundred years ago carried into effect, viz., "To assign the whole prat of any improvement to the person by whose activity it is carried on." If a landlord effects valuable im- provements, he should receive interest for his outlay, of course; but if a tenant does the work, he ought to have the full benefit of it gratis, and in the event of his leaving his farm he ought to be paid either by the incoming tenant or the landlord, for the value he is leaving in the farm, and which he put there. This brings us to the third "F," "Freedom of Sale of Tenant's Right," on which we have a prospect of early legis- lation, for the Prime Minister when at Leeds told us :—" I say emphatically that it is an object of capital and immedi- ate importance for the farmer to see that effectual and not abortive measures are taken to secure the wholisinterest of the tenant—not a part of that interest, but the whole in- terest,—his interest in his improvements, and his intereat, as the law may define it, in his tenure." If, a tenant has conferred upon him the legal ownership of that which al- ready belongs to him in equity, he ought surely to have the right to sell it. The result of such a system in the North of Ireland has been to place Ulster far ahead of the other three provinces for good farming, prosperity, and tran- quility. It is all rubbish to repeat with wearying mo- notony, "Freedom of contract —" "leave such arrangements to the landlord arid tenant." As a recent writer has said, "Until the depression in farming set in, a tenant farmer was unable to obtain a farm except under conditions which he regarded as unfair. Just now he may be able to make his own terms in some parts of the country, but not in others, and scarcely anywhere for a desirable farm. Wherever there is bread and cheese to be got by „farming, the landlord must have the upper hand in snaking a con- tract." Mr. Clare Sewell Read, ex-M.P., a Conservative, (argued before the Game Laws Committee of 1872-3 that the law already interfered with freedom of contract between parent and child, master -and servant, solicitor and client, debtor and creditor, tire., tire., and in 1875, while the Censer- vetiver; were in power, Parliament decided, by the Agricul- tural Holdings Act, that tenants are entitled to compensa- tion in the event of the termination of their tenancy by the act of the landlord, but added the power for the landlords to render the Act void by simply giving notice to the tenants that they (the landlords) would not be bound by the Act. The result was, as the landlords like to have their tenants 'under their thumbs," nine-tenths of them gave the neces- sary notices, and their tenants are still where they were be- f oie the passing of the Act. Well might Sir W. Vernon Harcourt speak of it at the time as a piece of "sham legis- lation." Tha Home Secretary during last Session said he hoped before this Parliament ended those who represented the Liberal Party would undertake to deal with this ques- tion on more intelligible principles, and upon a mote %lid foundation. Even Mr. chaplin, the Tory Member for fdid- Lincoleshire, described his own Bill, intended to amend the Conservative Agricultural Holdings Act, as interfering with "Freedom of Contract," for it proposed to deprive the land- lorctof the power to deprive occupiers of the soil of compen- sation for improvements they had made. The Earl of Fife, who, as already mentioned, has granted his tenants Freedom of Cultivation, has also established a rule on his estate that compensation will be awarded for all true improvements executed at the tenant's cost, even should he have to be evicted for non-payment of rent, in other words, there is to be no signiorial power of punishing failure by "confiscation." No wonder that the Scottish Clamber of Agriculture should recommend the general adoption of the "regulations and conditions of farm tenancy of the Fife Estates," embracing, as they do, equally liberal voluntary concessions on the subjects of game and the law of distress. Lord Dalhousie, better known perhaps as Lord Ramsay, owns 138,021 acres, and is giving a new lease to his tenants. which anticipates some of , the leading proposals of the Farmer's Alliance. The tenant is to have the power of as- signing his lease, subject to the landlord's right of pre- emption (i.e' . the right of purchasing before anybody else), at a price to be fixed by arbitration in default of agreement. There are liberal provisions about game, and complete free- dom of cropping will be allowed, subject to the provision that two white crops may not be taken in succession, unless I after three years'pasture, and that turnips and fodder must Ibe consumed on the land. Compensation for improvements 1 is rather elaborately arranged for under seven heads, such as buildings, lime, drainage, Sic., the principle being that the original cost will be repaid subject to proportional deduc- tions for each year that has elapsed since they were effected. Claims for compensation will be determined by arbitration. A tenant will not be removable without three years' notice. Now can anyone suppose that Lord Dalhousie will per- sonally suffer because he has given such fair terms to his tenants, BO M to give them every encouragement and MM. 1 rity to make the most of their farms? Most certainly he ' will not; and the time is fast approaching when what he and Lord• Fife, sagacious, far seeing men, have granted voluntarily from a sense of juitice, will become the law .of the land. The Land Bill of the Farmer's Alliance is framed to se- cure to every occupier of a farm in England the value of his nnexhausted improvements. moot extended it in 1867. (Hear, hear.) But they had every reason to consider, unless some unforseen accident Should bring the present Parliament to a close, that before another general election they would have been entrusted with the power. (Applause.) That was a natural conse- quence of the step taken in 1867. They in Golborne were quite as competent to exercise the franchise as the people of Warrington or Wigan. But it was not sufficient that the parliamentary franchise should be extended to the county districts. They must have an entire redistribution of seats. In the boroughs, at the present time, there were 1,850,000 inhabited houses, which give an electorate of 1,200,000 electors, who returned some 300 members to Parliament. According to the late returns there were in the counties 2,500,000 inhabie&l houses, giving a county constituency of was eahthouatt ait.soppreesreonetotth something like 1,625,000 electors, and the present county membersby the bo boroughs hlsBwoa.,thosereturned re turned by the counties. This was especially important to me members m thanbers Gol borne. He was not one of those who believed that the agricultural trade of this country was ruined. Agriculture, owing to a succession of unprecedently bad harvests—eight out of tp having proved deplorable—and to the foreign competition, was ins deplorable state, and the farmers could reasonably ask two things. First, that, suffering as they were, they should be allowed to buy whatever they required in the cheapest market. That they were allowed to do at the present time, but if the proposal of the fair traders were listened to, they would not be allowed to do so. Secondly, they had a right to demand that they should be relieved Of all unjust and unreasonable restrictions. Mr. Caird, who was the greatest statistical authority on the land question, had shown.that, notwithstanding the enormous imports of wheat from America, amounting to more than double the home production, wheat had only decreased four per cent in value. All other farm produce lead risen, and Mr. Howard had stated that the land of this country could be made to produce double to what it does at the present time by a proper outlay of capital. But there was no security for in- vestments, and before capital could be induced to return to the land, the tenant must have security tor his unexhausted improvements. Most of Scotland was let on a system of 19 years' leases, and he therefore took that as a favourable example. For the first four or five years the farmer wouldl, Us manuring his land, year by year increasing its value. In five years it was in good condition, and the next ten years it would ha in full bearing—he had got the full amount of produce out of the farm. For the remainder of the term he I did his best to exhaust the value of the improvements he had put in the land, not knowing whether he may be allowed the farm again or not. Consequently.there were only 10 years during which the farmer got the fullest return for his capital. The land to be fully developed, must be free from the restrictions of entail and settlement. The landlord ought to provide the permanent improvements, and leave the ' tenant's capital free to develope to the full the working of his farm. After referring to the law of distress, Mr. Fv-gu- son said these were three steps we should have to take be- fore land could be placed in a profitable condition,—(hear, bear)—and concluded by saying that every man had a right to a legitimate share in the Government of his country. (Applause).

Mr. G. H. rOWELT, secretary of the south West Lanca- shire Liberal Association, seconded the motion. Ile was glad to see that such a movement as khe one they were supporting, had beenstarted in the Newton polling district, and that the workingmen of South West Lancashire were preparing to demand their great right. They suffered more in Lancashire than in any other county in England by being deprived of the assimilation of the county and borough franchise. In Lanca- shire there was the enormous population of 3,454,225 and only 340,091 persons on the registers, leav- ing over three millions of people who were un- franchised. Supposing they made an allowance for invalids, children, and women, and say one in ten were entitled to vote, then there ought at least 'to be 311,400 snore people on the register for Lancashire. The Tories were con- stantly saying the people in the counties were not suf- ficiently educated to exercise the franchise with safety. (Laughter.) He remembered during the last election, he had one very obstrepolous Tory to deal with. He was a candidate for a county constituency, and at 12 different places he made the admission that be would vote for the ex- tension of the county franchise saying "if every person in the county was as well educated as you are, I would vote for it to-morrow." (Laughter.) Turning to Sir Richard Cross, the speaker said the London Water 13i1,1 was a wonderful pro- duction. (Laughter.) He thought Sir Richard had not said much about it in Lancashire. It reminded him of a nursery ryhme that most of them would remember. With a little alteration it read:—
Sir Richard Cross went up the hill To get a for water, But Cross fell down And broke his crown And the Governneent tumbled after. _ . _

(Laughter and applause.) In the resolution he had seconded, they wished to remind the Government that there were mil- lions of loyal, honest, hard-working citizsris without votes in this country, who did as much in their respective spheres to pay tae S as those who were on the electorate, and they demanded that right as citizens of a great and free country. (Applause),

The resolution was carried with much enthusiast. Mr. CIIARLES HALL (political secretary of the Glborne Liberal Association) moved : "That this meeting tenders a most cordial vote of thanks to the gentlemen who have favoured us with their presence this evening and for their excellent speeches." They had cn the platform, he said, men who were known throughout the country for their com- , mercial dealings, and who had clone much for the cause they ' had at heart. (Applause.) He could not understand why any working man should be a Tory,—(hear, hear,)—and if the Tory friend who was present would attend any meeting in Golborne, be (Mr. Hall) and his colleagues of the Association would be heartily glad to k ear him. (A ppla use.) The association had made a good start and they intended to continue it— (applause)—and to add their mite at the next election to return two Liberal members for South-West Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) They intended to send two men who would represent and not misrepresent them in the legislature. (Hear, hear.) Looking back at the achievements of the Liberal party for the last 50 years, he maintained that the Liberal party would have such a history to be recorded that would compare favourably with the history of any intelli- gent nation. The Liberal party was essentially the party of reform, of high commercial dealings, the party which be- lieved that commerce would best bind nations together, and was worthy of their support, and the best thanks they could give the gentlemen was by working for the advance- ment of thccause. (Applause.) As the Radicalism of the last generation was the Toryism of to-day, so he believed the Radicalism of to-day would be the Toryiam of the next I generation. (Hear, hear.) Last week they had an imposing demonstration of Tories in Golborne—(laughter)—and at which some of the Liberal party were denied admission be- cause they could not behave themselves. (Laughter.) He was glad they had not had to refuse their Tory friends —(hear, hear)—many of whom he saw present, and he nas heartily glad to see them. He did not believe in tickets and mystery. (Applause.) Mr. HOWARD seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation.

Mr. John UNswonnt proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman. They would all agree with him that they en- joy ed an enormous advantage in having such gentlemen at the head of affairs as Messrs. Gladstone, Bright, and Harcourt, gentlemen who were so completely informed in commercial matters.
Mr. P. M. CAMPBELL cordially seconded the vote which was onthusiastically carried, and

The CitAnntrar, in acknowledging the vote, said it had been a pleasure to him to be present at such an enthusiastic and excellent meeting, and he would give them a compliment. They flattered themselves in Warrington that they had the best towns meetings in England, and he thought Golborne came next. (Loud laughter and applause.) Mr. Harry Entwistle, of Manchester, then sang the popular political song, "The Pilot of the State," dedicated to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. The song was given with much effect and the chorus was taken up with enthusiasm by the audience. A programme of other music was arranged, but it could not be gone through owing to the length of the meeting. The proceedings closed with the singing of the National Anthem.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN, The Diocesan Sermons were preached in St. John's Baptist Church, morning and evening •,.and the revival services were brought to a conclusion at the Wesleyan Chapel. An in'eresting reading was given at the Vulcan School on Saturday evening, and a sermon at the same place on Sunday by the Rev. Mr. Fielding, when collections were made.

LONDON MISSIONAIN SoctrrY.—Sermons were preached in Crow-lane Church in aid of the London Missionary Society, on Sunday morning, by the Rev. Mr. Slater. Can- gregational minister, from Madras, who is in charge of one of the high class native churches there, and whose most thoughtful discourse was listened to with the greatest in. terest, and an address in the school with evident pleasure. Rev. J. Ward, of St. Helens, preached in the evening, and although the day was very stormy the attendances were fairly good, as well as the collections.

LECTURE IN THE INSTITUTE. —On Monday evening a lecture was given by J. J. Pope, Esq , of London. Subject, "Number one—his very good health." The chair was taken by the Rev J. Allatt, who humourously introduced the lecturer, whose syllabus was as follows: Number-one—who and what he is, how he lives and grows, his wants, fresh air, good eating and drinking, fair amount of work, some time to play, a suitable wardrobe, an easy mind, how he is to get and use these things, all of which the lecturer filled in in a very interesting manner. Himself being a good sample of some twenty-four stone weight, and a laughable contrast to some whom were on the platform with him. A most usetul class of lecture well and ably delivered and illustrated by diagrams.

THE FATAL POACHING AFFRAY IN
CHESHIRE. THE HEAD KEEPER AND TWO COMPANIONS CHARGED WITH MURDER.

SPEECHES BY MR. McMINNIES, M.P., MR. JOHN . • CROSFIELD, J.P., AND COL. McCORQUODALE. On Saturday a soiree was given in the Congregational School-room, Golborne, in connection with the Golborne and District Liberal Association. On the arrival of the 4-17 p.m. train, from which Mr: G. H. Powell, secretary of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association, and Mr. Shepherd Little, M.A., and other gentlemen alighted, a brass band was found to be in attendance, and a large crowd of persons in holiday attire lines' both sides of the street. From here a procession of several hundred membeas of the Liberal Association was fermed, each one wearing a rosette, and, headed by the band, proceeded first to the Liberal Association rooms and thence to the school-room, where a substantial tea had been provided. The number of persons, however, who attended was so great that accommodation could not be found for them, and consequently two or three "sittings" took place. The room had been very tastefully decorated for the occasion with banners and mottoes, among the latter being the following, which were conspicuously placed ,in front of the gallery : "Honour to Gladstone." "Justice to Ireland" "Bright," " Hartington," " Harcourt," " Granville," " Cobden," and " Welcome." After tea a public meeting was held, when the room was filled to its utmost capacity, while the proceedings were characterised by the greatest enthusiasm. Shortly before seven o'clock loud cheers out- side proclaimed the arrival of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. far Warrington, Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., and Colonel McCorquodale. who were accorded quite an ovation on entering the room. Mr. Crosfield presided ; and upon the platform were Mr. J. G. McMinniee, M.P., Col. McCorquo- dale, Mr. G. H. Powell, Mr. T. Shepherd Little, M.A, Mr. J. Johnson Ferguson, M.A., Mr. C. F. Bosomworth, Mr. C. Hall, Mr. J. Unsworth, Mr. P. M. Campbell, and a host of other prominent Liberals. Mr. HALL, the political secretary, read the following letters of apology : November 26th. Green Bank. Liverpool, E.—Dear Sir,—l am eatt emely sorry to say that I cannot be at your soiree on be 26th. I should have been very glad of the opportunity of meeting my old irienis in South-West Lancashire. but I have an engagement which I could not get out of. With warm, good wishes for the prosperity of your association, I remain, yours faithfully, WM. RATHBoNE. Springwood, Allerton, Liverpool, 24th November, 1881.—I very much regret my inability to be present at your soiree to- morrow evening. I sincerely hope you may have a full and successful meeting; for I am confident that nothing is more calculated to advance liberal and sound opinion in South-West Lancashire than submitting questions of public interest to the consideration of the electors, through the medium of public meetings held in the various centres of the district. With best wishes, believe me, dear sir, truly yours, Charles Hall, Esq. Taos. BROCKLEDANK. 25th November, 1881.—Dear sir,—To:my grief and disap- pointment I have been telegraphed for to London to argue a case before Lord Coleridge, and I am obliged to go up to-night. I am afraid that Icannot get back in time for the meeting to- morrow. I would telegraph to Golborne if I had the address of our friends there. Will you kindly do so for me? Yours, W. li. KENNEDY. The Cameleer, who was received with applause, said: adies and gentlemen, 'when I was invited to take the chair here to-night I eid not hesitate for a moment to accept the invitation, because I felt it WAS my duty if I could be of any service in helping you, nof to hesitate to come amongst you. (Hear, hear.) I have been, ever since I can remem- ber thinking about politics, an earnest Liberal—(hear, hear) —and I hope I shall be one as long as I live. (Hear, hear.) I rejoice to find that in this comparatively small place of Golborne you have such a body of earliest Liberals as I se, around me to-night—(hear, hear) and I imagine that if there was the same earnestness and determination through- out the whole of South-West Lancashire our friends Cross and Blackburna would soon have to walk the plank. (Laughter and cheers.) I never could imagine what could tnduce any working man to belongato the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) I don't know what Tories have ever done to improve the condition of working men. Their whole history has been one of opposition to every good measure that had been introduced by the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) They opposed the repeal of the Corn Laws, they opposed you having a vete, they opposed the repeal of the newspaper duty—in fact, they have opposed everything that I know of that has been good, and they have tried to push upon us a good deal that is evil. You have to thank the Liberll party to-day for having cheap food. There is no man amongst you now but who can get his daily newspaper and he well Informed upon every subject that comes before the country. You have to thank the Liberal party far that— (hear, hear) and you have to thank the Liberal party that you have the means to educate your children, which Is a very important thing. All these great measures have been passed by the Liberal party; and there is no man, living or jdead, who has done so much for thr working men of this country as that grand, noble man, John Bright. (Cheers.) What did the last Tory Government de for us—that grand Government of such great and eminent men as Sir Richard , Aesheton Cross? (Laughter.) They can't point to a single 1 measure passed daring the six years that they were in office that has been of any benefit to the people of this country. They plunged us into a wicked, cruel, and unjustifiable war In Afghanistan, a war that cost two millions of money, which was utterly wasted, and thousands of valuable lives were destroyed. (" Shame.") And that was done to find out what Lord Beaconsfield called a scientific frontier. Well, when Mr. Gladstone's Government came into office they abandoned that foolish and wicked policy. (Hear, hear.) They withdrew tbe troops from Afghanistan ; and we are a great deal better off now than we were with the Tory party in office. (Hear, hear.) The only thing they got that I know of was the island of Cyprus—(laughter)—an island with about 140,000 inhabitants; but instead of it being of value to this country, it has cost us a lot of money —in fact, if you notice the Day speeches now-a-days they are very silent about Cyprus. (Laughter.) They snubbed Greece. Mr. Gladstone has given Greece what she desired, and he has done that without fighting for it. Then the Tory party plunged us lute another wicked war, as unjustifiable and wicked as the Afghan war—and that was the war in Zululand, Ido not know anything in my life, that I ever heard of, more wicked and more cruel than that war. And yet Sir Richard Assheton Cross had, I was going to say the impudence, to come here, with ether Tories of South-West Lancashire, to 07 to "gull" you people that the late Government were in favour of peace. He must take you for a lot of dumble heads—(laughter)—to he gammoned by such stuff. Oh, but there was one thing-the Tories did. ‘'es, I forgot, there was one thing Sir Richard Asshetou Cross did. You know Colonel Blackburne says that he is the finest Home Secretary we ever had. There never was such a man. As to Sir Vernon Harcourt he was a baby beside Sir Richard Assheton Cross. What did Sir R. A. Cross do? When be got into power the first thing he did was to extend the hours for drink. Public-houses did not open until 7 o'clock in the morning before, but Sir R. A. Crossaald public-houses were to open at 0 o'clock in the morning. ("Shame.") Now, a good many of you are working men, and a good many of you know the evil of that one hour in the morning when a man is going to his work. We know it in Warrington pretty well. There's many a man gets tempted into the public- house. The publican is down to his trade, and he says, "If you will have a cup of coffee I will put two pennyworth of rum in it." The man goes in and very frequently stops drinking there the whole of the day, whereas if public- houses did not open until seven o'clock the man would get to his work at six o'clock and avoid the temptation. Well, why did Sir Richard Assheton Cross do that? The reason of it was because the Tories got into power in 1874 by means of the beer barrel. (Cheers.) The two greatest curses to this country are war and drink,—(hear, h4ar)—and take my advice, my friends, never votelor a man who is in favour of war and drink. (Hear, hear.) You vote for the man who is in favour of peace and sobriety,—(cheers)—and for that Government which will do something to rid this country of the enormous quantity of drinking houses, which are doing so much mischief. (Cheers.) We have heard a great deal of talk about the bad trade of this country. -- The three men Hitchens, Perrin, and Willis, were brought up at the Sale Police Court, on Monday, charged with night poaching at High Legh on the 6th November, and also with firing at Thomas Ford with intent to murder him. Originally the prisoners were charged with the murder of a poacher named Jennings, but this charge, as far as the prisoners are concerned, has been withdrawn.—Mr_Hockin again appeared to prosecute; and Mr. W..Cobbett 'defended the prisoners. Mr. Hockin said Hilt the course he was about to take he was bound to take in the interest of justice and in the in- terest of the prisoners themselves. When the case was originally before the Bench he said that the great desire of the prosecution was to elicit the truth, and no one had assisted more in getting at that than Colonel Legh himself, who had all the men before him, and had begged and im- plored all of them to make a full and true statement to the 'magistrates, and asked them if they were withholding any- thing to come forward and repair the wrong. Some of the witnesses had come forward and impressed a wish to have an opportunity of coming before the magistrates to make what reparation they could and correct their evidence, and as those statements would be in justice to and to the advantage of the prisoners, he had come that day instead of waiting until Thursday, desiring, as he did, to have the evidence tendered at the earliest possible moment. Walter Meech, head keeper to Colonel Legh, stated that on the night of the affray at High Legh he had in his pos- session a revolver, which he received a few minutes before closing in of the poachers. A young gentleman named Banks handed it to him. Mr. Banks volunteered to go with them on that occasion. It was the revolver produced. When Mr. Banks handed it to him he said, "Take this if you should want it." After the keepers and watchers had closed he removed it from his (witness's) pocket. Before be did so be had heard three firearms discharged and saw the flashes. He could not say whether they came from the poachers or the keepers. Banks teld him that two chambers of this revolver were loaded. He pulled the trigger and fired it off in the air, not at any person. He fired it in the air for safety, being unaccustomed to revolvers, for fear it should do some damage. Two men were on the ground at the time, one was the deceased man Jennings, and the other was the pris- oner Hitchens. He afterwards returned the revolver to Banks' who put it in his pocket. Mr. Ricketts was a little to the front of witness and he did not see him fire at all. He spoke to Mr. Percival after he gave his (Percival's) revolver to the police. Re told him that he had heard that the bullet found in the deceased did not fit Mr. Rickett's revolver that had been taken from him, and said "if you hsot at all it would possibly be from your revolver." He said "the one I gave to the police is not the one I had that night." He said it was a size larger or a size smaller. Mr. Ricketts said to witness the morning after the occurrence, "I am afraid it will turn out that man is shot, as I saw Percival shooting towards him as he lay on the ground." He did not use any stones, nor did be see anyone else do so. Cross-examined: He believed the shots were fired by the poachers. When he fired, two poachers were on the ground, and two were struggling with the keepers. He took the revolver from Banks, simply for safety. He knew his party had firearms the same morning. He stated before the magis trates on the llth Nov. that he had no firearms, and so far as he knew none of the others had; that was net true, and when he made the statement he knew it was untrue. He was certain no one had a gun. Charles Wellesley Ricketts, a young man employed in 'Colonel Legh's office, after being duly cautioned, as was the case with the previous witness, said that on the morning o the 7th November he had a revolver with him. It was a number seven pinfire six-chambered one. The six chambers were all loaded. He took the revolver from his pocket at the corner of Foulke's cover, but as they ran down the field he again put it in his pocket. When he got to Owen's farm, be withdrew the charges. He did not fire the revolver that morning. The revolver produced was his property. The same morning he saw Mr. Percival with a revolver, he saw the flash and heard the report. He had since ascertained that it was Percival who had fired. There would be about three yards distance between the man on the ground and the man who fired. Witness had since spoken to Meach, and said that it would turn out that Jen- nings, the deceased, wakshot by young Percival. The man on tround was a poacher, but he could not sari which of them. Cross-examined.: Before the shots were fired he knew that Percival had a revolver. To his knowledge no one but him- self, Banks, and Percival had any firearms. He did not hear any shots other than those he had mentioned. The statements which he made before the magistrates, on the 11th, that he had no firearms, and that his revolver was at his room, at High Legh, were untrue, and he knew them to be untrue at the time he made them. He remembered Inspector Leighton calling on him and asking him for his revolver and all his ammunition. He gave him 4 cartridges, the others were in a box. He told him that four were all be had, and believed so at the time. He did not know that any stones were thrown by his party. He did not throw any. William Percival, son of a farmer, having been duly cautioned, said that he was out on the morning in question, and had a central fire breech-loading six-chambered revolver with him. All the six chambers were loaded with ball cartridge. He fired his revolver twice that morning; the first time when 20 or 30 yards bbhind the poachers. That time he fired straight into the ground. A man named Arthur Cook stood in front of him. Previous to firing he heard three or four revolver shots, as well as three distinct gun shots. He stood for tWo or three seconds and then made a rush at the men and passed one who was on the ground. He saw a min 10 or 12 yards farther with a gun, which he appeared to be raising to his shoulder ; 'he was pointing it towards the keepers. Witness shouted ont, " Drop the gun," aimed at the man's legs, and fired. Ile did not know whether he hit him or not; be was not more than ten yards off when he fired. He put his revolver in his pocket, and did not take It out again until he got home. He gave the one produced to the police, as it was the first he could lay his hands on. Ile had two, both of Which fired the same I ball. He had four loaded chambers when he got home. He showed his revolver to Banks and told Ricketts that he had it. Cross-examined: There was no one near the man, who had his gun raised to his shoulder. Two of their men who had sticks rushed at the man just as he shot at him. He thought his shot reached him before the men. He got up to the poachers before they were captured and before the struggle was over. On the 11th Nov., when ex- amined before the magistrates, he stated that he had no firearm and that he was not up with the others when the struggle took place. That was not true, and he knew it was not true at the time. He heard the gun shots before the revolver shots. There was not more than a second or two between the last gun shot and the first revolver shot. Inspector Leighton at this stage of the proceedings ap- plied to the Bench for warrants for the arrest of Meech, Ricketts, and Percival for perjury and the wilful murder of the poacher Jennings. The Bench granted the warrants, and the three men were at once taken into custody. William Banks, a clerk in Parr's Bank Warrington, stated that he was out with Meech and the other men. He had a a revolver which he gave to Meech, and he received it back from him. He loaded it before he left him. He saw Willis and Perth' fire point blank at the keepers, and then saw Ford, the injured rnan, stagger. He next saw a poacher fire, who he believed to be Jennings. He knew that Percival and Ricketts had revolvers. The prisoners upon this evidence were remanded. Mr. Hockin said that he bad been asked by the prisoners Meech, Rioketts, and Percival, to ask the Bench to accept bail. Substantial bail would be offered on behalf of Meech and Ricketts, and Percival's mother was a substantial farmer at High L,gh. Meech and Ricketts were liberated on bail (£500). The Bench declined to accept bail in the case of Percival, who along with the poachers was removed in custody.
