div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3,188 i.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3,188 i.
LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT GOLBORNE.

dm and North-Western increase of receipts is something perfectly unprecedented. As the trade ef the country in- creases in that manner so the happiness and the comfort of the people increases. (Hear, hear.) Ido not believe that the working people of this country were ever in a better condition than they are just now. There is full employ- ment, there are good wages, and there is cheap food. (Hear, hear.) You reaped these under a Liberal Government remember. Now, if the working people of this country will reflect upon these things • they will take very great care whenever another general election comes, that they will not have the Torieti back into power. [Hear. hear. A Voice : " Give us the franchise." (Applause.) Somebody was kind enough to send me a copy of the Liverpool Daily Courier, I think the name is. (Laughter.) It is a paper that I don't spend a penny on once in 12 months, because I don't generally find much in it that is worth reading. But I suppose some kind friend sent me this paper that I might be enlightened with the grand speeches of Sir R. A. Cross and Col. Blackburne. Well, I read Sir R. A. Cross's speech through, and I must say that I never read such twaddle in my lEe. (Laughter.) If that be the speech of the greatest Horne Secretary that ever lived—well I could not believe it. It struck me what he said about Ireland was so unfair and unjust to our present Government—in fact he hinted as much that this Govern- ment of ours, composed of honourable, 'honest, conscien- tious men, positively rejoiced at the atrocities committed in Ireland. I thought it was an aspersion that was beneath Sir R. A. Cross. He has no right to accuse men like Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Bright—(cheers)—of rejoicing in the cruelties and murders that were perpetrated in Ireland. And he would fain make out that the Liberal Government are responsible for these things. The Liberal party hate murder and hate cruelty as much as the Tories do—(cries of "More so") ;—and the things that are happening in Ireland are not the outceme of to-day, last year, or the year before. It is the accumulation of wrong which has been gathering up for the last 50 years—(hear, hear)—and the landlords in Ireland have nobody to thank for it but themselves, ' (Hear, hear.) They have exacted enormous rents from these poor tenants, as is preyed by the cases which are in the Land Court. You will see for yourselves that nearly every tenant Nvho has applied to that court has had his rent reduced 25 to 50 per cent., showing that the landlords have been screwing rent out of these poor tenants in a shameful manner, and it has exasperated them until they have got to that state that they commit murder. Mind you I don't say a word in favour of murder and mutilation. Nobody has a greater horror of it than I have. But Coercion Bills won't cure it. The thing to cure it is a just law justly administered. There will have to be law for England as well as Ireland. (Hear, hear.) There will have to be a law to deal with English landlords. As to the Tory party their game is always to put money into the landlords' pockets at the expense of the people. (Hear, hear.) But the Liberal party are not going to do that, and if I am not very much mistaken, if Mr. Gladstone's life is spared, Mr. Gladsmne will give us a bill for England and will deal justly between landlord and tenant. (Cheers.) I shall not occupy your time any further, because there are plenty of speakers to come after me, and my friend Mr. McMinnies and I have to drive a long way after we leave this room. I am very much obliged to you for the patient and kind way in which you have listened to me, and I hope that this is not the last time that I may have the pleasure of meeting a lot of earnest, thorough Liberals such as there are in Golborne. (Cheers.) Colonel MCCORQUODALE moved the following resolution, which he said smuld no doubt be received with cordiality and approval :—" That this meeting desires heartily to ex- press its confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and, re- cognising the great value of their recent legislation, pledges them its support in dealing with the great questions to be introduced next session." In order to understand the advan- tages spoken of they would have to contrast the conduct of the late Tory Government with that of the present Liberal Government: They could not forget the sensational articles that they saw from day to day, and the uncertainty that existed three or four years ago, in consequence of which they were in alarm and did not know what to do in business matters. The Sepoys were transferred from Calcutta in order, apparently, to try to frighten Russia ; and this was done when Parliament was not sitting, to preventthe country offering any opposition. (Shame.) Had Mr. McMinnies been there on that occasion and not been during the recess, he had no doubt he would have called them to account. (Hear, hear.) But they did not frighten Russia, and the cost to the country was half a million of money. The Go- vernment thought to throw dust in the eyes of the people ' and carry favour with the nation. The Chairman had re- ferred to Afghanistan, and he (the speaker) considered it one of the most unprovoked and unjust wars in which this coun- try could possibly be engaged. (Hear, hear.) We attacked an orderly people, and destroyed the lives, to an enormous extent, of men, women, and children of that country, to say nothing of the bloodshed of our excellent soldiers, who were intended for better purposes. (Applause.) It was thought that by taking possession of that country we should be able to keep back Russia, but Mr. Gladstone had clearly shown that it was far better to have an independent nation between British India and any enemy that might venture to come forward. (Hear, hear.) But the Liberals believed there was no intention of an enemy coming forward and disturb- ing the position thus—(hear, hear)—and in whatever they did were actuated by feelings of justice, honesty, and pro- priety. (Applause.) In South Africa we had the Zulu war and the attempt to annex the Transvaal, against the wishes of the delegates and the people of that country, as was clearly explained by air. Gladstone in his /slidlothian speeches.. Those speeches had been termed "wild" by sir R. Cross. He (the speaker) bad the advantage of Sir B. Cross, and heard all those speeches, and if be had not been a Liberal before that time, they would certainly have con- verted him. (Applause.) They had heard a great deal about the Berlin Treaty. Lord Salisbury, at the time that treaty was signed, had a secret treaty in his pocket, tactics to which England had not hitherto descended. (Hear, hear.) A portion of the Treaty of Berlin was very impor- tant, but the late Government were quite indifferent to its provisions, atd it was not until Mr. Gladstone s Govern- ment went into office that Greece was freed. Under the Conservative Government we were eagaged in wars, but under the present Government we enjoyed the peace and friendship of the whole world; and were on better terms with the United States of America than we had been, he sup- posed, curing the memory of man. (Applause.) Many of them would remember the:trouble with America, owing to the degradations of the Alabama, and the conduct of the Liberal Government in referring the matter to arbitration, placed us on the best of terms with America, though they were blamed by the Conservatives for paying the bill. Ile had seen the report of the speeches in the neighbourhood last week—(laughter)—and the specters blamed the Govern- ment for not avenging ourselves in the Transvaal for the injury done by the natives when they thought we were going to force the annexation upon them. But these speakers sat at borne at ease and wanted our army to go out and fight. They did not volunteer to go out and risk their own lives. (Applause.) If a man would do that ene would fancy he was thoroughly sincere, but when he simply called for revenge, then one doubted the accuracy of the views he Advocated. (Hear, hear.) He thought they would have no difficulty in supporting the motion when they contrasted the present position of affairs with the state of matters during the administration of the late Government. (Ap- plause.) When lie last addressed them the country was a little alarmed about Fair Trade. One fact spoke for itself. When Mr. Gladstone was a young man, living on the Mersey, American built ships were the sight of the day, and carried four-fifths of the freight of the country ' • but now they onlyionveyed one-fifth of the shipping trade, the re- mainder, or one-half that of the whole world's, being car- ried by our ships. Mr. Gladstone said this was caused by Free Trade, inasmuch as we bought everything in the cheapest market, which could not be done by the Americans until they changed their laws. He need not allude to Ire- land, hut the motto before him, "Justice to Ireland," re- minded him of what he had heard forty or fifty years ago; and during that time, the Chairman had said, justice had not been done to Ireland. He was sure they had all the greatest sorrow and sympathy for the people of Ireland, and it was the wish of the Liberals and all good people through- out the country to administer justice. (Applause.) He hoped the Land Act would work well. He was glad not only to see that reductions in rent were being made, but that good landlords were coming forward to their tenants and offering to meet thorn without going into court. When one looked at the power the leaders of the Irish people had in leading the people, one was inclined to think it would have a wonderful effect if applied to all that was good and useful for their brethren. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by saying that Conservatives legislated for particular classes,—the Liberals worked for all classes. (Applause.)
Mr. SHEPHERD LITTLE, of Liverpool, in seconding the motion, criticised the measures introduced by, Sir Richard Cross whilst Home Secretary, and quoted the lines—
" Oh, he's a jolly good fellow, Whatever the Radicals think, For he shortened the hours of labour, And lengthened the hours of drink."

(Laughter and applause.) But he had another merit. He gave us the Artisan Dwellings Act. They had exceptional good advantages in Liverpool for judging of the advantages , of that measure. Having a Tory Town Council, they deter- mined to carry out thc bill, and pulled down a great many houses in one of the most populous parts of the town at great expense. No one would then build the dwellings, and at present there was not a'single house upon the spot, but the land was given up to the amusement of cats, dogs, and the small boys of the neighbourhood. (Laughter.) He felt it unnecessary to ask any man or woman in that meeting to ' kindly consider the condition of Ireland, and to look with sympathy upon her wrongs, and to endeavour gently to deal with those Irishmen who might consider that the Government were going the wrong way to benefit their country. Speaking of the rebellion of 1798, Mr. Little slid they could never wrong the masses of the people without making it Alicult in after times to treat them rightly and to do well for them. (Hear, hear.) There was no one knew the extreme difficulty with which it was possible to get in- formation of any crime in Ireland. This was in consequence of a class of persons employed during the rebellion as in- formers, who, Lord Cornwallis afterwards stated, were totally untrustworthy upon oath, and, unfortunately, a number of people, whom he believed to be innocent of the rebellion, had been executed upon their testimony. ("Shame.") In Ireland the name "informer" was worse than that of murderer. The present Government introduced a measure to prevent eviction, but the House of Lords threw it out, and they could not do wrong to a people without being punished for it, and without it being made more difficult to do right in the future. (Hear, hear.) The Irish Land Act came, not from the Land League, but from the people of Ulster. Whilst in England the Conservatives were crying down the bill, a Conservative, Sir Sanatel Wilson, went to London

derry, and had to say that he adapted the principles of the Land Bill in their integrity, and that he was prepared to give something further. Could there be stronger testimony of the justice of that bill ? (Applause.) It was a great mistake to be continually sending over to govern Ireland men who had very little sympathy with its past, and very little knowledge of its present. Their knowledge was almost ' entirely confined to reports received from magistrates and police. They ought to try how an Irish Home Secretary would do in Dublin Castle, and an Irish Lord Lieutenant— (applause)—because the people of Ireland would treat with greater respect a man who was a native of their own coun- try than a man whom they knew nothing about whatever. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Referring to the need of a bank- ruptcy Bill, Mr. Little said suppose a man went into the Bankruptcy Court with £6,000 assets and £lO,OOO debts, one would think the debtor would be able to pay 103. in the pound. But the greater part of the £6,000 would be Ab- sorbed in the law expenses, and the creditors would some- times receive a Is. in the pound and sometimes 3s. 4d. (Laughter.) The question of the redictribution of seats would have to be considered, for it was perfectly ridiculous that a miserable little town in the south should have agreater power in the councils of the nation than places like Liver- pool and Manchester. (Applause.) After referring to the improved condition of lndia under Lord Hartington, Mr. Little resumed hie seat amid cheers.

Mr. J. G. McMINNIEs, M.P., who was cordially greeted, spoke as follows :—I have great pleasure in supporting the ' resolution, because I believe that the present Liberal Government deserves the support of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) There will no doubt be to-night a good deal of repetition in the speeches. For my own part, I never object to that. It is a good thing for those who have to listen, if it be a bad thing for those who have to speak. (Laughter.) You have heard a good deal to-night about ~the difficulties that this Government had to contend with in connection with the foreign policy of the country. You have heard about the unsettlea state of eastern affairs in Europe, about the annexation of the Transvaal, and about the Afghan war. I have no obj!ction at all to these things being said again and again, because I believe that you can- not understand the difficulties the present Government had to contend with, and the manner in which they have got out of those difficulties, without bearing in mind that great heri- tage of woe that was left them by their predecessors. I shall not, however, go into the matter of foreign policy, because you have heard a good deal about it, and I think it ex- tremely likely that you will hear a good deal more about it to-night. The domestic legislation of the present Govern- ment has not been of a very large amount, but it has been of very great importance. Last session but one we had the Hares and Rabbits Bill, and we had the abolition of the Malt Tax. During the last session we have had a bill carried by ! the ability and energy of Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—which, in its importance, entirely, I believe, orershadows every legislative measure of recent ,imes—l mean the Land Bill. (Cheers.) It is too soon to say what the success of that Land Bill may be. We believe, and we hope, that it will be successful in removing the great grievances that have existed in Ireland. (Hear, hear,) We think and we hope that the grievances that have af- flicted the tenantry in Ireland will be removed by this bill, and that there may be a season of quiet, and repose, and con- tent for that oppressed and misgoverned country. (Hear, hear.) We hope, and every man who does not wish to see the disaffection continued in Ireland ought to hope, that through the influence of that bill, and the influence of time, which may make perhaps even Irishmen forget the wrongs that have been mentioned to-night—we hope and believe that perhaps at no distant period any Irishman will be con- tent to stand side by side with any Englishman and any Scotchman, believing and knowing that he has equal power to govern and rule the United Kingdom. (Cheers.) Sir Richard Cross—(laughter)—l think in this very district said that the Government no longer possesses the confidence of the country—(A voice: It's a lie.)—and if the country had known as much as it does now the present Government would not have been put into power last April but one. Well, now, I don't believe that Sir Richard Cross and his colleagues are good judges as to the opinion of the country. They believed up to the last moment at the general election that the country was in their favour, and would continue them in power by as large a majority as they were placed in power by in 1874. They lived in a kind of fools' paradise up to the last moment—(applause)—and believed they were popular in the country. The fact is they got their informa- tion from London—about the very last place that you should take as a test of political opinion in the country. (Hear, hear.) They believed in the London press, in the London clubs, and in the London singing saloons—(laughter); and I believe that any man who takes his information in refe- rence to the ideas the country has of politics from London is almost Certain te be misled. (Hear, hear.) One thing, however, is quite certain—Sir Richard Cross has no confi- dence in the Government. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There is a very rude' ungallant, and libellous couplet that I I have sometimes heard quoted to this effect—

There's nothing right they say, there's nothing right they do." "We men have many faults, but women only two; (Loud laughter and cheers.) Now, lam sure the ladies present will excuse me to-night. This is what I have called a libellous couplet, and I only quote it because I entirely disbelieve in it, and because I think it represents exactly Sir Richard Cross's opinion about the present Government. (Cheers.) Ido not think there is much to be said against the tone of Sir Richard Assheton Cross's speeches. Sir Richard has been a Cabinet Minister. He will be a Cabinet Minister again probably. [A voice: I think not. (Laugh- tar.)] He speaks with a certain sense of personal responsi- bility, and you do not find him uttering those rash and foolish speeches that we sometimes hear from political midgets like Randolph Churchill. (Laughter.) Neverthe- less, I think Sir Richard Cross misrepresented Mr. Bright very lately in a speech that he made, I think, at Stockport, or it might be in this place. [A. voice: Stockport.] He said that Mr. Bright had called enquiring workingmen knaves and fools, and he said that Mr. Bright had insulted workingmen. He was alluding to the question of Fair Trade and Free Trade; and I think it not unlikely that Mr. Bright did say something of this kind, not about working- men, but about men who, for their own personal and politi- cal objects, were endeavouring to delude the workingmen in reference to this question of Free Trade. (Hear, hear.) The fact is that workingmen generally have never been deluded on this question of Fair Trade—(a voice: Never will.)- -the Reciprocity craze, as one of our writers has called it. But, however that may be, it is impossible for us to think that the man who has spent a long political life in the service of workingmen, and the man who a fortnight ago saw that wonderful exhibition of affection entertained by the workingmen of his own town—(hear, hear)—it is jai - possible that a man like this is capable of stigmatising workingmen as knaves and fools. (Hear, hear, and cries of "He never did.") Sir It. Cross claimed for the late Govern- ment great praise, inasmuch as they have reduced taxation upon land. He says that they have reduced the rates upon land by something like a million and a half, and have placed it upon the imperial exchequer. Well, if the late Government have reduced rates upon land by a million and a half, they have increased the rental of the landlords at the expense of taxpaying people. (Hear, hear.) Any and every relief of taxation upon land goes ultimately, and in the long run, into the pockets of the landowners—(hear, hear)—se that I do not think the tax-paying community have very much to thank the late Government for in reducing rates upon land. Now, before anything of this kind is done, I think that a good deal is to be said about the incidence of taxation upon land ; and I hope that a good deal more attention will be paid in our public meetings in reference to the land tax, and the incidence of that tax, and the juggle by which that land tax has been reduced. The tax upon land, as it was fixed in 1692, was supposed to be 4e. in the £—(hear, hear)—and an annual bill was passed in 1798, in reference to this land tax, that the tax of 4s. in the £ was to be levied upon the then valued land. But the fact is that the tax of 4s. in the g has been all along levied upon the rental of 1692. The land tax, where it has been redeemed, has been redeemed on that basis; and the fact is at the present time the land tax only reaches something over £1,000,000 a year, whereas, if it were levied according to the intention of the Legislature up to 1798, it would realise £/2,000,000 a year. Now, of course it is quite impossible that this thing can be changed, but it ought to be a reasen why the taxpayers of this country should resent and resist any attmipt of the landowners to take from the pockets of the people anythisig to redeem the present taxation upon land. (Hear, heir.) Sir Richard Cross says that we charged them with being the cause of all the bad trade that has afflicted this country during the last six years. Now, we did not charge them with being the cause of all the bad trade, but we did say that, by their wars and by their con- stant intermeddling with continental affairs, and with affairs in Africa and Asia, they did aggravate that bad trade. (Hear, hear.) In reference to the future: we do not know very much about the future legislation of the present Government. We have some reason to believe that we shall have the Bankruptcy Bill, which was interrupted by the press of business last year. We shall very likely have an act for the prevention of floods. We shall have an act for the remedying of corrupt practices at elections. (Hear, hear.) We shall, I hope, before very long—perhaps not immediately—have an England Land Bill—(hear, bear)— and we shall, no doubt, before three or four sessions have passed, have an extension of the county franchise. (Cheers.) I do not know, of course, what order these measures will be taken in at present, although I hope they will not make that mistake which Mr. Bright said they made and attempt to drive six omnibuses abreast through Temple Bar. They could not do that now, because Temple Bar is gone; but I have no doubt at all they will do whatever they can. I have no doubt, also, that what they do will be thorough; and I think we may have confidence in them, considering what we have seen them do already. (Cheers.) I believe I shall have to bring my remarks to a close, but I cannot do it without congratulating you upon the SUCCESS of your efforts in this district in connection with the Liberal cause. (Cheers.) I hope that those efforts will be continued. I hope that they will be successful ; and I hope that your efforts, and what you do, will stimulate other portions of the county, so that you may redeem South-West Lancasiiire from the disgrace of returning almost exclusively Tory members—(cheers)—and you may relieve me of being the only Liberal South Lancashire representative that you have at the present time. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was carried, with two dissentients. Mr. J. E. JOHNSON FFRGtSON, M.A., of Kenyon, moved, "That this meeting believes that the time has now arrived when the Government should extend the franchise in the counties, and give to a large class of most respectable and loyal Englishmen the right to which they are entitled, and prays the Government to give this subject their early con- sideration." He said be felt ho should be offering an insult to his Golborne friends were he to attempt to argue that that they were equally as fit to be entrusted with the fran- chise as any of those to whom the Conservative Govern-

div.head: AMONG THE PIANOS.
div.p: AMONG THE PIANOS.

How little we know, and often how little trouble we take b Inquire, about the great manufactories and industries of Eng land. aror instance, a piano stands in the corner of the room, beautiful to look at in its case of rosewood or Italian walnut, Polished and perfected, fitted with keys and strings and sound- ing-board, with all the new improvements and patents, a per feet check repeater action, a perfectly new system of tuning, a sostenente board for the conveyance of sound, an exquisitely in- genious method of changing the key without the musician's science; and still how seldom anyo se can tell where the wood came from that gives the instrument tone and finish and fielleacY how much was done by pure machinery, and how much by handicraft; what pressure was required to cli-cipline the soft felt into those curicesetoyslike little hammers or how it came about that some pianelpire soinfinitely superior to others, not only in tone and style, but in the ultimate advantage tf wear and tear. Many of us have passed a huge manu- factory to the Orafton-road, Kentish Town, where will be found the perpetual hum of business literally from morning till night. With the advance of years thebuilding has grown storey. by storey; it is stretcheig itself out to the adjacent streets, Strange sounds of melancholy music come from it, a hum of mingled machinery and music, yet we scarcely inquire what is going on within those busy wales. And yet it is a very hive of Industry, a wonderful sight, for here they make the music for the million ; here they turn a pine-tree into a piano, and here Mr. John Brlnsmead and his clever sons are demonstrating to thtworld that the best work is that turned out by the best workman; and that 'the way to excel in the great competition of pianos is to love the instrument and to supervise its manufacture in the smallest detail with scrupulous care. The uninitiated are not aware how much the piano is indebted to the example of that king of Instruments, the violin; how the delicate and sensitive manipu- lation of the sounding-board is an anged, altered, and improved Upon, in accordance with the principles of the undisputed model; and the thoughts of those who visit Messrs. Brins- mead's manufactory senile back to those old days of Cremona, when the manufacture of a mus'e at instrument was a matter of pride, and, in a certain sense, a labour of love. The essence of a first-rate piancforte manufactory Is the grand doctrine of setection. A piano as it stands before us, tried and perfected is the "survival of the fittest." Every plank, every joint, every board, every screw, every wire, and every hammer, has been the best of its kind, tried and not found wanting not a precess in the manefacture has been devoid of mathematical and geometric accuracy; and before a piano can to made, machinery and handicraft must join hands and fortunes. A poetical idea flits across the brain as we stand amongst the wo d stacks of the pianoforte manufactory. The trees of every country under I heaven have been ransacked to make up the contingent parts of a piano, and the best trees of their kind. But what is the tree that makes the music, and from whose branches cames that exquisitely sensitive sounding-board Why, the Swiss pine, that for years has been played upon by the wind in its moun- tain home, and that is cut down and sent careering down the mousitain torrent in the forests to bring music to our homes. Pan cut down the reeds to make his pipe; and the Swiss forest trees are musical to the end. We may remark in passing that the entire stock of timber, seasoning and awaiting the drying. room, and subsequent machines and steam-saws, is little short of a value of £20,000. The working world cannot live without music; every household at home or abroad must have its piano. It would take a far larger space than is at present at our dis- ;Niel to describe minutely the va,i ins departments and pro- cesses which ensue from the time that the piano is a mere log of wood to the moment when the symmetrical instrument, be It centennial oblique, upright iron grand, or boudoir grand, is deposited in the "chamber of horrors" or examining-rocm, to be diagnosed and examined .by experts before it can go out to the world with the name of " Brinsmead" upon it as, a tribate to its excellence and fine constitution. The visitor would have to go to the furnace where the iron frames are bronz.d till they shine and glisten like busnished gold; amongst the steam saw mills and whirling machinery, where each numbered and registeecd particle of a piano Is prepared for the finishing touch of the artist; to examine the deleate process of veneering, where shreds and stries of the warty excrescences of . trees found in Persia and Oircassia are artificially arranged Into those beautifnl harmonies of woadwork that we admire in pianos; to the store room, where are kept the ivory keys, the striugs, the felt, the Pegs, the appliances, and the tarried legs necessary for the busy manufacturers; to point out what varieties of key making and stringing are required for pianos seat to Iturmah, to India, to sea, and to all hot or damp climates, where ivory starts and wood yields to clinsate ; uetil. when the 350 sets of parts, of which most pi nos are oomposed, are satisfactorily adjusted, the instrument fashioned and modelled with so much care, is ready for the inquisition; and then, a-, this supreme moment. woe be to the department in which the slightest flaw or slip is detected. It is essential to the 'first principles of the Brinsmead manufactory that na piano goes forth to the world without a "clean bill of health," and being pronounced sound In wind and limb. At the last stage of the intecate manufacture countless tuners are at work, with sharp ears and educated taste, though the tuner's labour will be considerably modified by an ingenious In- vention recently patented by this ente-prisine firm, which will bring the tuning proee.s; within the range of all who are in the Colonies or at distant stations. So popular have become the Brinsmead pianos, owing to the faulmess care in their manufacture, the headwork and direction of the practical mem- bers of the firm, and the advantage of numerous secured patents, that orders press up-in the manufactory from all parts of the kingdom, and it is estimated that about 3.000 instru- ments a year are turned out of this mental...story. This 'a wonderful enough when we remember that foreign planes are notsubject in England to any duty whatever, whereas every English piano is handicapped when exported to a foreign mar- ket. But the principle of the Brinsthead firm is to give the hest piaao of its kind the best of materials, the best of care, the best of taste, and the best of finish; and this is why the manufsctory in Kentish Town sends down to Wigmore-street so many pianos perfect in scale, sustain:d in tone, static ia bulk, with Wel and responsive touch, and, in fact as near as possible to that ideal that all usual. °jos must require—" a thing of beauty" that is "a joy for lever. '.--plustrated London News, Oct. 22, 1881. '

iSCIENT/FIC. ASSOCIATION. Tho fortnightly meeting of this association was held on Tuesday evening, when Mr. iVilliam Gamble presided. Mr. WILCOX, chemist, Duke-street, read an essay on "Chemistry of mind." In his opening remarks he said that his subject might be new to them, but the thing itself had kept company with man ever since time began. At the same time it was not difficult to conceive that our minds were not in the same condition always as they now are. Changes were con- tinually going on in the chemical world, and it was so in the case of mind. Geology applied itself to the larger or greater change, and chemistry to the smallershinge but none of the less important of the elements. Matter was made up of ' elements such as hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, &c., and as irf matter compounds were formed, so anger, hatred, love, dis- gust, vanity, respect, courage, admiration, jealousy, revenge, temerity, contempt, dm, united to form compounds. His (the essayist's) compounds were the men and women who peopled this earth, and who, of course, possessed the various qualities he had mentioned. Men and women were born compounds, and immediately on entering this world their minds acted upon each other. The minds of the father and mother influenced that of the baby, and were people not continually insisting upon mankind adopting their particular tastes and habits? Were not some people crying out most unmistakeably that they would not endure this, and insisting upon the other? What was the difference between a wild and a tame animal? One had been influenced by the mind of man, and the other had not. A child had fond parents • who lavised upon it their affections, and led it to imagine that it had a right to gratify every wish ; and by failing to administer due punishment the child attributed such im- munity to its own importance. By and by it was sent to school, and subjected to a line of conduct very disastrous to that of the parents. Another influence had been brought to bear upon the mind of the child, and that influence tended to mould its character. Speaking of opposites in chemistry and their relation to each other, such as acid and alkali 1 compounds, producing a harmonious chemical combination, he asked if they could conceive of any mind more opposite to that of man than the mind of a woman. Yet how strongly man and woman were knitted together.tA couple might live happily together, but-their peace of mind might be destroyed by the introduction of a third person. There was also a heavenly attachment and holy communion mingling with and running by men throughout their whole life. Some men, the essayist said, were described as " boiling with rage," or "full of gratitude," which showed the different conditions of mind. Dr. TWYFOBD said he had been very pleased with what he had heard. They had had a good deal of chemistry but very little mind, and he must confess that he saw no con- nection whatever between "chemistry" and "mind." Dr. Gnossstax agreed with Dr. Twyford's remarks. He could not see in the comparisons given how it affected chemistry at all. He could not see from the parallel cases given what mind had to do with chemistry. When the essayist was attributing an unfortunate marriage to the power of another influence, he was certainly at a loss to know whether thal,influence arose from chemistry or mind. As to the expression "boiling with rage," chemistry as a science dealt with alterations that go on in matter. For in- stance, the heat and melting of sulphur was not a chemical action. If they took water and boiled it on the fire, it was not a reaction; it was a physical alteration that was going on. If they disposed of it by the aid of the electric spark, or split it up into its several parts, that would be a chemical reaction, but boiling was not. lie could not even agree with Dr. Twyford. He could not see any chemistry in it, and he could not see any mind in it. (Laughter.) Mr. 13noox proposed, and Colonel GAMBLE seconded, a vote of thanks to the lecturer; and this was carried. Mr. Wir-sow, in responding, said he wished to point out in his lecture how minds were built up by the action of one on the other.

div.p: SATURDAY EVENING CONCERTS AT ST. HELENS—There was a good programme gone through, on Saturday night, at Mr. Barton's concert in the Town Hall. The artistes were Miss Parry, Mr. George Barton, Mr. H. Broadley, Mr. T. A. Barrett, and Mr. Lester Barrett. Miss Parry sang very effectively the pieces suited to her voice, '' Home they brought her warrior dead," "Kathleen Mavourneen," and "In the gloaming,' which latter was sung in response to an enthusiastic encore which greeted the conclusion of "Kathleen MaiFourneen." Mr. Barton contributed " The bay of Biscay" in his customary manna, and also joined Miss Parry in the beautiful duet "The sailor sighs," which was rendered in admirable style. Mr. T. A. Barrett executed a couple of pianoforte solos, in which he displayed excep- tional ability; and his brother, Me. Lester Barrett, fully maintained the reputation he had gained at a previous con- cert, as a faithful exponent of Dutch character. He also gave in character "Professor O'Toole's science lectures " and " McLann is the man," both of which provoked much merriment, and secured loud encores. Mr. Broadley's singing of "The scout " was followed by an encore, and in response he sang The minstrel boy." The concert was brought to a close by Mr. George Barton and Mr. Broadley singing " Flow, gently Devil."
T. BUTTON, Auctioneer.
By ..dessrs. H. THORNTON 4. COMPANY.

liavroN Mums Lamovmssarr Socrarr.—On Mon- day evening, Mr. T. Miller read an eassay entitled—" The Miracles of Christ a Proof of His Divinity." Mr. J. li. Gamon, in the absence of the president, occupied the chair. Messts. A. E. Davies, S. Barrow, and J. Looker made short speeches at the close of the paper.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meeting was held in the Girls' schoolroom, Halton, in connection with the above society, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. R. Hughes rad a paper, entitled "Women's rights, politically," Mr. C. W. Brown occu- pied the chair, and there was a very good attendance. A lively discussion followed the paper, in which thelollowing gentlemen took part :—The Rev. 1. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Gamon, T. Wright, C. W. Brown, J. Hancock, G. Walton, B. Haddock, J. Lucre, R. Tandy, and S. Barrow. The vicar made the following proposition, which was seconded by Mr. Hughes, and carried :—" That in future the mutual im- provement class in connection with the Parish Church be thrown open for the attendance of ladies as well as others." SALVA.TION ARMY " FAREWELL MEETING" AT RUN. com.r.—The departure for America of Captain Inman and Lieutenant Wass (Happy Charlie), the two late leaders of the Salvation Army at Runcorn, was made the occasion of a large valedictory meeting on Tuesday night to commemorate the evolt. A large procession paraded the streets, and when the meeting commenced the Public Hall was densely packed. An address was delivered by Mr. George Marshall, who is becoming more closely connected with the Army. Happy Charlie, and Captain Inman also gave addresses, and alluded to the work ,done in Runcorn. They had laboured there with pleasure, and should never forget the happy times they had had, atthough thousands of miles might separate them Captain Inman remarked that be was very fond of Run- corn. The proceedings terminated about. 10 o'clock. The two officers leave England on the Bth to join the American division. _ .

Tun SOCIETY OF CHEMICAL Isnosrnv.—The first meet- ing of the Liverpool section of this society was held in the Royal Infirmary School of Medicine, on Wednesday, and was. largely attended. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. K. Muspratt, who in a short inaugural speech stated the aims of the society, and introduced Dr. Hurter, of Widnes, who delivered a highly-Interesting and intricate lecture on the dynamical theory of the manufacture of sulphuric acid, in which he demonstrated that it was possible to arrive by mathematical calculation at the exact conditions upon which this manufacture could be most satisfactorily and economically carried on. The results which he arrived at by his method exactly coincided arith those which have been proved to be the best by the practical and hard-won expe- rience of a century of workers. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought this highly-successful meeting to a close. TOWNSHIP 31P.ETING AT WIDNES.—A public meet- ing was held on Thursday in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, for the purpose of passing a resolution authorising the over- seers, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, to hire furnished premises, to be used as an office to transact their business' in. Mr. J. W. Carlile occupied thrg chair, and there were also present Messrs. J. W. R. Fowler, T. F. Allen, W. H. Kershaw, S. Owen, J. Taylor, and :L. S. Rigby.—The Chairman said the notice calling the meet- ing stated the resolution was to empower the overseers to "hire furnished premises," but it had been thought advis- able to rent a room or rooms, as was found necessary, and purchase their own furniture. The laiv, in such a case, only allowed the expenditure of £I2 annually for the rent of rooms.—Mr. Kershaw said it would be a good plan if the overseers were to have an interview with the medical officer and relieving officer' and see if some arrangement could not be come to about the different bodies each having offices in the same place. He moved that the overseers be empowered to rent a room for the pee of the overseers of the township. —Mr. Fowler seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—lt was farther proposed by Mr. Owen, and seconded by Mr. Kershaw, that the overseers should be em- powered to spend £lO in furnishing the rooms.—This con- cluded the business. TILE FARNWOETH AMATEUR MINSTRELS.—Tbis body of local performers gave their second concert for the season on Monday evening, in the boys' schoolroom, Farnworth. " I'se a gola ' was well rendered by A. Whitfield, and A. G. Davies made a decided hit in the comic song "Dinah Duck." The ballad " Ah ! he kissed me when be left me," was taste- fully and effectually sung by W. Brown. In the comic piece " Lucinda " F. C. Davies scored one of the successes of the evening, and certainly earned the hearty encore which was accorded to him. An almost equal measure of success rewarded J. Evans rendering of the ballad "Scatter blessings as you go." In "The comet of the west," T. Davies succeeded in amusing the audience, whose repeated laughter testified to their enjoyment. T. Whitfield's "Old toll sate" came in for its share of applause, and another comic song given with considerable spirit and vivacity, by T. Foreman, brought the first part of the programnae to a conclusion. In the second part, T. Davies and S. Smith gave a song and dance very successfully, and Arthur G. Davies added to the pleasure of the programme a "Stump speech," in which he very successfully caricatured some of the absurdities of platform oratory. Next Caine the perfor- mance of a farce, In which the characters were sustained by T. Foreman and the Brothers Davies with their customary success. A "plantation walk round by the whole cons- pony" brought the entertainment, which was well attended, to a telmination.
A.T WIDNES.—On ThIITS-

day evening, the dramatic performance on behalf of the Railwa y Benevolent Institution, which has been repeatedly referred to in our columns of late, came off at the Volunteer Hall, Widnes. The work of organising the entertainment, which must have proved a very navy task indeed, was. undertaken by Mr. E. Sansom, the station master to the London and North-Western Railway Co., at Widnes, a gen - tleman who, we understand, in his earlier days took great interest in theatrical matters, and at one time had the pleasure of playing several minor parts in Liverpool in com- pany with the great actor, Mr. Barry Sullivan. The room Was capitally filled, although the price of a ticket in the first seats was 55., and in the second 2se6d. The expenses in- cident to such extensive preparations as were made, must have been very considerable—indeed, we believe they amounted to no smaller a sum than £5O. The performance was under distinguished patronage, and amongst those pre- sent were—Colonel Newburn, Mr. Brunner, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Dr. Cooper and party, Mr. IV. H. Kershaw, Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. Booth, Mr. T. F. Allen (clerk to the Local Board), and Mr. A. E. Smith and party. I The production of the plays was carried out under the superintendence of Mr. W. S. Bransom, an actor of very lengthened experience, who, from his manner upon the stage, would not give any one the idea that so many winers had passed over his head. He was supported by Miss Alice I Finch, of Birmingham, and the other performers, with the exception of Mr. Sansorn, were amateurs. The music was by Mr. Pow ell's band; and the scenery and costumes, which were both very good, were provided by a Liverpool firm. The programme consisted of selections from Shakes- I peare's "As you like it " and "The Merchant of Venice," Sheridan's "'School for Scandal," and Mr. Leopold Lewis's adaptation of the French drama, "The Bells," by M. M. ErckmanneChatrian. The seleotion from "As you like it " was the forest scene, and the characters were as follow: Duke, Mr. R. Lewis; Jacques, Mr. IV. S. Bransom ; Amiens,- Mr. J. Morrison; Adam, Mr. H. B. Shores; Orlando, Mr. E. Sansom; First lord, Mr. J. S. Rigby; exiled lords, the Farnworth Glee Club. Mr. Lewis took his part very fairly; Jacques was admirably' played by Mr.Bransom ; and Mr.. Sansom's Orlando was very pleasing indeed. The piece passed oft very well, on the whole. The acting was certainly a little too formal, as could hardly but be expected under the circumstances; but this was atoned for in the next piece, the trial scene from "The Merchant of Venice." The caste i was—Antonio, Mr. R. Lewis; Gratiano, Mr. H. B. Shores; Bassanio, Mr. E. Sansom; Shylock, Mr. Brimpom ; Duke, ' Mr. Oakden ; Salarino, Mr. J. W. White; Salanto, Mr. J. S. Rigby; Clerk, Mr, J. Carver; Portia, Miss Finch; and Nerissa, Miss Oakden. Mr. Bransom gave a representation of Shylock according to that which was so popular before Mr. Irving's new rendering, which some people have the audacity to consider most unnatural. Mr. Bransom was deservedly well received, and the passages where Shylock compliments the advocate on a wisdom beyond his years, were loudly applauded. Mr. Shores possesses considerable merit as an amateur actor. Miss Finch, as Portia, was, on the whole, exceedingly good, though her reading of the lines "The quality of mercy is not strained," was rather poor, from an elocutionary point of view, there being too much self-consciousness imparted into the declamation of the pas- sage. She was exceedingly well received by the large audience. Mr. Sansom gave the part of Bassanio in capital style. This gentleman's acting is worthy of special praise ; but nature has • not gifted him with the full, resonant,tones which would, coupled with his dramatic power, have probably made him one of the kings I of the stage. His voice is husky, and his enunciation very I indistinct; but his power to utterly forget himself in the re- presentation of a character—the great secret of all good act- ing—and i for the time to imagine himself the man he is representing, s excellent. THE .EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1881.

Tan Wunizs Itaxmomtwns' Assommox.—On Wednes- day evening, the members of the Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Association met at the Simm's Cross Hotel, when they unanimously requested Mr. Samuel Owens to become their secretary, to which he consented. Mr. David Wright, of Warrington-road, was _elected presideat, and Mr. , Thos. Sadler vice-president of the association. The members turned up in tolerable strength, and discussed with much animation the proposed library question. ENLARGEMENT OF RUNCORN NATIONAL BOllOOLB. This work, to which we referred last week, is now being carried forward energetically. The plans have been prepared by Messrs. F. and G. Holme, and the builder is Mr. William Farrell. The style of the architecture will be broken Gothic, At present it is only intended to enlarge the old building which stands between the new school built some years ago, and which presents a good frontage to Church-street, and the infants' school. The present accommodation in the boys' school is for 220, and for the girls 170. The alterations, when completed, will increase the accommodation in the boys' department to 332, and in the girls' department to 224. A handsome entrance will lead from the street to the girls' schoolroom, which will be approached by a broad flight of stone steps. More than ordinary attention will be paid to the lighting and ventilation of the building. The total cost of the work will exceed £OOO.

SHOP ROBBERY AT HUTTON QIIARTAT.—OR Sunday evening the shop of Miss Woodward, crockery and earthen- ware dealer. Huyton Quarry, was entered while she was at church, and a sum of money amounting to nearly LIO taken away as well as other articles. ST. HELENS WEf3LETAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT Asso- cuertow.—Mr. Critcheson presided at the weekly meeting of this association on Wednesday night, when a paper by Mr. J. Lyon was read, entitled "A Cruise in the Annie," being a description of a sea voyage along the Irish Coast, to the Shetland and Orkney Islands; and back again to Liver- pool. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Lyon at the close.

ATTEMPTED &NOME IN S. HELENS.—A young man • named John Haselden, about 24 years of age, a barber in College-street, attempted to commit suicide. For a long time he has been in a poor state of health, and having the idea that his illness was incurable, this so preyed upon his mind that he became very much depressed. On Saturday he inflicted a wound upon his throat by pressing it with both hands, but the wound was a very insignificant one, the knife, in fact, only having cut the skin. In the shop at the time, with Haselden, was a man who prevented any further attempt, if one was contemplated, and the would-be-suicide was taken into custody. He was, however, released on ac- count of his weak state of health.

PERFORMANCE OF THE CANTATA " DANIF.L " AT Wucens.—The musical cantata " Daniel " was given on Wednesday eveni.ng at the Lacey-stseet School-room, Widnes. Mr. Lamb was the conductor, and Mr. Andrews the musical director. The following were the principal vocalists and the parts taken by them :—Miss Thomas (soprano), who took the part of the Queen; Miss E. Cooke (mezzo-soprano), the sister of Azariah; Mr. Walsh (tenor), Azariah ; Mr. D. Jones (baritone), Daniel; Mr. Betney (bass), the King. The opening scene of the cattata was laid in Babylon, end the life of Daniel was followed throughout its varied and exciting phases, including the story of the lions' den and. the fiery furnace. In the first part Messrs. Woodward and Jones and Mr. Betney distinguished them- selves by the taste and spirit with which they rendered their respective pieces. In the second part a special word of praise must be given to Mr. D. Jones' rendering of the piece, "Hear the voice of our cry," which was equally dis- tinguished by musical power and happiness of interpreta- tion. In the third part, "How lovely is Zion" was given in a praiseworthy manner by Miss Thomas, who possesses a soprano voice of great sweetness and considerable compass. The choruses throughout were given in a manner which leave e little scope for improvement, and speaks well for the training and musical talents of the performers. There was a good attendance, and the audience evidently appreciated the musical treat provided for their delectation. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. A lively and interesting debate was listened to on Tuesday, at the usual weekly meeting of this society, upon a bill brought In by the Home Secretary for the removal of Parliamentary Ifisabilities. The debate was opened by the President of the Board of Trade who supported the measure, as did also the member for Walsall and the Secretary for War. The mem- bers for Windsor, Gloucester, Birkenhead, and Warrington strongly opposed the bill. On the motion of the member for York, the debate was adjourned. The Leader of the Oppo- sition, at the commencement of the debate, wished to know whether the current report as to the resignation of several members of the Cabinet was correct. The Premier said it was quite correct that one member—a very important mem- ber—of the Cabinet had thought it necessary to retire, owing to the introduction of this Bill on the part of the Go- vernment, and that was the Solicitor-General; but Ale assured him it was simply through the difference of opinion which existed rather than disaffection from the Liberal party in general. The member for Birkenhead, who was absent at question time, asked (with the permission of the Speaker) if Her Majesty's Government bad opened negotia- tions for the restorition of Cetewayo as king of Zululand. The Colonial Secretary replied that no negotiations had been opened with the view of re-establishing the Zulu king upon the throne in Zululand. There might be some design concerning that individual, but as yet it was not sufficiently matured to enable him to say anything further upon the subject. The new registers for Lancashire show that there are 86,700 county voters in the four divisions of the county, being an increase of 2,200 over the numbers shown at the last registration.

TEMPERANCE- MEETING AT ECCLESTON HILL, ST. HELENS.—On Wednesdiy evening, Mr. William Sampson, Liverpool, addressed the first meeting in connection with the Eccleston Hill Mission Sunday School Band of Hope. The Rev. Mr. Green, of St. Helens, occupied the chair, and the rem was nicely filled. Mr. Simpson gave an earnest address on temperance, and referred to a statement made at the recent Liverpool Assizes by Mr. Justice Kay to the effect that 50 cases out of every 100 were directly traceable to strong drink. Mr. Wainwright proposed, and Mr. J. Jones seconded, a vote of thanks to the lecturer. The proposition was carried with acclamation ; and Mr. Simpson, respond- ing, said he had been pleased with his visit to Eccleston Hill, and he should be glad to come again. He remarked that he had be.en the guest of Mrs. Job Lyon. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close. Twenty-four persons accepted the temperance pledge.

Lon Buts IN PAELILMENT.—Wednesday being the last day on Which the plans of private bills intended for the consideration of Parliament during the next session could be depositad, no less than 310 were deposited, con- sisting of 127 railways, 35 tramways, 88 miscellaneous, and 60 provisional orders. Last year there were only 244, com- posed as follows :-87 railways, 17 tramways, 52 miscel- laneous, and 88 provisional orders. The session altogether will be one of the heaviest for private bills that we have had for many years. Plans, sections, and books of reference re- lating to the bills named below, wkich will be submitted to Parliament in the ensuing session have been depasited : St. Helens (Corporation) Water, Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company, Manchester Corporation, Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, Oldham Borough Tramways, Accrington Corporatian Tramways, Accrington Extension and Improve- ment, Accrington Branch Canal, Southport and Cheshire Line, West Lancashire Railway and Blackbarn Improve- ment.

Mn. PETER RYLiNDS' Ammer, ADDRESS. —The mem- ber for Burnley, Mr. P. Rylands, delivered his annual id- dress to his consLituents on Monday. He alluded at length to the question of obstruction in the House of Commons, and said there were two ways of putting a stop to it—one by limiting the rights of minorities, the other by silencing the offenders. He was in favour of the latter course, and would suggest that the punishment for obstruction, instead of being the mere farce it now is, should be suspension for the le- mainder of the session, or until the House shall otherwise determine. Referring to the overworked coLdition of the House of Commons, Mr. Rvlands suggested that the speeches delivered there should be "shortened," that grand committees should be constituted, that local authorities should be in- vested with more power, and that county boards should be established. In dialing with the present condition of Ireland the hon. member expressed the opinion that the outrages in which the offenders remain unknown are so numerous as to lead him to believe the Dublin Castle authorities and the Irish constabulary are not d,,ing their duty in endeavouring to secure the protection of life and property in that country. He had, however, so much faith in the Irish Land Act that he believed it would ultimately overcome all obstacles. A vote of confidence in Mr. Itylands was unanimously passed at the oonclusion of his addras.

KNUTSFORD COMMERCIAL SCHOOL.—Master James Sim- I cock, of 011erton, aged 15 years, educated at this school, has just passed his first examination for a surgeon. He is placed in the second division. At the age of 13, while at school, he was successful athis first pharmaceutical examination. COMMIES& MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCTETY. —The fifth meeting of the session was held on Monday night when an essay was read by Mr. John Blease entitled" Fruits of perseverance," upon which an animated discussion took place after which the essay was approved of by 22 to 4. Mr. place, presided. THE SHOCKING END OF A WARRINGTON WHITESMITH. —The inquest on the body of William Abrahams, who com- mitted suicide under circumstances detailed in our last issue wall held in the Parade Room, Police Station, on Saturday. last, by Mr. C. E. Driffield. The evidence was in accordance with the facts previously stated, and a verdict was returned to the effect that the deceased died from the effects of an overdose of laudanum taken voluntarily whilst suffering somewhat under temporary insanity, following a " spell of drinking." •

LEOTIMB AT NV/GROVE, ST. HELENS.—On Monday, a lecture was given in the Wesleyan Chapel, Nutgrovet by the Rev. W. G. Pascoe, on "Before marriage and after.' The Rev. R. R. Moore, of Ravenhead, presided, and in opening the meeting wished the friends success in the work they were trying to accomplish, viz, the erection of a new chapel. They deserved success as they had worked hard and earnestly. He felt an interest in the old chapel which was erected some 70 years since, and which was then considered a very imprztant building. The congregation had so grown, that it required enlarging 30 years ago, and now they were going to dear out entirely. He hoped God's blessing would rest upon them. (Applause.) The lecturer commenced by commenting upon marriage generally, and the feeling of individuals regarding marriage. Ho traced the characters of different individuals of both sexes in our every day life before marriage, describing the various tempers, accomplish- ments, inabilities to perform necessary matters pertaining to the comfort of both in marriage, and ability to do what was not necessary or essential to the comfort. His opinion was that love and marriage should be more lacked and discussed in home circles by parents with their families. In passing on and looking after marriage, the lecturer stated that the young wife was unable to improve self-culture, and could not keep up in the race of intellectual development with her husband. He stated woman's first charm was her de- , votion to God. He condemned the parents in chosing young I men who were immoral and depraved in their ideas and habits, for their young and virtuous daughters. He des- cribed the practices which he thought necessary for the young wife to carry out in order to make the home comfort- ! able, happy, and cheerful, and impressed upon the young I men to spend their time at home and increase their love as the years of marriage deepened instead of allowing it to decrease. He pointed out that home wah only a home where love existed, and that the prime element in a young man's , character was his godliness; and that love deep and true was ' essential to the success of marriage. The chapel wa3 well filled and the lecture was evidently thoroughly enjoyed, it being interspersed with humour and wit throughout. A collection was made in aid of the building fund for the new chapel after which Mr. Fogg proposed and Mr. Hitchin seconded a vote of thanks to the lecturer. Mr. Pascoe thanked those present for the manner in which they had listened to his lecture, and proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, remarking that be was glad to meet a Church of England clergyman presiding over them and hoping that prejudice and bigotry might soon be, totally vanished. This was seconded by Mr. Hopton and carried unanimously. Mr. Moore remarked that he was glad bigotry was dying out. He had been much interested in the lecture, and was sure all had profited. MISSIONARY MEETING AT Sr. HELENS.—On Sunday the annual sermons in aid of the London Missionary Society were preached in the Congregational Chapel, Ormskirk- street, in the morning by the Rev. Mr. Walker, of Huyton, and in the evening by the Rev. J. Peill, a missionary from Madagascar. The collections taken at the close of the services amounced altogether to £2O. On Wednesday even- ing the annual missionary meeting washeld in the Assembly Room of the school in Brook-street, presided over by Mr. W. W. Pilkington. He was supported on the platform by the Revs. J. Peill, T. C. Slater (missionary from India), R. J. Ward, and Mr. J. J. Dutton, secretary. The secretary stated that his efforts had not been so successfulin the past year as he had wished. Rainford had contributed £1 Ss. as com- pared with £5 the amount of collections made in the first year. From St. Helens they had a total of £lB5 12s. id., which included £24 10s. 9d. the Sunday collections o, the previous anniversary, and £8 4s. at the public meeting after- wards. The Sunday school collections amounted to £4l 4s. 3s; collected fer the Widows' Fond, £5 12s. In ad- I ditlon to that there had been subscribed :—Mr. W. W. Pilkington, two years subscription, £100; Mr. R. Pilkingtcn £s,Sathaniel Moxon £1; total £lB5 123., less expenses, £2 1.83 6d., which left a balance of £lB2 13s. 7d. There had been collected at Peaslev Cross Sunday Schools for the Rev. T. T. Mathews, of Madagascar, £4 151 4d. The whole of ' St. Helens district which includes Ashton-in-Makerfield, Golbourne, Huyton, Newton-le-Willows, Warrington and Widnes, had collected £461 15s. id. The Rev. Mr:rein delivered an address on mission work, and the rise and pro- gress of miesions in Madagascar especially during the last eight years: thd period of his connection with the work. He had a district about the size of Lancashire, with 80 churches which were under his own control. There was only one missionary to look after the wants of the natives tn that district, and that was himself. In that wide district there was not a single school for the education of children. He went on to speak of the persecution of missionaries, prior to the Queen's conversion, and the destruction of the national idols. When the Queen burned her idols the people followed her example, and barnt theirs also. Although this had been done there were vast numbers unconverted, and appeared to be without a God in the world. They had built churches, ar.d appointed the head men of the town as preachers, although they knew nothing of the Christian religion, having only a very obscure idea of what they were doing. In almost everything the Government interfered, but 90 far the churches had enjoyed an immunity from such interference. In Madagascar they bad 862 scoools, 43,904 scholars, 26,000 parents able to read, 25,600 children who had passed as able to read; altogether in that , mission they had 50,000 people who were able to read. They had 700 churches throughout the island, and 71,000 members. As an evidence of the zeal manifested by the natives in the , cause of the true religion, he mentioned that Eine° the burn- ing of the idols they had contributed £40,000 for the carry- ing on of missionary and educational work; and since that time there bad been 20,000 copies of the Scriptures sold at • one shilling each.—Mr. W. W. Pilkington in the course of his remarks impressed upon the audience the importance of I missionary work, and said that pocket money spent towards ' its furtherance was well applied.—The Re it R. J. Ward also addressed the meeting.”-A collection was made at the close.

• MR. PETER RYLANDE, M.P., Os PRIVATE CLUBS.— Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., on Wednesday received a deputa- tion from Burnley Licensed Victuallers Association, who asked him to obtain a return relating to private clubs in which intoxicating drink is consumed. The hon. member said he was glad that, so far as he knew, these clubs were ; confined to Burnley and a few other Lancashire towns, but he agreed with the deputation that if they flourished in a Ifew towns the danger would be that they would extend to other towns. He had already asked members of the Govern- -1 ment to get a return, but they thought they had no means of doing this. He would again bring the matter before the Government.

MILITARY RIOT AT FRESTON.—There was an exci leg dis- turbance between a number of soldiers of the 72nd and 101st Regiments, from Fulwood Barracks, Preston, and bodies of Preston constables, on Wednesday. The row started outside a beershop named the Fighting Cocks, Fylde-street. The ' inn was full of soldiers, and something having occurred with a policeman outside, they rushed upon him with the cry "Belts off." Other constables came and then there was a general melee. One policeman named Swarbrick had all , his front teeth smashed and his face badly injured. Police- constable Howard, a very big-built man, had his shouldier dislocated and his head and face wounded. The men were just assembling for parade at the station, and they ran down and arrested every soldier they could find. Over eventy I were taken to the station. There was much excitement.

NINTH LANCASHIRE RIFLE VOLUNTEER BALL.—The non-commissioned officers of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers held their annual ball on Monday evening. The Drill Hall had been nicely decorated for the occasion, and the ball was stated to have been one of the most enjoyable and successful the volunteers bad yet held. Amongst those present were Captain Bolton, Lieutenants Hogarth, Thomp- son, and Gooch, Sergeant-Major O'Brien, Sergeants Venn and Baines, and Sergeant-Bugltr Plinston. The latter effi- ciently performed the duties of M. 0., and Sergeant Venn , was the secretary. Dancing was continued until 3 o'clock to the strains of Mr. T. Boldsworth's quadrille band. Sergt. Tunks supplied the refreshments.

A strong gale sprang up suddenly on Saturday an d raged throughout the night. The barometer was ex- traordinary low on Sunday. On Sunday night in this neigh- bourhood the forte of the wind was very great. On the Lan- cashire coast the gale did considerable damage, and some exciting scenes were witnessed at Blackpool and Lythatn. From the south and east coasts several disasters to shipping are reported. At Plymonth the Asiatic steamer arrived with the Cape mails, but owing to the storm was unable to "call," and proceeded to Southampton. At the back of the Isle of Wight a large steamer in distress was seen to cast anchor, and shortly afterwards she disappeared. Signals of distress were seen on the Goodwins but the weather was so boisterous that the lifeboat could not go out to render assistance. At Margate the roof of the Corporation Gasworks was blown off, and crashed in upon three cottages. At 'lull a chimney stack was struck by lightning, and fell through the roof of a house, seriously injuring two young men who were in I bed.

EXECUTION OF TIM PRESTON MITRDEJIER.—The man Simpson, condemned to death for the murder of his sweet heart at Preston, was executed at Manchester, on Monday. No reporters were admitted to witness the execution. From the evidence given at the inquest it appears that the convict made no confession, though he did not deny his guilt, and had admitted the justice of his sentence. The coroner's jury unanimously made a presentment in favour of representa- tives of the Press being admitted to witness executions in future. Similar protests have been made before in Lan- cashire, but without effect. The law as it stands gives power to the High Sheriff to exclude reporters, in which 1 case the only persons present at executions are the gaol officials 1 In Lancashire for the past two or three years the death I penalty has been carried out in secret. The offer of an ex- High Sheriff to admit reporters to an execution in Liver- pool on condition that they only published an official ac- count of the scene was rejected, and on that occasion like- IVISA there was a strong protest against the total exclusion of outsiders. The law will probably remain unaltered, as the Home Office authorities have shown no inclination to in- terfere in the matter.

He did not know that they should be altogether dis- heartened. There was certainly room for very mach humility, and prayer, and belief, but he did net know that there was any room for despondency. The religious state of this country might be very bad indeed, but they remembered the time in past history when Christianity was I in a worse plight than it was now. It was indifference rather than open hostility to religion that had caused the neglect of public worship. He believed there was little Atheism after all in the land. There might be a little among well educated people, but there was very little amonget I workingmen. The only cause was indifference. They were never disposed to reject the truth. When sickness came they liked the minister to come, and in case of death they like to give their friends religious burial. There must be some great temptation in the way that men were so indif- ferent to these truths, and he would mention one or two causes. First of all he did not hesitate to believe intemper- ance was one of these. So long as there were so many public- houses and gin palaces scattered abroad cast over the land they need not be surprised that there were so many empty places of worship on Sundays. (Hear, kear). They were told that as men sowed so they would reap, and if they sowed public-houses he thought it need not astonish them very much if they reaped intemperance. (Hear, hear.) Besides this there was another cause of the irreligion, and that was that a good many people were moving about from place to place. The populations of our towns and cities were not by any means stationary, and people when they went into new places of worship were a long time before they connected themselves with the congregations. It was more from want of thought that they did not go to places of worship. There was no thought, and there was a want of definite church principles. They had heard a good deal that evening about going back to the purity of the past, and although there was truth in that, there might also be error as well. There was no doubt about this, that people had not the same firm con- victions about the church being an institution of God that they had in former years. It was all very well to be tolerant, and tolerance was a very good thing in itself, a virtue of Christian life; bat, at the same time, there was another kind of tolerance, which was only indifference, that was to say, a great many people were convinced that one denomination' or one system of church government, was as good as another. Although that might be very charitable, In the meantime it very often came to this, that no church government was as good as any; and many of our working- men were content to attend mission halls and evangelistic services, which were really good in themselves. but unless they brought people into their churches he did not think latter all such work could do very much good, that was to say, while evangelistic services had their proper places they only could show cake side of the Gospel. But he did not think any Christian would care to live all his lifetime listen- ing to those addresses. They must be brought into the churches. He expressed his pleasure at being present, and wished that the congregation might go on and prosper, and that it might become a great spiritual force in the town. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Pruutxsi gave Mr. Moore a welcome to that locality, and hoped he would be the means of great blessing.; and that the church under his ministration would grow and flourish most abundantly. He referred to the religious census, and said they could not overlook the alarming facts that had been placed before them by the chairman. It was surely the duty of every thoughtful believer to take these things to heart, and if they could but individually and unitedly' take them to heart he felt sure that much good would result. He, for one, most heartily, earnestly, and prayerfully would consider the facts that had been put before them, and if they. as pastors and churches, unitedly could consider and devise all means they possibly could to alter this state of things it was possible some good might yet be done. They wanted to get at the people and would have to be contfht to go into the highways and hedges to carry the truth. If they did that they would have their heart's desire and the religioi census when it was next taken would present a bet tlf aspect (Applause.) He hoped the church would have reason to bless the day that saw Mr. Moore ordained as their pastor. (Applause.) - Mr. S. H. Minna moved, and Mr. E. Mooan, senior' seconded, a vote of thanks to the ladies who had assisted at tea, which was carried. The Rev. E. Moortu, in proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, said although be did not believe in letting the sphere of politics overlap his proper duty, he believed it was a ministers duty to take an interest in the politics of his time, and one of the first questions he asked when he came tA Warrington was—what sort of a man is Mr. McM innies ? He rejoiced very greatly when that magnificent wave of Liberalism swept over tha country—(applause)—to see that amongst the great downfalls of " beerocracy," Warrington took a for emost place. (Applause.) But apart from any personal kindness which the chairman had shown to him and the church with which he was connected, he was proud of the man who could overturn the man who had so long represented this borough in the interest of drink as the late M.P. for Wallington. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WALLINGTON cordially seconded the vote of thanks. (Applause.) I The proposition was carried with enthusiasm.

1 ORDINATION OF A BAPTIST MINIS- TER AT WARRINGTON. , Ordination services were held on Monday afternoon, in Golborne-street Baptist Chapel, in connection with the settlement of the Rev. E. Moore as pastor. There was a moderate attendance. The Rev. E. Parker, President of the Baptist College, Manchester, asked the minister the usual questions respecting his call to the ministry, and the reasons which had led him to accept the pastorate of the church, to which Mr. Moore gave satisfactory replies. Mr. T. Hall, one of the deacons, explained, the circumstances which had led to the invitation given to Mr. Moore, after which the President asked Mr. Moore the usual questions with regard to his religions belief, in responding to which he explained at considerable length his religious faith, and the doctrines which he had resolved to teach. The Rev. E. Parker next delivered "the charge" to the newly-appointed minister in an eloquent and impressive manner, basing his remarks on Acts xx., 24, and recommending Mr. Moore to take Paul's life as an example. The Rev. Sidney W. Bowser, of Birken- head, offered the ordination prayer, which was very lengthy. The Rev. J.T. Marshall, M.A, classical tutor of Manchester College, then delivered a long address to the church, taking as his text Phillipians ii., 29. After the service, which lasted two hours and a half, a tea meeting was held in the school- room, which was attended by a very large number of per- sons The room had been very tastefully decorated for the occasion, a prominent feature being a number of black pro- file portraits of eminent gentlemen. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Parker Mrs. Moore Mrs. Hall, Mrs. Crowder, Mrs. Bamford, Mrs:Johnsen, Moore, Baxter, Mrs. Merrils, Mrs. Longshaw, and Mrs. Whitham. MR. McMINNIES M.Pe, ON RELIGIOUS OBSERVANCE. • In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel, and was well attended. Mr. J. G. McMinnies'M.P., presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. T. Marshall, MA., G. M. W. Carey MA., D. Jenkins (Liverpool), W. Pilling • (Hill Cliffe), P. Parker (Rochdale), H. Davies (Lymm), J. Warnock M.A.8.D., J. G. B. Maisson (Birkenhead), Mr. Her- bert Watts M.A. (Liverpool), clic. siThe CaArnetate, who was warmly applauded on rising, said :—Lidies and gentlemen,—There has been to-day, in ,connection with this church and congregation, a very inter- esting ceremony. I dare say I need not tell you that the Free Churches of this country do not attach supreme impor- tance to the ordination of their ministers. We esteem and respect ontoministers as men of culture, as men who, having i Studied religious subjects, have the ability to give us advice and instruction; and we reverence them for their work's sake. But we do not acknowledge that our ministers have any control over our faith. We regard them with great esteem as I have said, and we look to them in affliction for sorace and comfort. But if they were to pretend to have any contrcel over our individual convictions we should assert the right of private judgment, even in the face of our ministers—(hear, hear) ; and I think if they made any pre- tensions of that sort, we shoald pay no more regard to them than a clergyman of the Church of England pays to the opinion of his Bishop. (Laughter and applause.) Now, I have no doubt at all that our friend Mr. Moore is very much better for what has happened here to-day. He is a better eV a happier man for having met his friends in the ministry, for having heard what they-have said to him, and for having the opportunity of expressing his convictions before his brethren and before this church and congregation in reference to religious matters. The venerable minister who pronounced the ordi- nation prayer said on that occasion "we lay our hands upon the head of out young brother, but, oh Lord, thou knowest there is nothing in it."
