div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Press Association Aberdeen corre,pondent telegraphs : —An extraordinary discovery has just been Made at Dunech House near Aberdeen, the seat of toe Earl of Crawford MA Balcarres. Yesterday morning it was found that the body of the late Earl had been stolen from the private mortuary attached to the chapel. The Earl died in Italy a short time ago, and the body was brought home a short time since. An anonymous letter was sent stating that the body had been stolen, but no notice was taken of it. c At Blackburn yesterday, William Thompson cotton manu- facturer, Boundary. Mill, was summoned for a breach at the Factory Acts. Two women were found working in the mill at half-past seven o'clock on the night of the 15th nit; two hours past their time. The Inspector Characterised it as the worst case he had ever had. The full penalty of £3 and costs in each case was imposed. James Almond and Ca were fined £9 2s. for employing ten young persons during breakfast time.

The three men, Perrin, Willis, and Hitchen, poccernedist the fatal poaching affray at High Legh nn the night of the 6th„ tilt, were again brought before the county justices at Altrincham on Thursday. Ford, the injured keeper, who is an inmate of the Manchester Infirmary, was present and able to give evidence, though with difficulty, a portion of his lower jaw having been shot away. He identified Perrin as the man who fired at him, and who inflicted the injuries from which he was suffering. Other evidence was given confirmatory of that previously reported, and the prisoners were again remanded. The serious charges against Meech, the head gamekeeper, and the young men Percival and Ricketts were not opened, but the men were called before the Bench and informed that their case would be proceeded with next Thursday. Bail on behalf of Percival, as well as the other prisoners who are charged with murder and perjury, was applied for and granted, but was refused to the poachers.

FRODSRAM. FRODSHASI AND HELSBY DRAINAGE DOARD.—A meeting of the Finance and General Purposes Committee was held In the Board-room, on Friday, when there were present : Mr. James Reynolds, chairman; 31,ssrs. R. Bate, John Challoner, W. E. Davies, W. Booth, and Charles E. Linaker, clerk and surveyor.—The Clerk reported that the auditors, Messrs. F. Thorneley and T. Davies, had on the 7th ultimo, audited the accounts of the Board for the year ended 29th September, 1881, and bad found the same correct, the balance sheet and statement of account, as printed, being in their . opinion a true statement of the affairs of the Board.—it was resolved that the Chairman communicate with Captain Park Yates's agent with a view to co-operation in the proposed work of improving the Hoolpool Gutter, and constrUding new cloughs to prevent the influx of the tide.—The Clerk was instructed to write to several of the land owners re- questing them te call upon their tenants to clean out their side ditches, and enclose them copy o 2 a circular addressed by the Marquis of Cholmondeley to his tenants with reference to this matter. CHURCH TEMPERANCE MEETING. A meeting of the Frodsham Branch of the Church Temperance Society was held in the Girls' School, on Tuesday, when the Vicar pre. sided, and addresses were given by the Rev. G. T. Penrose, rector of Gawsworth, near MacclesflOd, and.. Mr. James Tom- kinson, J.P., of Wellington Hall. A collection was made at the close of the meeting in aid of the funds of the Society. FRODSHAM AND FIELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD.—The first annual statement of accounts for the rear ended 29th Sep- tember, 1881, has been issued. The amount of rate levied was £509 ss. 10J., of which awn .£l4 12s. 7d. remained un- collected. The interest from the hank was 13s. Cid., the • total actual receipts were. therefore. £495 Gs. 9d. The total amount expended far the maintenance of watercourses was £259 14s. Bd., including tbe cost of renewing and reco4- structing Platts, cost of obtaining provisional order and Act of Parliament, £130; books, etc., £lO 16s. 141.; salary of 'clerk, collector, and surveyor, and office rent, £52 108.; balance in hand,,£42 Sc. ; total, £495 es. 9d. LECTURE AT THE METHODIST .FREE CHURCIL—A lec- ture was delivered in the Methodist Free Church, on Thursday evening, by the Rey. R. Trotter, entitled "Little Folks and Big," when the chair was taken by Mr. Thomas Ft,gby, of Frodsharn Bridge, and there was a moderate at- tendance. The lecture was very interesting.

div.head: CHESHIRE FARMER'S SAD • HISTORY. '
div.p: A CHESHIRE FARMER'S SAD • HISTORY. '

On Thursday last, within ten miles from Warrington Can the comity of Cheshire), there transpired an occurrenee which, if true, brings the possibilities of oppression Sand hardship under the English land tenure within "measureable distance" of the tyranny of the now amended law of land- lord and tenant in Ireland. The tenant of a farm had held possession for 19 years, and for 17 years he had paid rent at the rate of,, £8 an acre with regularity and promptness. No improvidence or had management have been the cause of the difficulties which have now overtaken him. He does not drink nor smoke, and his neighbours are unanimous in speaking to his industry and carefulness, and that his wife is equally laborious. On :Monday she has worked with him ,in the fields, and at night gone out "charring." On Tues- day worked in the fields again, and at night made up her butter, &c., for market, and on 'Wednesday attended War, rington market with the same for sale, and so on through the week. Nor has she been guilty of extravagance. Since her marriage (16 years ago) she has only had one new dress and one new petticoat, the latter having been given to her. It as simply been a matter of getting just enough out of the land to pay thb landlord his exLortionate rent, and then to drag on a bard existence on the paltry balanc,. But when bad' seasons came there was nothing to livetn, and not enough for the rent. Two•years ago a !Auction of £2O win made in the rent, bet burdened with the conditions that £lO worth of manure should be pat on the farm, and must not sell any hay or straw, so that no benefit was gained fromthe reOuction. It is alleged that competent judges daclare there is not the slightest excuse for saying the land has been stacived,but on the contrary there is no land near "in better heart." For the last four years the tenant has been obliged to sell a cow each year towards paring the rent, and if the rent went a short time in arrear he was charged five per cent. interest on it. This year has come the crisis. £4O was paid towards the rent. More was still due, which would have been paid bad atime been given. Last week the tenant was offered £2B for a stack of hay, and he proposed to hand over the amount intact to the landlord. The landlord, however, refused to allow the amount to be touched, and without warning put in the bailiffs and adver- tised the produce for sale. The sale took place, and the stack, for which £2B had been offered, went for £l6. The sde was remarkable from the fact of handbills being dis- tributed and bills posted by an unknown hand, to the following offect

BOYCOTT Tlle LANDLORD I By refraining from purchasing the Induatrion Man and Wife's Produce and Cattle. Rent has been too high. Impossible to pay so much and makes living. GO HONV. WOE! to the First Bidchr. The man is now turned out into the lanes, okl and bent with rheumatism, and must seek employment as a labourer in order to support his hungry and scantily clad family, whilst it is stated that the landlord, who has wrung ES an acre out 1 of his tenant, pays for land occupied by himself £3 an acre.

WARRINGTON CATTLE AND !longs Fain.—The November cattle fair was held in Winwick Street on Tuesday. There was a large number of cattle offered for sue, and a good many buyers being present, the animals freely changed hands, at prices varying from £lB to £2O, for mulch cows, and £8 to £l2 for heifers. The horse fair held the following day (Wednesday), was the best fair that has been held of late years. Nearly all the animals which were of a superior class, were English, and were principally draught horses. Business was almost confined to this class, many anirrals found purchasers, from £5O to £6O being the prices realisett. WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.—The monthly meeting was held at tte Workhouse, yesterday. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Rylands, and the other members present were 'Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. Harrison, Derbyshire, Plackhurst, Cooper, Houghton, and Gibson, together with J. C. Sutton (clerk.) The Chairman said he could not let the business commence without some reference to the loss they had sustained by the death of one of their members—Mr. Winstanley. He had been a member of the committee, he thought, from its formation ; be had attended most regularly, and they all knew what amount of informa- tion and zeal he brought to the business of the Assessment Committee. Of course their loss would be small compared with the loss to Newton; but he ' for one could not resist expressing his regret that they would never see his face again. He moved a vote of condolence to the family. Col. McCorquodale seconded the motion, and endorsed what had been said by the chairman. Ile felt sure they would all miss Mr. Winstanley very much indeed. He was a most useful man, and had devoted a great deal of his time to public busi- ness. Mr. Darbysbire and Mr. Cooper supported the vote of condolence, which was unanimously agreed to. A CORRECTION. Sir,—ln regard to a football match played between Manor Ems School, Frodsham, and Collegiate School, Runcorn, published in your columus last week, allow me to make cer- tain corrections as to the result, which lam sure must have been inadvertently stated by our opponents. The result was Runcorn Collegiate School, two tries, one poster, and four or five minor points ; Manor House School, two tries, one touch in goal, and three or four minor points.-1 am, sir, yours respectf ally R. P. P. MANSFIELD, Captain. Frodsham, 28th Nov., 1881.

AN APPEAL. Sir,—To most of your readers who have resided for some years in this district the honest face of Johnnie Harrison, Commodore of Runcorn Fcrry, must have been familiar i• the good old man altar 45 years steady and faithful service as boatman is now permanently disabled by old age and Isfiranity, with no alternative but the workhouse unless kind friends come this aid. subscription list has been started, to which the London and North-Western Railway Company have given Ton Pounds. Other smaller sums are promised ; and I venture to hope that the inhabitants will respond liberally to the appeal now being made on behalf af an old and trusty public servant. Yours, itc., J.D. Widnes, November 30, 1881.

TEE *RELIGIOUS CENSUS OF WARRINGTON. 1881 AND 1851 COMPARED. Sir,—The statistics published in your paper a few weeks ago in reference to the numbers in attendance at the various places of worshipin Warrington on a given Sunday, have used quite a sensation in the minds of many earnest and thoughtful persons who take a deep interest in religious matters. Since the year 1851, when the last religions census was taken, the municipal borough of Warrington has just doubled its population, the numbers (roughly speaking) being in the year referred to 22,000, against about 45,000 in 1881. The numbers attending religions services have not, however, increased in anything like the same proportion, as after deducting 23 per cent, from the gross attendance at all services in 1851, the nctual number of persons present was 10,142, whereas in 1831, taking the same basis of calculation, we have only 11,108. The qbestion naturally suggests itself, how do the two religious sections, viz, Church and Dissent, stand in relation to each other as regards the figures previously quoted? The following table will best mower such a question :- 1851. 1881. Gain. Loss.

March of England. TotaLattendance ... 5,523 ... 3,971 ... 'Various Dissenting Churches, including Roman Catholics. Total attendance ... 4,619 ... 7,134 ... 2,515 ... This analysis shows a remarkable state of things. The Church of England, with double the number of places of worship she had in 1851, not only fails to show any increase but shows an absolute decrease of more than 1,500 persons, although she has had double the population to draw from. A similar—in some instances worse—state of retrogression has been. exhibited by the census recently taken in many ether of the populous manufacturing towns of the northern and midland counties. In 1851, the nett result of the census taken was to prove beyond all question that not only had the Church of England ceased to be the church of the nation, but that the majority of the inhabitants of our coun- try belonged to the various Dissenting communities, and to- day proof positive is given so far as the figures have been ascertained that the adherents of the establishment are in a very considerable minmity. The Church of England has long ceased to be anything other than the church of a sect, and as such her disestablishment and disendownfknt is desirable as a matter of equity. But another question remains to be answered and the interference suggested by it applies only in a lesser degree to Dissenters as well as Church people. Who is responsible for this unsatisfactory state of things? The Church of England certainly. She has not even held her own, but has by wilful neglect and criminal carelessness lost a great proportion of her former numbers. Dissent had decidedly progressed (considering the figures for 1851) to a large extent, hut by no means equally to what ought to have been the case, and it remains to be seen whether in the face of the Lets adduced the present religious indifference and apathy of the great majority ol our fellow townspeople will be allowed to continue withow efforts for improvement being made.—Yours, • Warrington, November 28th, 1881.
MAX.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. Ttrssnia.—Before Mr. E. Greenall and Mr. Matson. UNWHITEWASTIED FARMS—Charles Heaton, farmer, Grappenhall, was charged that being registered as a milk salesman he neglected to lime-wash his shippon in accor- dance with the regulations of the county.—Sergeant Booth visited the defendant's farm on the Bth November, and found the shippons in a dirty state, not having been lime-washed since February, when the defendant had his cattle affected with foot and month disease.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs.—For a similar offence Mr. William Bradford, farmer, was mulcted in the sum of ss. and 93. 61. costs.—A similar penalty was imposed upon Peter Woodward for a like offence. Ctsious CLAIM FOR Foorts' Rh:rm.—Mr. Benjamin Ben- nett, of Greenside Farm, Hatton, was summoned by Mr. William Tipping, assietant overseer for Walton Inferior, for a, poors' rate of £ll is. 2d., levied en the 4th November.— Mr. Tipping said he demanded the rate from the defendant on the Bth November.—Cross-examined by Mr. Burton, of Runcorn who appeared for the defendant, witness said he knew defendant had filed his petition in liquidation. He was present at the sale of his effects, when the trustee paid him the rate for the previous half-year. He Lad net demanded the present rate from the trustee, as Mr. Bennett was still on the farm.—Mr. Burton contended that defendant was not liable for the rate, as all the property was vested in the hands of the trustee, who had received the money from the sale of the crops and of the milk. The defendant was now simply the caretaker of the farm, and not the occupier.-LHe called the defendant in support of this statement, and the Bench ordered Mr. Tipping to obtain the rate from the trustee, Mr. Thomas Bennett. OTTENCE AGAINST THE HIGHWAY ACT.—James Smith was charged with erecting a steam threshing machine too near the highway at Grappenhall.—On the 24th November defendant was working a threshing machine on the high- way near Reddish Hall, Grappenhall.—He was fined 103. .and 98. CI costs.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

- ADVANCE IN COLLIERS' WAGES.—The colliery proprietors in the Somerset Coalfield have, in answer to an application from the colliers for an increase of wages, conceded an advance of 5 per cent., to begin next week. Last evening ao adjourned meeting of master,' and deleg- ates of the whole of the North Wales collieries was held in Wrexham. They considered the demand of the workmen for an advance in wages of 5 per cent. The masters stated that the price had not advanced since the date of the last meeting but that trade was duller, conseqaently they could not ac- cede to the request of the men •, but they would meet the delegates in three weeks, and if the prica of coal was raised in the meantime, they would advance the men's wages accordingly. The weekly pay commenced on Saturday last. THE STRIKE IN STAFFOUDSHIRE.—The great potters strike in Staffordshire has now entered upon the third week, and both masters and men are more determined than ever not to give in. Less than one third of the 30,000 men out belong to the Union, and only one or two branches have funds capable of supplying the men for "any length of time. The operatives' federation is paying a small sum weekly to those non-union men who give in their names for relief from the public subscriptions which come to hand. Those not in the Union are estimated at over 20,000, and their pay must be very small indeed.
ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. FIUDAT.—BefOre His Worship the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington and Mr. W. Blinkhorn.

---- - SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST THE POLICE.—A man named Burton, who said he came from Birmingham, and had travelled about this part of the country for 25 years with a knife g,,ieding machine, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. George Young, whilst in the execution of his duty, on Thursday afternoon, in Rainford- road.—The officer stated that he found the prisoner so druok as to be unable to take care of himself and machine, and he took him into custody for safety. The prisoner became so violent that witness was obliged to handcuff him. Prisoner Will resisted, and while they were Struggling together P.C. Pickup came up. Prisoner attempted to bite and kick both the officers.—P.C. Pickup said prisoner kicked him in the ribs and on one of his legs.—Prisoner said the officers threw him into a ditch of water, and illused him very badly; indeed he believed they had broken one of his ribs, and his wrist was very mach strained. They used him very badly indeed when they got him to a place where nobody could see them—Superintendent Johnston and P.C. Carter, who locked the prisoner up, said this was the first they had heard of the matter.—P.C. Young said they used no more violence than was necessary.—Prisoner said he had no right to get too much drink, he was quite aware of that, but at the same time it was not his right to be abused and illtreated.—Por being drank he was fined ss. and costs, or seven days ; and Ll and costs or one month for the assault upon the police. —Prisoner: Where's my barrow.—A Policeman : Never mind that.

TRAVELS IN THE EAST. BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SpEcteL.3 30EVLI. DA N . Quoting now from my note-book, Monday, 3rd April.— " I am now writing at the source of the Jordan at Dan. Since reeving Sadesh this morning soon after seven, we have come down, not the steepest, but the roughest and m mountain aide in all the journey. Two of the unhorsed by the ponies losing their feet most ed wiPe Pertri gently and rolling them off behind. Neither suffered the- slightest i,jury. After reaching the extensive plain on which, to the south, is the Lake Hula or Merorn, and into which all the Jordan unite and empty themselves, we had to make a circuit in order to avoid the marshes that surround it, in which great herds of buffaloes were wallowing. This took us nearly three hours to accomplish, and instead of coming on at one stage to Dan, and resting at noon amid its cool shady nooks, its rushing streams, and rich foliage laden with perfume, we lunched under the shaele of an old, bridge, under which one of Jordan's tributaries was flowing. A little above where I now sit at Dan, the water comes boiling out of the base of the hill—one of the spurs of Hermon— beneath a tree and forms at once a large and tepid stream, one of the main sources of the Jordan. C/ESAREA PHILIPPI. "Coming on to Banias (Cmsarea Phillippi), one hour's ride, we find another source of the Jordan, equally wonder- ful as respects the body of water that gushes from the base of another spur of Hermon. It is said that the water originally issued. from a grotto, now shown as the Grotto of Pan, and on being dammed up there formed a wide-spread vent through the large bed of gravel close by. Thence, indeed, it now issues, more like a stream running over the pebbles than one spring- ing from under them, and forms a deep and rapid river a few yards below. I now hear the dash of it as .1 sit in the tent, and as it rushes under the narrow bridge over which we pass from our tents to the town. It Here, then, we are at Cesarea Phillippi, having reached the bounds of the Holy Land, and being about to enter Syria. It was from this place that the Redeemer went forth on His last journey to Jerusalem. It was on one of Hermon's peaks, probably after receiving the confession of Peter, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God; that he was transfigured, and thenceforward set His Face steadfastly towards Calvary', His soul in the pains of travail for a world's redemption. Just as the Jordan takes its departure from this extreme end of Palestine, and rolls a flood of life and fertility from one end of this symbolic land to the other, so did that last flow of love and power take its rise here, and;rolling on through the dark and troubled scenes of Israel's social life, send forth its healing streams, not only over this favoured land, bat- opened to the whole world a fountain of living water which runs from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth." Cmearea Philippi, now called " Baneas," both names from its historical associations with Greece and Rome. It was anciently ca lled.Paneas. Black and yawningat the foot of the rock which overhangs the ruins of the city is an im- mense cave or grotto, dedicated to Pan, the Sylvan Ged of the Greek mythology. Josephus relates that Cresar Augustus, on his visit to Palestine, 13. C. 20, gave Herod the Great the province of Paneas. At a later peliod the city was in- cluded in the territory of Philip, who rebuilt it and gave it the name of Cmsarea, in honour of Tiberias Cazsar, adding " Philippi " to distinguish it from Cresarea on the coast. Porter remarks: "But the name Paneas had become too deeply rooted ha the language of the country to be changed at the will of a prince. It clings to the place still under the Arabic form Baneas, while the Greek name has been long forgotten." Josephus also relates that "After the destruc- tion of Jerusalem, Titins made Caesarea Philippi the scene of great rejojcings, and amused the people with gladiatorial displays in-Which the jewish captives were made to fight with each other and with wild beasts." The place retains many monuments of its ancient nower and grandeur. Ablve the grib of Pan, and along the face of the cliff, are several niches and slabs bearing Greek inscriptions. An old castle ' wall encloses the few wretched houses that now compose the village of Baneas. We walked round the walls in the evening, and among other things that deeply interested us were several huts raised on poles, 15 or 20 feet from the ground, and apparently wrought together with willow and palm leaves. I have wondered since, whether these were the sort of tabernacles Peter proposed to build for Jesus and his two distinguished servants Moses and Elias, on the Holy Mount! Such a position, heaven and earth, would be quite befitting the desire to elevate them above the earth, and yet enjoy their companionship. On the south of the town are the ruins of an old castle in fine preservation. Its walls are composed of materials taken from buildings of much greater antiquity. Massive stones, bevelled in the ancient Jewish style, and mixed with fragments of broken columns, have been utilised by the Roman and Saracen in raising these heavy bulwarks to resist assault and invasion We passed across the age-worn bridge that spans the moat, and beneath a gateway which had evidently been guarded by a portcullis. Three corner towers of the castle are still preserved. Beyond the citadel to the south the ancient city must have extended to It Con- siderable distance, as broken columns still mark the site. Rising out of the southern ridge of Hermon and directly to the east of Cxsarea Philippi, is a rugged peak a thousand feet high, crowned with the castle of Sabeibeh, one of our company scaled its sides-and stood within the ruins of the castle before breakfast. His long continued absence, while we were preparing re to start, filled us with many fears for his safety. At last he came in sight, just as we were about to mount. I think I see the culprit, with the fragments of bread and omelette on his knees, bearing like a martyr the wrathful looks of his of his relieved but reproachful companions. But, after all, what would not some of us have given for the amazing vitality and vigour our friend displayed? He seemed to know nothing about nerves or nervousness. No, sooner was his head down on his pillow than he was in, a sound and snoreless sleep—say a sleep as sound as a top—and then, with the first sign of life in the morning, he was np at his ablutions, and soon after was bounding away to re- connitre the.mountry so as to enliven the breakfast table with his discoveries. But the mountain—the exceedingly high mountain on which the Lord of life and glory was transfigured. Where was it? Not on that single peak of Hermon! No; for there stood this fortress of Phemcian origin, dating far back into the history of the world. But behind, and reaching far above the cliff that overhangs Ctesarea Philippi, the majestic Hermon rises until its snow- clad summit seems to touch the heavens. Far up over its verdant slopes and ridges must the Saviour have led the chosen three, until the silence, so profound on exceedingly high mountains, bad been reached. Then the face and robes of the Master began to glitter; two shining ones were seen to stand at His side, and in that silence, so profound, begin , to talk with Him "on the decease Hewes to accomplish at Jerusalem." Then, as they close the conversation, the voice of the Eterial Father comes forth from the out shin- ing glory and pr ef laims "This is my Son, the Beloved, in whom I delight, hear ye Him." Was all this done to elevate the thought and confirm the faith of the poor trem- bling disciples in the prospect of Calvary's dark and soul- crushing scenes, and in view of their bearing a life-long witness to His Divine Majesty? Such, indeed, was one object of this wonderful manifestation, as declared by Peter long afterwards, but surely it was not the only one! Who shall speak of the sustaining power of that sublime scene over the spirit of Him who was the subject of the manifesta- tions? We know that between the glistering garments on the Holy Mount, the face glowing with celestial light, and the torn raiment dripping with blood from His mangled brows, was but a few days; but we know not, and no human heart can ever know, the consoling sustaining power of the Father's words down to the very moment of the bitter cry, I "My God, my God, why Last Thou forsaken me?" What but the Father's boundless joy and love in the contempla- tion of His atoning work could have strengthened the Son and "'so pressing on before the disc,iples with His face steadfastly set towards Calvary ?" As connected with these last scenes in the Saviour's life, Cmsarea Philippi stands before my mind as only second in interest to Jerusalem itself. It was here, probably, beneath the shadow of this towering rock, and with water gushing from its base, that the Saviour sat while lie drew from His disciples, through Peter, the grand confession of the faith which it had been the labour of His ministerial life to plant in their souls—" Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God." And not less likely is it that when he descended from the Mount, and found His disciples had failed to cast the demon out of the poor lunatic boy, He pointed to this conspicuous mountain with its castle-crowned summit, when he said "It ye have faith as ii grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, 'Remove hence to yonder plum,' and it shall remove." (To be continued next week.)

ALLEGED ASSAULT BY A PtmucaN.—James Kenyon, landlord of the Black Horse beerhouse, was charged under a warrant with assaulting Mrs. Charlotte Marsh.—The prose- cutrix said she went into the prisoner's house on Tuesday night for a glass of beer, when he "caught her by the throat, struck her on the nose, and knocked War senseless 4— Prosecutrix had no witnesses to support her statement, and prisoner called three persons, who stated prisoner simply put the prosecutrix out of the house, and that she had her ' "nose busted" by a woman named Taylor.—The Bench discharged the prisoner.

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT ST. HELENS. On Wednesday evening the prizes won by hte members of the 21st L.R.V. were distributed in the Volunteer Hall by the Mayor of St. Helene (Major R. Pilkington). He was supported on the platform by Colonel Gamble, Major and Adjutant Wilcoa, Mr. A. Sinclair; the Misses Gamble, the Mayoress, Mr. and Mrs. W,Gamble, Miss Sinclair, and others.

Colonel Gamins said they were met together to distribute the prizes which had been won in the members shooting con- tests of the year of their own range. He had hoped that Colonel Pigott, the officer commanding the regiment of the district would have been present, and he regretted very much to receive a telegram from him saying that in consequence of the delay in trains he had been obliged to send that tele. gram that he could not come. He was very anxious that Colonel Pigott should come, because he wanted him to hear what they had to say as to their shooting. Colonel Pigott had taken a great deal of interest in the shooting of the district under his command. He was the representative of General Cameron, who had had a great deal to say as to the improvemeat of practical shooting of the volunteers. He was anxious that Colonel Pigott should hear what they had done hitherto, and what they proposed to do to meet his views as to • some change in the mode of training volunteer shooting in the future. He thought this was an occassion that was peculiarly appropriate for reviewing what they had done during the past year in the way of shooting. They had the Mayor of St. Helens to distribute the prizes. That of course was no new thing, but it was a very new thing to have a volunteer officer of twenty years standing in that positon. Thee" knew that it had never occurred before to have an officer in that position, who, in the year 1861, won the first prize away from home. He was very happy that they had such a representative of the regiment and St. Helens in one person that evening. He was quite sure they would join with him in congratulating Major Richard Pilkington on the position he holds as the chief magistrate, and also to congratulate themselves that they had a representative in that position. (Appian se.) It was now 21 years since they considered themselves a shoot- ing regiment. They were first sworn in in August, 1859. In that year they did no shooting for prizes, but the following year was considered their great year, for they then won prizes to the amount of £379. At this point Colonel Pigott' entered, and Colonel Gamble proceeded to state the prizes and honours won sines the formation of the corps in 1859:- National Rifle Association : Queen's Prize with gold medal, won in 1879. Men in the first sixty for Queerth Prize : One in 1861, 1862,1863, 1871, and 1879, two in 1880, and one in 1881. St. George's Badges: One in 1869, 1871, 1878, two in 1880, and two in 1881. Grand Aggregate Badges had also been won in 1879 and 1881. In the inter-regi- mental matches (average shooting of 2 per cent, of efficients), first in 1867, 7th in 1876, 3rd in 1877, second in 1878, and first in 1879. Lancashire Rifle Association : Grand Chal- lenge Cup, first in 1862,1863, 1867, 1868, 1870,1876, and 1878, and second in 1880. Battalion Challenge Cup (10 men), third in 1879, second in 1880, and first in 1881. Leigh Challenge Cup, first and second in 1862, first in 1864, and second in 1865. Bury Challenge Cup, first in 1880.' Volley Prig)/ first in 1861 and 1862, first and second in 1864, third and fourth in 1865, second and third in 1866, first and second in 1867, first in 1869, third in 1874, fifth in 1877, second in 1878, third in 1879, second in 1880, and fifth in 1881. County Badgesosecond in 1864, first in 1865, 1866, 1867, 1868, 1869, 1870, 1876, 1880, and third in 1878. National Rifle Association bronze medals, Vet in 1862, 1883, 1867, 1868, 1870, 1876, third in 1878, and first in 1880. Men the international match, one in 1865, 1886, 1867, 1869, 1870, 1871, and three in 1881. Matches with other corps, including regulars, one in 1861 and won by the regi- ment, two in 1883 one being won, two in 1864 and one won, succosses in 1873 and 1874, one out of two in 1877,five matches in 1879 winning each, two in 1880 winning both, and four in 1881, being victors in all of them. Money and value of cups won in contests from home :-In 1861, £7O; in 1862, money £l9O, cups £lB9-total, £379; in 1863 money £BO, cups £lO5-185; in 1864, money £270, cups £B4-354; in 1865, £167; in 1868,1148; in 1867, money £l6B, cups £lO5-4271; in 1868, money £9l; cups £lO5-196; in 1869, £100; in 1870, money £7l, cups £lO5-176; in 1871, £53; in 1872, £25; in 1873, £4O; in 1874, £6O; in 1875, £45; in 1876, money. £lOl, cups £lO5-X203; in 1877, £102; in 1878, money £l4B, cups £lO5-253; in 1879, £350; in 1880, money £250, cups, £3l-281; in 1881, money £242, cups, £lO5-347; making a grand total of nearly £4,000. Colonel Gamble then said he had gone through this record for the informa- tion of many who had not joined the corps in the early years of its formation, and had not taken part in the whole of the shooting of these twenty-one years, and also as a stimu- lus to those two who had not yet made any mark. He (Colonel Gamble) was not sure, but he bad not heard any- thing which had lel him to think that any regiment had a better record for shoot* than this (applause). Their secretary for nineteen years (Sergeant West) had been con- nected with most of the shooting movements of the country, and he believed there was no such record (loud cheers).- Sergeant West then read the report, which showed that the total amount of money prizes won away from home this year was £242 15s. against £250 last year 1880), but, in- cluding the challenge cups, dm., it stood this year at £347 15s. and four badges, against last year 0.880) £2BO, five badges, and an N.R.A. bronze medal. One very satisfactory fact was that they had more individual winners in number this year at the three large meetings than last, showing that the number of proficient shots who were able to hold their own against all corners bad increased.-The Mayor thou proceeded to distribute the prizes The Mayor then proceeded to distribute the prizes. DRILL Palm (value £25, given by commanding officer) awarded to the non-commissioned officers and men-exclud- ing members of the band-who have attended the greatest number of battalion parades of the corps, or brigade drills, from the-beginning of March to the end of August, and who have completed their class firing by the latter date, and attended the annual inspection, unless absent with leave. div.head: WARRINGTON POLIOE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLIOE COURT.
SATUSDAY.—Bef ore the Ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclongb,)

- and Alderman Burgess. ROBBERIES BY A GlRL.—Mary Jane Bunting, a girl, was charged with stealing from the Ladies' Industrial School, Smith-street, on Monday afternoon, a girl's brown ulster, value OW., the-property of Esther Molyneux ; on Wednesday, the 16th November, a girl's grey ulster, value ss, the pro- perty of Edward Webster; and on Thursday, the 18th November, a small shouldier shawl, value:3s., the property of S. Branwood.—The Chief Constable said the prosecutrix was Miss Jeffrey, mistress of the Ladies' Industrial School, which school the prisoner attended. On Monday last an ulster was missed, and on the previous Wednesday and Thursday an ulster and shoulder shawl were taken. On Thursday morning he received information and on making inquiry it was found that on Monday between four and five o'clock prisoner went to the shop of Mr. Morton, pawn- broker, Latchf rod, and offered an ulster for pledge giving the name of Elizabeth Jackson, Green-street, Sankey-green. The pawnbroker was net satisfied, and refused to take the articles in. On Friday morning Evan James, employed at the pawnbroker's shop, was taken to the school and he idetnlfied the prisoner as the girl who offered the ulster in pledge on Wednesday. He then took her into custody and charged her with the robberywhen she said " Yes, I did it." She also made a statement to the effect that she had pledged two ulsters and a woollen handkerchief for 2s. 6d. at Mrs. Woods's. These articles were pledged in the name of Elizabeth Jackson.—The mother said the prisoner was a very disobedient girl, and a similar character was given her by the school mistress.—The prisoner was committed to prison for one month, and then to a reformatory for five

years. 13Earrrn wine His Law.—James Renshaw was charged that he being the servant of one Thomas Bridge, did on the 24th November steal a quantity of salt, chalk, and rubbing stones, value 75. 10d., the property of Thomas Bridge.—The prisoner had been employed by the prosecutor since January and on Thursday morning prosecutor gave him orders to go to a wholesale dealer named Thomas Taylor for 7e. 10d. -ivorth of rubbing stones, Sic. Prisoner went for these goods. and then proceeded to Winwick and Leigh where he dis- posed of the property, and at night sent a lad who accom- panied him home with the pony and cart prisoner having spent the money in dr:nk.—The prisoner said Bridge "trusted him with the goods."—The magistrates' clerk: It is larceny by a bailee—a new offence since you studied the liw. (Laughter.)--Prisoner was committed for one month's hard labour. . MoNDAY.—Bef ore Councillor Fairclough andiPouncillor Crosfield. Tax "Orr aXD CARVED " MAN.—Joseph Battersby was charged witn assaulting his wife Jane.—The prisoner went home on Friday afternoon, and not being pleased with some- thing his wife had been doing, struck her on the head with his fist, and "knocked her twice over the table."—The prise- ' ner stated that his wife ran him to the door with the poker, and that his wife had "cut and carved him many a time, as they could see."—Prisoner was] bound over to keep the I peace for six months. CnnEtys TO HORSES.—Peter Atkinson, farmer, Comber- bach, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse whilst in an unfit state. Inspector Harper, R.3.P.C.A., said he saw defendant's horse in a cart on the 16th November, and it was totally unfit for work. Defendant was fined 5s and costs.—A similar charge was made against John Grant', a carter. On the 16th November defendant was in charge of a grey horse, in a greengrocer's cart, in Sankey-street. It was in a "skeleton condition," and although the day was very cold the exertion of drawing the empty cart caused it to perspire profusely. The horse, it was stated, had been now destroyed. A fine of lOs and costs was imposed.—William Smith was mulcted in the sum of 5s and costs for allowing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state.—The case against John Little, who had driven the horse was dis- missed. Inspector Harper said the horse was unfit to walk in the street. It was one of the worst cases of cankes he had seen. A BIRMINGHAM Borrow: SAVAGE ASSAULT ON TSB POLlCE.—Patrick Walden, a rough looking young fellow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horse- ' market-street, and also with assaulting P.C.'s Chantler and Hollingworth.—The prisoner was seen by P.C. Chantler to knock a man across Buttermarket-street on Saturday night To the officer's inquiry for his name and address, prisoner replied, "Find it out," but promised to go to the police station. For a few yards he walked quietly, and then he attempted to throw Chantler and Hollingworth by getting uoffinelceerrsthmeiorsltegrsioleUnittlyirtTelhyeyh! however, succeeded,g oand h kicked toc r per's-brow, when P.C. Monaghan came to their aid, but the p-isoner, who "though a little one," was very strong, threw the officers again. With his sharply pointed clog, prisoner kicked Chantler on the elbow, inflicting injuries which will disable him from performing his duty for some time.—P.C. Chantler said from some papers prisoner had in his pocket he appeared a person who took part in the great fights at Birmingham.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, said he came from Birmingham.—He was committed to gaol for four months with hard labour. AN UNGRATEFUL RETURN.—Robert Helsby, 3 joiner, who, it was stated, lived on drink, was charged with having, on the 21st November, stolen from Messrs. C. Cartwright and Co. a joiner's bass, containing two planes and other articles, valued at £2. It appeared that Major Cartwright, seeing the prisoner in the Workhouse over a month ago, felt sorry for him and gave him employment at his works. On account of his irregular conduct prisoner was, however, discharged a fortnight ago. He went on the night of the ilet November to Mr. Walter Cartwright's house, in Orford Avenue, and asked for the bass of tools, which were given him. He after- wards attempted to pawn them, arrd on Sunday gave himself up to the police.N-He was fined 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment. NEGLEII'L L PARENTS.—The school attendance officer, Mr. Riley, summoned the following persoas for not sending their children regularly to school, and a fine of 55. was in- flicted in each case :—Edward Hardman; Peter Sutton, .wire worker, 44, Hardy-street ; John Wright, wire worker, 4, Turner-street ; Wm. Litherland, 81, Win wick-street; John Carley, forgeman, 15, Kerfoot-street ; Mary Bagley, 22, Dolman's-lane ; Joseph Whitlow, butcher, Dial- street; Thomas O'Brien,'chemical labourer, Fairhu-st's-yd. ; Wm.* Gibson 116, -Pierpoint-street; Henry June, 387, Knutsford-ro;d. Tulsnay.—Before Captain Litton and Councillor Monks. ' ROBBING THE LADIES' CHARITY ASSOCIATION.—AmeIia Pessell, a married woman, was charged with stealing from the dwelling house of Frances Scarisbrick, 40, Rolleston-st., on Saturday, two sheets, the property of the Ladies' Charity Association.—The prisoner had lodged for a few weeks.with Mrs. Scarisbrick,mt whose house the materials of the Ladies' Charity Association are kept. On Saturday night about ten o'clock, she presented herself at Mr. Morton's pawnshoji in Latchford, and offered the sheets for pledge. Mr. Kerr, the manager, found the sheets bore the name of the Ladies' Charity Association, and questioned the piisoner who left the shop to fetch the woman who she stated had sent her. As, however, she did not return, on Monday information was given to the police who visited Mrs. Scarisbrick's house, and that lady found two sheets had been stolen. The prisoner was then apprehended.—She was committed for two myths imprisonment. A NEGLIGENT FATHER. —William Preston, who was brought up on warrent, was fined ss. and costs for neglect- ing to educate his child Margaret. The girl, although 12 years of age, has not as yet passed an examination. WEDNESDAY.—BJore Alderman Davies and Mr. Ziba
_ ArMange.

--- THEFT FROM A LODGING HODSE. -- John Bottoroley, a silk dresser, from Lancaster, was charged with stealing a pair of cord trousers value 10s., from the lodging house of Thomas Hines, 8, Hill-street.—The prisoner had lodged at prosecutor's house since Friday, and on Tuesday Mrs. Hines went out of the house at noon, leaving the stolen trousers on a rail. Prisoner was then in the house. bht on Mrs. Hines' return, be bad departed, and the trousers could not be found. At night the prisoner was captured, and P.C. Jones discovered the prisoner was wearing the trousers under his own. When charged with the theft he said " It is a -- lie."—Prisoner said his wife told him Mrs. Hines had given her the trousers, and he thought it best to put them under his old ones.—Mr. White (magistrates' clerk): Do you generally find lodging house keepers give away good pairs of trousers? (Laughter.)—Prisoner: I don't know. lam strange to this part of the country.—He was com.nitted to gaol for a month. WHOLESALE SHOP ROBBERIES. Joseph Corcoran, and ' Thomas McHugh, both of whom the Chief Constable said never worked, were charged with stealing from the shop of Mr. Thomas Dale, draper, Bridge-street, three grey woollen shirts, of the value of 7s. 6d.—A. young woman named Maria Frances Marsh, whilst passing from Friars' Green to Rose and Crown-street on the previous afternoon, saw Corcoran take from a hook at the prosecutor's shop door, three woollen shirts, which he placed under his coat. He then joined McHugh who was standing on the other side of the street, and they went into Leyland's Court together. The shirts had not been recovered, and the Chief Constable asked for a remand which was granted. Five robberies of a similar character were committed during the same day. TaultsnAv.—Before Captain Litton (chairman), Alderman Webster, and Councillor Milner. A BATdH OF SCSPICIODS CHABACTERS.—MichaeI Burns was charged with being in possession of a watch and chain supposed to be stolen. From the Chief Constable's state- ment it appeared that the prisoner offered the watch and chain in pledge at Mr. Greaves', pawnbroker, Church-street. Mr. Calvert, the manager, discovered that the watch exactly corresponded to a description of a watch stolen from Liver- pool in March. Prisoner stated he had purchased it in Liverpool for £3 105, but when taken into custody by P.C. Jones he stated he had purchased it for 18s. 6d. p.m a person at Whitley, in Cheshire. Mr. Hunt telegraphed to the Liverpool police, and the owner of the stolen watch came to examine the watch, but though the number was the same and of the same description it was much smaller. Mr. Hunt said he should retain the watch and chain. Prisoner was liberated, and bound over to appear when called upon.— Margaret Lathom and Mary Ann, Steadman, respectably. dressed women, were charged with being found frequenting the Market Place with intent to commit a felony. Prisoners were observed by Mr. Place, the market inspector, to be pushing amongst women in the market on Wednesday, sometimes together and at other times separately, and acting altogether in a suspicious manner. Receiving information of several robberies troll) satchels, he gave the prisoners into custo lv. They stated their husbands were horse dealers, but refused to give any account of themselves other than that they came from Liverpool at three o'clock. They were seen by Mr. Place shortly after twelve. Latham stated she had about 50s. in her pocket on arriving at Warrington, and had spent about 10s. in presents for the children. When told

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. J. Fidler, W. Tyrer, J. Matthews, T. Bohol', J. Leatherbarrow, J. T. Hall, Jos. Jackson. Jas. Buckley, John Lowe, James Fisher, E. Syder, W. Birchall, T. Saddler, W. Gerrard, W. Swift, G. J. Paris, J. Kenwright, and W. A. Meadows; with Mr. Hartley, clerk..

THE BAPTISING OF CHILDREN IN THE WORKHOUSE. The Clerk read the following entry from the report book of the chaplain (the Rey. B. A. W. Norrie):—" Thursday, Nov. 24th. I have this day handed to the workhouse governor the numbers of all Protestant children baptised privately in this house between September 29th, 1878, and September 29th, 1881, to enable him to make a return as moved by a member, from which it will be seen thatlin 1878 9 there were five, in 1879-80 five, and in 1880-1 none. Lest these figures should be misunderstood or misinter- preted, I beg leave to remind the board that the Local Government Board's Consolidated drder, Article 211 (a) says a chaplain is not required to baptise children in the workhouse except under circumstances which would justify the administration of baptism in a private house. Children should be baptised in the Parish Church. Guided, there- fore, by these instructions, I have since 1870 baptised only six children who were reported to me as being dangerously , ill, or whose mothers were unable to take them• to church. The rest, by my directions, have been taken to Rainhill, Whiston, or Prescot Church, according to circumstances." —The CLERK remarked that the Rev. J. Barnacle had asked for the returns, and perhaps it would be better if the matter was left till he was present.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS acquiesced, and observed that the statement which had been read must be considered satisfactory. He would merely ex- press a hope that when the new chapel was open children should be baptised in it instead of being taken to Rainhlll, Whistonrand Prescot Churches. (Hear, hear.) THE BOARD IN FINAIICIAL DIFFICULTIES.

The CLERK reported that there was only a balance of I £lB4 Bs. ed. in the treasurer's bands, which was net suffi- cient for out-door relief purposes. He then read a state- ment showing the amount owing by each township on the call made November 10th, and from which it appeared that Only £2,409 had been paid out of a call of £23,539, leaving a balance of £2l,lso.—The Clerk was directed to write to the overseers and assistant overseers of each township, urging immediate payment of the arrears. IRE GUARDIANS AND THE "LIVERPOOL COURIER."

-- Mr. FIDLER called the attention of the Board to a leading article in the Courier of last Monday, referring in strong and pointed language to the pamphlet that had been issued by the Board with regard to out-door relief. The article was written in such condemnatory language that he, as a member of that Board, felt it most keenly. It appeared to have been written on the assumption,that the Guardians took the initiative in publishing the pamphlet, but they had not done so. The Bolton Union had been issuing them for years, with beneficial results. Besides, the Local Government Board empowered them to publish such returns, and the writer of the article was evidently not aware of that fact. He thought the advantages arising from the pamphlet were very great, and his opinion had been confirmed since it was issued. Ministers of almost all denominations had made application to him, for copies of the pamphlet. Ile had placed one in the hands of a ,popular man in St. Helens, who was almost as well known as the Mayor, and that gentleman had pointed out to him (Mr. Fidler) some of the grossest cases of imposition. The Courier seemed to think that for the offence of one 99 should not suffer, and he quite agreed with that, but as a matter of fact the proportion was very much greater. He was sorry that a paper wielding the influence of the Cormier should pass such condemnation upon the con- duct of that Board. The fact was there bad been a great many able-bodied men unable to get employment, and the strain upon the officers and the drain upon the exchequer had been simply astounding. He gave instances of how the Guardians had been imposed upon, and mentioned the case of a man who was employed to wheel stones, but who was too lazy to do the work himself, and got his eon to CIO it. The man drew the money and eat the food purchased by it. If they were to suffer and be pointed at as the scorn of the country and written down as Guardians who had made them- selves the laughing stock of other unions, he, for one, in order to preserve his character as a gentleman and an honest man, should stay away from the Board. (Heart hear.)— Rev. T. (InetrisEns said he had read a letter arising out of the article to which Mr. Fidler had alluded. The corres- pondent, who signed himself as "a lover of justice," after referring to the pamphlet issued by the Guardians, went on to say" Now I contend that to complete this paupers' list we ought to have a special return of the cost of dinners of the Guardians, so that we may compare the two together, and let the ratepayers see where the money goes, and how it is spent. Itcertainly does not all go for paupers. At one time the dinners cost 15s. to 203. per head, and the cost of maintaining a family consisting of eight to ten is estimated generally at 225. per week. What a contrast! 205., one I dinner a guardian; 225., one week's keep for a family of ten 1 persons; and yet they have the presumption to publish a list of paupers with a view to detecting and preventing im- position." He (Mr. Chambers) would not have condescended to notice the letter except for this reason, that a great many ratepayers would really take in all that was said in the letter, and credit the Guardians with appropriat- ing the money. Whatever the Guardians might have done in times past to render themselves ludicrous in the eyes of the world it had nothing to do with that. He wduld not sit there and allow them to be called dishonest. They might have done foolish things, but they were not dis- honest. He could testify that during his three years' ex- perience no dinners of the Guardians bad cost the rate- payers 205,; in fact, so far as he knew, their dinners had cost them nothing, except when the Guardians had been living frugally visiting the asylums. The sum of is .3d. had been the outside cost of the dinners of the Guardians before they 1 were wisely stopped, and that Is. 31 was paid by the Guar- dians out of their own pockets. Now with regard to 225. only being allowed for the support of a family of 10 persons, no such family of 10 children existed on the books. The Guardians were doing their best to save the ratepayers' money with regnard to out-door relief, and they certainly paid for what they eat and drank out of their own pockets. —The subject then dropped. MISCELLANTODS. Messrs. W. Tyrer and W. A. Meadows were appointed as a deputation to attend the Poor Law Conference, and to form part of a general deputation to wait upon the Local Government Board to present copy of resolutions passed at a Poor Law Conference held in Rochdale.—lt was resolved that Mr. James Houghton be appointed assistant overseer for the Bold district at a salary of £4B per annum.—A com- munication was read from John Owen, one of the inmates, requesting that he might be supplied with tobacco and more food. Ile had applied to the master, but the latter had told him he had nothing to do with it, and referred him to the doctor. He (Owen)' thought the master was above his post.—Owen was called before the Board, and in answer to questions he admitted that he had never had his allowance of bread weighed, although he had seen others weighed, and they were short. He also admitted having asked the doctor for tobacco, but the latter went away and did not make any answer.—The Board considered there was no ground for their interference.

tence, and it behoved everyone to push forward the great work. The proceedings terminated with the customary votes of thanks. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. - -

PRIMITIVE METHODIST HOME AND FOREIGN MISSIONS. The annual meeting of the Runcorn branch of the above soeieter was held on Monday, in Greenway-read ChaPel. Mr. Robert Shaw occupied the chair, and was supported by the Revs. C. gmansean (Deputation), of Ludlow, J. Pickwell (resident minister), D. Schofield (of Frodsham), and Messrs. Ring and Ruscoe. The Rov. D. SCHOFIELD (secretary) in reading the report, said it afforded him very great pleasure to be able to say that their labours had not been in vain. From every district of their missionary operations, Canada excepted, an increase was reported; and the decrease of four for the year in Canada was accounted for by the unsettled and migratory character of the population. In south Africa, notwithstanding the dis- turbed condition of the country, the mission work had been successful both among the natives and the settlers. The work of education, secular and religious, was also-progres- sing, beisg carried on by trained and competent coloured teachers. In Fernando Po, western Africa, several causes had operated to diminish the membership, and retard their efforts, but the grace of God had been equal to them. After filling up all vacancies caused by death, a small increase was reported. Tbe schools at Santa Isabel, which were closed by the Spanish Government, had been re-opened, and the gentle training of the missionaries was shoving itself. The George's Bay Mission, which was in the bush, was also doing exceedingly well. The principles of total abstinence were being inculcated along with scriptural knowledge. Several young men had been trained to public speaking, and nine persona had been baptised who were giving satisfactory evidence of a renewed moral nature. In south Australia they had 14 circuits, and nine mission stations, 107 con- nexional chapels, and 23 other places in which the Word was preached. There was alsre an increase of CO members for the year. The report of the Melbourne district showed an increase in the membership of 90 for the year and an in- crease of 318 scholars in the schools. New South Wales was also prosperous, the report showing an increase of 140 mem- bers. • There were also 3,478 scholars who were taught by gratuitous teachers. Queensland, being a comparatively new colony, and of vast extent, did not compare very favour- ably with some of the older colonies. Yet there they had 83 places of worship, 31 of which were connexional property. In New Zealand they had 16 stations, which included 61 places, 18 ministers, 131 local preachers, 33 connexional chapels, and 1,111 members, being an increase of 44 on the previous year. In the dominion of Canada the missions were almost entirely eenfined to Ontario, where they had property to the amount of £73,000. In the Home Mission district, which included Great Mritain and Ireland, they had 88 stations, 402 preaching places, some of which stations became self-supporting at the last conference. The mission had, at the present day, OS ministers, a membership of 8,946, with an increase of 379 for the year. He was sorry to have to make the statement that financially the same succees had not been realised. The total receipts for the year, both for home and colonial stations, was £19,368125. Id., being £4,000 less than the previous year. But there was no doubt that the cause of this falling off was the commercial inactivity and general depression of trade. He was, therefore, very hopeful that when the cloud was lifted the missions would flourish as of old. The local collections were as follows : Collected by the children with books and boxes, £5 19s. 10d.; colleated at the services, £5 ss. ld.; total for the year, £ll 43. na-, being an increase of 14s. 3d. over last year. The CHAIRMAN said that the work which by their presence there they countenanced was a very great one. The education of the young people in our own country was a vaat work, and one worthy of all support. Evil was ram- pant amongst them, and wound its way into their Sunday schools, and even into the midst of their family circles, un- doing the work which loving parents and friends had been trying to do. To accomplish so great a design as the con- version of the young people of this country, men and women were devoting all their energies; but thework they had come to discuss that evening was a far more difficult one, and con- sequently nobler than even this. They bad to go into countries inhabited by people who entertained a suspicious feeling against the white man. This suspicion would in many cases have been eradicated by this time, had it not been for the dishonest dealings of many of their country- men, for it was a deplorable fact that while the missionaries were carrying the Gospel to the heathen, their own nation had been carrying the sword and sowing theseeds of discon- tent. They had therefore to contend with difficulties of their own creating, as a nation, as well as the natural repug- nance that was always felt by the savage nations towards white people. But the grace of God enabled the missionary to overcome all difficulties which beset his path. '1 he work was progressing, and he entured to say it would progress, in spite of all the machinations of the enemies of Chris- tianity. The Rev. C. SMALLMAN (the deputation) said Christianity was the best system in the world. The only way to prove this in a satisfactory manner was by studying the effect it had upon the livee of those who imbibed its principles. They must, however, be careful as to the person whose character they studied, because some who by their profes- sion had been identified with the chuich of God had proved themselves utterly unwortby of that bononr. He would make choice of an individual with whom bethought no one could find fault. Ile referred to the Apostle Paul. Ile would not dwell upon the incidents connected with the life af that noble man, but at once direct their attention to his death. He was under the power of the most cruel monarch the world ever saw, who tortured the Christians by covering them with inflammable matter and setting fire to them for the purpose of itluminating his pleasure gardens at Rome. Under the pdwer of this tyrant lay the Apostle of the Gen- tiles. It was here he gained the summit of the spiritual Pisgab, and as he looked back upon his life he had nothing to regret. Unlike many sceptics who, as they enter the "valley of the shadow of death," quake with fear, and wish they could only live a portion of their lives over again. Paul could look back upon his life and say, "I have fought a good fight ; I have kept the faith." Unlike the sceptic, he had nothing to fear for the future, for he could look death calmly in The face and say, "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give to me at that day." He (the speaker) thought there could not be a more enviable position, spiritually, than that of St. Paul when he uttered those words, and he therefore concluded that a system capable of making a man happy in such adverse circum- stances was well worthy of being embraced. It was this system they were endeavouring to carry to the heathen. He might just observe en peasant, that the object was not so much to make people conform exactly to their way of thinking, as Primitive Methodists, as to get them to become Christians. They had heard from the report something of what was being done in the various fields of labour, but nothing had been said with respect to the states of America. But the missionaries were doing a good work there. They were carrying the gospel to the Rd Indian in his wigwam, and to those white people who had emigrated. There were to be found amongst that number people from Germany, Sweden, Reload, England, and Norway. The work was rapidly spreading, and the time would come when churches, dsc., would be built, not only in Canada, but right across to the shores of the great Pacific. Mr. Smallman next alluded to the work in Australia. The aboriginal tribes of that continent were the most degraded people on the face of the ' earth. They were utterly ignorant of the arts of civiliza- tion, and of the future state of the soul. They supposed that the soul of their departed friends would enter into the body of a white man. He told a story of an English settler who was lost in the bush, and whilst wandering about, be SaW a raised platform, and upon examining it, he found upon the top of it the skeleton of a human being, which subsequently proved to be a chief of one of the tribes. As the settler was descending from the platform, he received a blow on the back of his head which rendered him insensible. I When he recovered he found himself in one of the hovels of a tribe of aborigines, who, after feeding him, brought an ugly old woman to him and made signs that he was to espouse her. Upon his expressing his disapprobation of the amiable lady, they brought a beautiful yourag girl to him, and placing a club in his hand, motioned to him to knock her down. After parleying with them for some time, he let the club drop very lightly upon the head of the girl, who had sense enough to fall to the ground, upon which they appeared satisfied. By keeping a sharp look out he at length found means to escape, and return this settlement. The explanation to this strange story was that the natives, supposing he was the old chief metamorphosed into a white man, had captured him and offered himhis widow, the old woman, but upon his refusal, they brought the belle of the tribe to him and requested him to perform • the marriage ceremony by striking her to the floor with the club. Such were their notions of a future state. The mis- sionaries were carrying the "glad tidings" to these be- nighted people and they were being instructed in the principles of religion, which would dispel the foolish ideas they held with respect to the future state of the soul, and which would teach them a better way of going " sweet- hearting " than knocking down the object of their affections. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) There was another feature to be looked at in the Australian mission, and that was that a great number of Chinese came to the gold diggings, and the Gospel was preached to them, thus effecting what would take years of hard labour if their efforts were confined to RAINHILL WESLEYAN Staerav Senooto—The aunt- China itself. Another portion of the population in Australia versary tea meeting in connection with the above Sunday were those men who had been transported from England, and school was held on Wednesday, about 150 persons sitting had since been released, having fulfilled their sentences. Many of these ms were very wealthy and respectable, and down to an excellent tea. The following ladies presided at it was only right that the Gospel should be preached to the tea tables :—Mrs. Conning, Mrs. Hoperoft, Mrs. Meadows, them, who had, as it were, been tossed out of the lap of their Mrs. King, Misses Brown, Thompson, Hoyle, Stead, Webster, own country. Ile thanked God they were not idle at home. 1 Woods, and Scaddon. After tea a public meeting was held There were several things that were absolutely necessary to in the chapel, Mr. J. Hewitt, of St. Helens, in the absence ensure success. Amongst these were perseverance and of Dr. McNicoll, presiding. There were also on the plat- energy in pushing forward the work. lie urg.ed them to , form Revs. S. Taylor, W. T. Pascoe, Mr. T. Brown, Mr. continual plodding aria persevering labour, and concluded Hoperoft, and Mr. Makin (secretary.) After brief speeches by quoting the well known lines of Longfellow, entitled ' by the Chairman and Mr. Hoperoft, the secretary read the "Excelsior." report for the twelve months ending September 30th, from The Rev. J. PiCRWELL, in the course of a few remarks, , which it appeared that five scholars had become members of said he Could not help sometimes looking at the gloomy side the society. The number of scholars on the books was 119, of the question as regarded Runcorn, and remembering that showing an increase of 5 upon the previous the chapel was in debt. He, however, took heart when he year. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday aftenoen, at the Workhouse, Dutton. Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs.
