div.head: FRODSTIAIR SEWERAGE.
div.p: FRODSTIAIR SEWERAGE.
The following letters were real by the Clerk : "ii, Clegg-street, Oldham, 24th November, 1281.

Dear Sir,— WRIGHT IND RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. I, Referring to your statutory notice of the 19th January, 1880, ' to our client, Mr. Edward Abbott Wright, and to the plan which accompanied it, and to your letter to him of the 7th July, 1881, and to the plan and section shewing one man-hole, and one lamp-hole which accompanies that letter, and to your letter to us of the 29th October last, defining the easement re- quired by the Sanitary Authority; we are instructed by our client to inform you that the amount of his claim for compen- sation in respect of that easement •is the sum of £l4O. We are likewise instructed to inform you that unless the Sanitary Authority is prepared to pay him that amount, he claims a reference to arbitration, and is ready at once to nominate an arbitrator on his behalf. We will thank you to acknowledge the receipt of this communication, and remain, dear sir, yours faithfully, WRIGLEY AND MORECROFT," H. Linaker, Esq., Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, Frodsham. 'B3, Mosley-street, Manchester, Nov. 28, 1881. Dear am obliged for yours of the 25th inst., inform- ing me the amount of Mr. Wright's claim, and, in my opinion, the Ant hmrity will now have no alternative but to submit to arbitration. You ask if I could suggest any ore likely to act forth@ Authority. Mr. Patterson, land valuer, of Albert-square, Manchester, would be a most competent man. I am not aware it he is known to you, but he was the Land Valuer and Agent for the Duke of Bridgewater's Trustees up to the time the canal was purchased by the Limited Co. He has had con- siderable experience in settling this class of claims —Yours truly, HENRY BANCROFT." By. Linaker, Esq., Frodsham. Mr. ASHTON : It we have to pay Mr. Wright.£44o and Mr. Dutton £340, it would, perhaps, be better to go the other

way. Mr. CHALLONER : But we are only going to pay Mr. Wright £5O, and Mr. Dutton-about £2O. Mr. ASHTON : IS it not likely that before many years elapse, Netherton will have to be drained? The CLERIC : Yes; but it would come in the same drainage

scheme. Mr. CUALLONER remarked that the road had been newly laid, and in order to go down to the depth of 261 t., they would have to materially disturb it. 1 The CLERK was of opinion that by putting a drain in the road it would very much improve it. The CEIAIRMAN considered that the only matter really before the Board was the appointment of an arbitrator. The CLERK : Yes, because if you do not appoint the arbitrator within a certain time, the gentlemen concerned can select one within 14 days, and be can act without your permission. The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Bancrof t suggests Mr. Patterson. The CLERK : Yes, and I think that you could not have a better man. Several members of the Board know him well. Mr. REYNOLDS, J.P. : Yes, I know him well. It was unanimously resolved, on the proposition of Mr. ASHTON, seconded by the Rev. J. W. N. TANNER," That Mr. Patterson, of Manchester, be and is hereby appointed arbi- trator on behalf of the Authority in the matter of Mr. Wright's claim for way-leave required for sewerage pipes in connection with the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Drainage Scheme, and that the Clerk be and is hereby authorised to have a personal interview with Mr. Patterson, and obtain all necessary evidence and legal assistance, and , generally to take such steps as may be found necessary to . represent the Authority, and submit the complete case to I the arbitrators." Mr. FARRINGTON, nuisance inspector, laid before the - Board his report; after which the proceedings terminated.

WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY . DEBATING SOCIETY. The House -e-assembled on Monday evening, when Dr. Huson-More (the speaker) occupied the chair. At the time for the commencement of business there were only 23 mem- bers present, and under these circumstances the Premier moved that the House go into committee to consider urgent business, and that the standing orders excluding, strangers be suspended. The hon. member for BCCIINGHAM, having been voted to the chair, read the minutes of the Council meeting, from which it appeared that after a long discussion it was resolved that the Speaker should invite the leaders of each party to a conference with a view to an amicable arrangement tieing arrived at. Pressure of business, however, had prevented him from attending to the matter earlier, and he expected thit the leaders had not received the letter until that even- ing. In the course of the following week replies would probably be received. He suggested that six gentlemen should be appointed on each side to confer as to the future carrying on of the society. No one wished the society to be abolished, and therefore it behoved all those who had its interests at heart to do all they could to keep it together. (Hear, hear.) The PREMIER could only say personally that he should be glad if they could smooth down difficulties consistently with the maintenance of their own rights and their own self respect. The President of the Board of Trade had told him that one of the opposite party informed him that at a meet-. big their friends the "enemy" reflected strongly upon the conduct of the Speaker, who it was said, had shown partiality. It was further said that the Liberals had broken a promise—which certainly was never made in his hearing or to his knowledge, and which would have,been indignantly repudiated—a promise that they would bar the hon. member for Northampton from bringing forward his motion. Such a promise, he said, was not made. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid that they had not got the whole of the reasons from i the other side and that they were really working in the dark. ' He hoped there would be the freest discussion that evening, \and that there would be no mistake or misunderstanding as to what was the feeling of the Liberal party on that occa- sion. He had prepared resolutions expressing confidence in the Speaker, which he intended to bring forward at the last 1 meeting, but withdrew them in deference to the wishes of , the Speaker, but in opposition to his own judgment. The SPEAKER said he undo stood that one member of the Opposition did complain of his conduct. The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE observed that one member (Mr. Westwell) stated that one of the reasons why the Conservatives had absented themselves from the meetings was that the Speaker had shown partiality towards the Liberal party. The member for NORTHAMPTON thought it appeared that the Conservative party had been dissatisfied for some time. They had found fault with everything. He thought if they were to discuss questions from a " childish " point of view, if they were to be afraid of hurting the feelings of their opponents, they might as well "shut up" at once and go home. The members on the Liberal side of the House had by this time largely increased, but there were only about 5 or 1 0 on the Opposition benches. The member for BOSTON said the Opposition complained ,of the tone of the debates, and he agreed with them. ("Oh, ' oh.") The quotation which was regarded as offensive was not withdrawn. All the member for Northampton did was this—he said that he had not stated that the quotation re- presented his opinion. What the Conservatives asked for was a withdrawal of the expression, and he should have been pleased if the member for Northampton had seen his way Ito withdrawing it. (Several voices: "It was withdrawn.';) The SPEAKER : It was withdrawn even as a quotation. The member for NortnumProx : I said "If the words displease our friends I withdraw them. It makes no difference, as the facts are matters of history." The member for BosTorr said he was prepared rather than that the society should be dissolved, to move that the mem- ber for Northampton should no longer be a member of the House. (Loud cries of "No, no.") He thought it would be much better that they should lose one member than fifty. After a brief discussion, in the course of which Liberal and Conservative members expressed their surprise that any member should think of proposing that the member for Northampton should be expelled from the House, six Liberal members were appointed to meet the Conserva- tives with a view to an amicable arrangement being arrived at. ...._ _

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMBER 3, 1881 LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMBER 3, 1881 LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY.

The annual sermons on behalf of the Runcorn branCh of the London Missionary Society were preached in Bethesda Chapel, on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. J. Bedell, of Lymm ; and in the afternoon and evening by the Rev. J. Sadler, from Amoy, China. The annual meeting took place in the same place of worship on Monday evening. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, presided, and there were also present the Revs. T. E. Slater (the deputation), E. Williams (Calvinistic Methodist), J. Bedell, and Mr. Wm. Handley.

There was a good attendance. After devotional exercises, and a few remarks from the Chairman, the meeting was addressed by the Rev. T. E. Slater, formerly missionary in Madras, India, who attended in the place of the Rev. E. H. Jones, who had been attacked with illness. Ile Speaker first referred to the chief geogra- phical features of the country, and slightly to its theological systems. The population was ten times that of England and Wales, a little short of all the inhabitants of Europe. It was very difficult for them to form any conception of such a vast number of people; but if they were to begin that night to try to count up, the inhabitants of India, and continue to do so at the rate of sixty per minute, it would take them some seven or eight years. Indeed, the people of India formed more than a fifth of the wholeluman family! The English and the Hindoos both at one time belonged to the Agrian race. The majority of the Hindoos professed the Brahminical faith. This had flourished, in the world for thousands of years; it arose before the birth of Ahraham, and had a place of its own in the world's history ever since. At one time this form of religion was pure, but now the majority of the people pro- fessing it were idolators and grossly superstitious. Since the time of Christ, 3,000,000 people had been sacrificed in reli- gious practices by the bill tribes, of which, however, large numbers had now embraced Christianity. It was computed that there were about a half a million of Protestant Chris- tians in India, and the Roman Catholics numbered one million more. The Christian Church had advanced most rapidly in the South of India, and especially during the last few years. As many as 90,000 persons had given up this idolatory and embraced Christianity in the Madras Presi- dency since 1877, when that divisicn of the country was visited by the terrible famine. This interesting and most important movement towards Christianity bad been very largely the result of charity and sympathy shown by the British nation in the thus of that great calamity (Hear, hear.) In this, as in every other case, God, at times, brought good out of evil. In a country like lodia, many of the re- sults were, of course, of a general and indirect kind; and so one had to understand the people, and look below the surface, bef are he could guage the result which had been achieved. Christian education had done a wonderful amount, and made an impression upon the minds of thousands of Hindoos who had not yet professed their faith. Many had joined the Bralmohmo Sonaag—a name which meant the association which worshipped the one true God. They had exchanged Indian Polytheism for Theism,—the belief inc personal God; and he thought they could not look upon such a movement i as that without hopefulness. These people met together n places of worship, and sing, read, and prayed like ourselves. There were others who went further than this—nho had faith in Christ in the same way as evangelical believers. They were Christians at heart, but were prevented from making an open profession of their belief by reason of the strong social difficulties which stood in their way. They had no idea in England of the obstacles connected with the existence of caste. It was still considered a disgraceful thing by a Hindoo family when any of their friends or relatives became Christians. If a Hindoo of caste ever em- braced Christianity, he was thenceforth cut off from all privileges of his caste, and very often driven entirely out of , the family circle. There was no subject which the iiindoos I were so fond of talking about as religion. In the sacred city of Benares there were as many temples as there were thousands; and religion went right through the whole life of a Hindoo. Their system of algebra, which was very elaborate, was a religious one. They said their musical notation had come from the gods. Thera were four princi- pal notes in Hindoo music, and they were assigned to four of their deities. He believed that the nation of India was too religious at the core ever to become a kingdom of Atheists, though infidelity was spreading from the reading of English infidel and rationalistic productions. Within the last fifty years as many as 8,000,000 copies of God's word had been distributed in India in 25 different languages. Let them 'think of that, and remember that God had declared that this was the word which should not return unto him void! The time would come when from Cape Comorin in the south to i that hold of winter—the Himalaya n the north—Christ would sway His sceptre over the whole of the great land; i but God wanted them to share n this vast work, which had only just begun. Think of the enormous population of .the country ! 270,000,000 were waiting to receive the gospel ! Each of them could help, and take away one stone at least from the great temple of Hindooism, and lay one The the (Applause.)AtleßmxpAlesoefaiCdhtrhiset.Leedenfiee onary Society had been in existence a little over 80 years, and i the mission n the South Seas was started at the commencement of the organisation. The missions iin Africa and n China were now between 50 and 60 years old: The number of English missionaries engaged by. the society was 139 ; and there to-day 365 native ordained ministers, 4,679 native preachers, 92,474 church members; and 343,708 native adherents associated with the organiza- tion! (Applause.) The total sum raised and appropriated at mission stations last year was£lB,7Bs, which, be thought, they would all be of opinion was a considerable sum for the native converts to raise. In Amoy, where Mr. Sadler laboured, there were not fewer than 20 native churches which were self-sustaining, and which bad been brought into existence through the blessed operations of the London Missionary Society. (Applause.) The Rev. J. S. WaLIAMS, formerly a missionary in Bangalore, and now the pastor of the Congregational Church, Mold, also delivered a stirring address on the work in India. He remarked that there were 330,000,000 gods acknowledged by the Hindoos—more gods than the number of people. (A laugh.) He would point those who said that missionary work had proved a failure to the facts that in India there were 135,000 scholars assembled in their schools; there were 600 native preachers; 2,000 catechists preaching the Gospel every day of their lives ; and he was, therefore, pre- pared to maintain that instead of being a failure, the work had been a most glorious success. The Hincloos believed in the transmigration of souls, and when asked what was the i great end of life they would say t was to reduce the number of 8,400,000 births to which they were liable. A Hindoo believed in the next birth be might be a cockroach— (laughter)—an owl, otassume any one of a thousand other forms. Therefore he would not even tread upon an ant , which might be upon the footway, because that little ant huTwpehhoel upon speakerhe hg thete ehbe otu urcesi oeenndteodal pee fewm; ile mightcondemned months t nnbh tells htss strong gnhgogerla terms %d,i fhgahot th e hr e; tthh ee d might be his grandmother; the monkey which chattered lei .t.wle cm t knew? the e 011 (Laughduet ot ter.)h English Government who would not in the school books allow the slightest reference to Chris.tiartity,though it would permit of remarks as to the filthy system of Mahommedan- ism. (Applause.) In conclusion, the speaker urged those present to increased exertion in the missionary cause. Mr. Wm. HANDLEY read the financial local statement for the year, which was as foil ows:—S unday school, £2l 12s. 7c1.; subscription to widows' fund, £2 25.; collections on Sunday and at public meeting, £8 16s. 3d.; missionary box, £1 14s. 6d.; annual subscription, £2 65.; total, £3O Ils. 4d. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the deputation and other speakers, on the proposition of the Rey. E. WILLIAMS, seconded by the CHAIRMAN; and after the singing of a hymn, the proceedings terminated.

The meeting in connection with the Widnes Branch was I held in the Simm's Cross Congregational Chapel, on Mon- I day evening. Mr. Eustace Carey presided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. T. A. Carver, J. Tessyman, and T. Peters, and Messrs. Glover and Shuttleworth. The Rey. J. Sadler was present as a deputation from the London I Missionary Society. The CHAIRMAN having delivered an address, introduced J. Sadler, a Chinese missionary. The Rev. J. SADLER said he wished that night to talk a little about the Chinaman from his cradle to his grave. The Chinese were a very peculiar people, and their habits were very different from ours. Their houses were only one storey high, and their chimneys were of such a curious description that the houses were always smoky. Ile had spoken of describing the life of a Chinaman from the cradle to the grave. But in China most of the children had no such things as a comfortable cradle and were ushered into the world in a very rough and ready fashion. He then proceeded to allude to the dreadful prac- tice of infanticide. In China he had found the body of one of these little children being devoured morsel by morsel by a dog, and a friend of his one morning found one at his door —its body rotting away beneath the heat of the sun. The girls generally suffered the most. When a boy was born the father's face was covered with smiles, but in one case be instanced when a girl was born the father killed her, and kindled a fire over her remains, hoping thereby to drive I away the unlucky spirit which had caused so many girls to. be born to him. Mr. Saddler went on to speak of the opium traffic, which was a curse to China Government as the drink traffic was* a curse to us. But there was one fact which they could not look over, and it was that they, the English people, were mixed up in it, and could not divest themselves of responsibility for the evils it occasioned. (Hear, hear.) Passing to another subject they would be astonished at the manner in which a Chinaman lived. He subsisted very often on what they would consider no better than offal. The Chinese manner of dress was also peculiar. They had all heard of the Chinese pigtails—though why so called he could not imastine—and no doubt had laughed at them. But he had seen some young ladies wearing pigtails in this cour.try. (Laughter.) They would wonder of what use these pigtails were—but if they had seen a Chinese policeman secure a fugitive thief by his tail then wonder would cease. (Laughter.) The Chinese girls were full of foibles and follies. Would that they would only pay mere attention to their minds, and less to the trivialities to which he referred. In the North the Chinese nreefienont,daynthneore- civilised people, and manufactured silks w present would be ashamed to wear. Travelling iCI n iina was attended by all sorts of discomforts. The mosquitos for not pleasant companions, and the instance were habits of the people were in everything so dirtv. It was very difficult to teach them the benefit of cleanlinese. The speaker then again adverted to child-life in China, and said there wis little of the happiness and joyous fun which they saw u England. What a hard, cruel thing this heathenism Was! In China the mother did not care whether her child's face was happy with smiles or puckered with frowns or wet with tears. Let them be thank- ful that they lived in a Clwistian land. Then the system of

education was most unfortunate. They had lesson books in China which were 2,000 years old, and it was almost impos- sible to convince a Chinaman they were antiquated. A China- man's head was screwed on the wrong way, and he looked backwards and not forwards. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The Chinese people had some curious songs and chants, of which Mr. Sadler gave some examples. Their idea of geography was curious in the extreme. In a Chinese map China occu- 1 pied the lion's share of the space, and Europe, Africa, and America were hidden in the corners. The Chinese customs in regard to marriage and courtship were full of evil. In fact there was no such thing as courtship. It was all arranged by the parents or by intermediaries, and the wishes of the parties concerned were never even consulted. When the time for the marriage came, a red chair was sent for the bride, and then if the bridegroom was a timid man he accepted her, however unsuitable she might be. If on the other hand he were a bold man he might perhaps take courage, refuse to have anything to do with her, and send her back to her home. Another mischievous practice was the habit of a ' bride going in most cases to live with her mother-in-law— (laughter)—but in China the case was different, and the arrangement was a most objectionable one. Another great ' evil in connection with marriage in China was polygamy, the evils of which he scarcely need demonstrate. Poly- gamy, he was glad to say, was now being checked. Yet another evil was the facility for divorce in China. A woman might be divorced in that country on the slightest pretext— this being part of the general system which there prevails for crushing womanhood. Still even in China there was a brighter side to the picture. Wherever you went you met with monuments spanning the roads, erected to some faith- , ful mandarin, some true daughter, or dutiful son. He would next speak of the occupation of the Chinese. At some things they were very clever and ingenious. Referring to old age and death among the Chinese, the speaker said that the for- mer was universally respected in China. An old man was venerated, no matter who or what he might be. With regard to death, fatalism was very general in China. In conclusion he pointed out the responsibility which we had toward this people. After a few remarks from the Revs. J. A. Tessyman and T. A. Carver, and Mr. Glover, the proceedings terminated.

GOTERMIENT INQUIRY AT ST. HELENS. IMPORTANT DISCUSSION, The Town Council of St. Helens having applied to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £2,896 for works of street improvement, Mr. J. T. Harrison, one of Her Majesty's Board of Trade Commissioners, attended at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, to inquire into the application, and to take the evidence of parties interested. There were present the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington), Mr. T. thewis (town clerk), Alderman Cook; Councillors Hanson, and J. C. Gamble; Messrs. Johnson ',(borough treasurer), J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk), Jas. Hart (borough engineer), and Peter McKinley. Mr. BREWIS said he appeared, on behalf of the Corpora- tion, to support the applications. One of the applications was to borrow money for the purpose of purchasing a piece , of land, belonging to the Holy Cross Church, to widen the street near the church mentioned. The corner of the church was very ugly and inconvenient, as would be seen from the Surveyor's plan. The cost of the land including the widen- ing of the street, which would be done by the sellers, who were now engaged in making some alterations there, would £296 45. The other application was for power to borrow £2,600 for the purpose of paving the street on the line of tramway in Church•street and Raven-steet ; and also portions of Corporation and Hall streets. The Tramway Company paved inside the rails and a foot outside, the rest of the street to be done by the Corporation. Mr. Herr' said that the Holy Cross people, for the sum of £296 4e., would give the up land and execute the work. I They were now waiting for the consent of the Corporation to enable them to proceed with the improvement. The reason for the improvement was to be found in the fact that the corner was a very sharp one, and the road at that part was not 14 yards wide. The area given up comprised 145 square yards at 20s. a yard. In the matter of the other im- provement, they intended paving from a point near Bridge- street, along Church-street to the canal bridge in Raven- street, along Warrington Old Road to Parr-street. 8050 yards were to be paved at 163. 6d. per yard.—The Inspector having asked if any gentleman wished to say anything Mr. MCKINLEY said he thought the present setts were n fit for the purpose. INSPECTOR: Are they not sufficiently good? Mr. MCKINLEY: No, sir; nor are they suitable. INSPECTOR (to Mr. Hart) : Will you explain more dis- tinctly the character of the work. Mr. HART said they had a foundation of concrete, and then a bed of slag, macadam, and gravel from about six to seven inches thick. When arrangements were being made between the company and the Corporation, the company submitted Mr. Beloe's system, which is a steel rail laid upon a wooden sleeper, but the Corporation objected to that, and insisted upon a more substantial system, and ultimately the Corporation got Barker's system. The paving setts were Haslingden Blue Lonkey. The INSPECTOR : But the objection is not to the nature of the material as to the size of the setts. Mr. HART: Ours are of the seine size as those of the Tramway Company, seven inches long, five inches broad, and six inches deep. Mr. MCKINLEY: Don't you think the setts are too large for the purpose; too large for horse drawing or driving? • Mr. HART: I do not think so. Mr. MCKINLEY: But as they are the horses do not have a proper grip of the setts. If they were less they would be able to grip them. Mr. HART: I have not seen a horse down. Mr. MCKINLEY: I do not say anything about the horses going down, but if they had a grip they would be able to draw better. I have not seen this size of sett put down, except in St. Helens. If the setts were of the same size as those in front of the 'fown Hall they would be much more suitable, and would look much better. Mr. HART: In some portions of the borough we have some severe inclines. We have an incline extending four or five hundred yards, and others from 118 to 123 yards, and in winter time it be positively dangerous to use a bad class of material. Mr. MCKINLEY! Why not put the best setts in Church- street; it is in the centre of the town, and is level. And as to the horses slipping down, they would be more likely to do so on a surface of seven inches than on a surface of four. The INSPECTOR: They are similar to the others. Mr. MCKINLEY: But there is no reason why they should commit a mistake twice over. The INSPECTOR : Oh, no; but it is for the Council to find the best paving, sett, and I should consider that their judg- ment was better than mine. If you can show to the Council that it is dangerous to use the present sett, they might, perhaps, make a change. Do you consider it dangerous, Mr. Hart ?

Mr. HAIIT: Not at all, Sir. Mr. HANSON: They are not fixed close together. There is the space of three quarters of an inch between them. After a specimen had been examined by the Inspector he said it did not appear to him to be large. Mr. HART: That is an average, sir. Mr. McKINTET It is larger -than in any other town, with the exception of Earlestown. The setts in Liverpool, Manchester, Wigan, Blackburn, or Preston were not so large. INSPECTOR: I cannot say positively, but I think so. Mr. HARP was understood to say that in some portions of Liverpool setts 61n. by 4,Pn. were used, and were similar in quality to their own, which came from Haslingden, in the Bacup and Rossendale district. It was a very hard nell stone, without grit. INSPECTOR: Is it from the coal formation? Mr. BART: Ito, air; it is a whinstone. INspEcron (to Mr. McKinley): You can make a sugges- tion to the Council, and if they think it is desirable they wilt do so. I don't suppose the expense will he much greater. Mr. HART: Very much; greater by half, at least. This is 14s. a ton, and if you use Irish or Scotch granite you will have to put 245. down ; if Welsh, 283. IsspEcron : It is not the size that makes that difference in the cost. Mr. HART said the less size would be more on account of the waste in cutting. INSPECTOR: This does not look like whinstone. Mr. Hata : It is of the nature, sir. INSPECTOR: It is a stratified rock out of the coal forma- tion I think. Mr. CRAM gave the rateable value of the town at £224,000, and the population 57,000. Mr. JonNsoN, in answer to the Inspector, said that the Local Govcrnment Board had sanctioned the borrowing by the Corporation, altogether, of £71,084; and they had bor- rowed £75,804. Of that only £1,400 had been repaid. INSPECTOR: How is that? Mr. JOHNSON: Because it is not long since we borrowed. The first borrowing was in 1874, when £1,450 was borrowed, and that was to be repaid in thirty years. INSPECTOR: How much of that has been repaid? Mr. JouNsoN Only £2OO, but a portion of the remainder is in the sinking fund. INSPECTOR: And where is that? Mr. JOHNSON: In the bank, sir. INSPECTOR: But it ought to be refunded. Mr. JOHNSON: The next loan was in 1878, when £35,000 was borrowed. Of that £29,000 is put to the Public Loan Commissioners, and they make us pay that yearly. The remaining £6,000 is also in the bank. Mr. MCKINLEY: I believe they are drawing against it, sir. INSPECTOR: It will have to be stopped and put into the funds. Mr. MCKINLEY : They have promised that before, and they have not clone it. FORMATION OF A BRANCH OF THE GIRLS' FRIENDLY SOCIETY AT RUNCORN. A meeting for the purpose of inaugurating a branch of the above society, was held in the ante-room of the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday afternoon. Lady Mary Egerton oc- cupied the chair, and was supported by Lady Brooke, and Mrs. Lyon, of Appleton Hall. There were also present Miss Brooke, and the Misses IV. and L. Brooke, Mrs. Wilkinson (Warrington,) Miss Barclay, Mrs. Tomlinson, Mrs. Martin, Mrs. Preston, Miss Warner, Mrs. Pierpoint, Mrs. Mouritz, Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Crossby, Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Fitzsimon, Mrs. Lake, Mrs. Gregory, Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Johnson, and Mrs. Yates. Lady BROOKE, in opening the meeting, said it was estimated that there were in Runcorn about 3,000 girls above the age of fifteen, and of these about 150 wer e em- ployed as milliners, dressmakers, and shop assistants. There was no room in which they could meet, after business hours, for the improvement of the mind ; no place where they could assemble with friends to advise and help them. She was sure that all would see the need there was of an institution which had for its object the providing of these means of amusement and improvement for the young women of the town. She had very great pleasure in introducing Lady Mary Egerton to the meeting, and requesting her to give them some particulars as to the working of the society. Lady MARY EGERTON said that before touching upon the advantages of the society, she would ask those present if they had not felt the need of some organization for girls. The report for the year ending December, 1879, showed that there were branches of the society all over the British isles, Jersey, Guernsey, and also some in America. The number of members for that year was 62,000, and she thought it must be almost double by this time. The speaker referred to cases in which the mistress of a girl had a friendly feeling towards her, but upon the girl leaving her Service, she had no hold upon her. One advantage of the association was, that a mistress in such a case could write to one of the lady-asso- ciates of the association in the particular town to which the girl was going, and she would then be brought into a circle of young people of her own age, and also ladies who in- terested themselves in the work ; and thus the girl would feel quite at home at once, and her former mistress would be freed from all'fear on her account. Girls were very liable to go astray, and the society did all in its power to train them in ways of morality and religion. To commence a branch they only required a secretary and a few lady associates. The associates pledged themselvea to do their best for the promotion of good amongst girls. If a girl was out of a situation it was the duty of one of the associates to do her utmost to find her one. In many towns the society had a registrar, who eittier advertised in the society's own news- paper, or in some of the other journals. It was not to be expected that every one could do all this but there were other ways of aiding the soc iety. One of these was to look after girls who were strangers in the town, and who, when taken ill, had no one to go to. They could then give them an order for admittance into an hospital. Some might under- take to provide occupation for workhouse girls. They would by these means confer very great good upon young females who lived in the town. The society also encouraged their members in habits of thrift, and the feeling of sympathy one with another. In her own parish they formed a class for assisting the poor of the neighbourhood. She often read a story to them while they were working at their needles, making clothes for some of the deserving poor. She often found it very tryinglo keep up to the standard of the work, but it was one well worthy of support, and the success that it met on every hand was very encouraging. Mrs. LYON gave an idea of the actual working of the society, referred to the experience of Mrs. Wilkinson, who was the head of a branch in St. Paul's ward, Warrington. It had now been in existence for several years. A number of dressmakers, shop-assistants, &c., bad beovone i.cecices. Some of them, she believed, were earnestly trying to lead good and useful lives. The branch had prospered so well that now they numbered about 140 members. They ad- mitted none wliose characters would not bear investigation. As regarded the work, it'was of a very simple nature, and what she thought ought to be carried on everywhere, viz: the encouragement of regularity at church and the Sunday afternoon classes. - Miss BARCLAY : You say that the girls must bear a good moral charrcter ? Lady BROOKE: Decidedly. Miss BARCLAY : Unfortunately the girls who most need help are those who do not bear a very good character. Lady BROOKE: I think that is because they have not been looked after early enough. Lady MARY EGERTON said the girls must bear good moral characters otherwise they would corrupt each other, and the object of ;he society was to provide the girls with suitable companions. The "central" rules Were as follows :-1. "Associates must be members of the Church of England (but no such restriction is made as to the members), and the organisation of the society is to follow, as much as possible that of the church, being diocesan and parochial.-2. Asso- ciates (working and honontry) and members to contribute annually to the funds ; the former not less than 2s. 6d. a year, and the latter not less than 6d. a year. Mem- bers payments to go to the 'central fund.'-3. No girl who has not borne a virtuous character to be admitted ass mem- ber; such character having been lost the member to forfeit her card." After a rather lively discussion, it was resolved that a branch be formed in Runcorn. Several influential ladies gave in their names expressing themselves willing to take upon themselves the responsibilities of associates. Votes of thanks were accorded to Lady Brooke, and Lady Mary Egerton for their services, and the proceedings ter- minated.

WEDNESD AL.—Before Messrs. Geo. Pilkington (chairman) and John Brock. THE CARTER AND His VISIT TO "THE GRAPES."—James Bancroft was summoned for a breach of the Highway Act •by allowing his horse and cart to stand in Widnes-road for an unreasonable time, without any one in charge of them:— An officer was called, who said that on the 18th ult, he found the defendant's horse and cart at the front of the Grapes Inn. He went to him and told him that he should report him for his carelessness, which might have resulted in an accident, when defendant took high ground, saying that he had a perfect right, as a free born Englishman, to call for "a drink," and no one could interfere with him.— Bancroft was ordered to pay 7s. ad. and costs; and there is no doubt that by this time it is beginning to dawn upon him that he knows more about beer than law. INTERESTING LEGAL POINT FOR GAS CONSUMERS—Win. Bolton was summoned by the Widnes Local Board for an account of 65., alleged to be owing for gas.—The Bench held that the Board had no ground of action against the man, as he only owed 65., and they had in their hands a deposit of his amounting to I.o3.—The summons was dis- missed.

A PRESOOT WIFE-BEATER COMMITTED SIX MONTHS.— John Barlow, rag-gatherer, Kendal-street, Prescot, and who formerly lived in Widnes, was charged with brutally assaulting his wife.—Complainant said she had to maintain herself and two children, owing to her husband's idleness and fondness for drink. At four o'clock on the previous Friday morning he came home drunk, and awoke her to ask for money. At first she said she had none, when he struck her a violent blow with a heavy stick. Finally she gave him 4d., aid lie went out, but came back at noon, when she handed him 411, which he spent in drink. In the evening he returned, and said, "I will have your money or your life." She replied, "I have no more ;looney to give you,, on which he told her she would have to find some, even if she pawned the few clothes or furniture they had left. She said she would not pledge anything more, on which he struck her a severe blow on the back of the head with the poker, which caused a wound which bled very much. He then went out for' the purpose of pawning the only spare , sheet there was in the bouse.—Prisoner pretended that the disturbances between himself and wife arose owing to her having had a child by another man before she was married.ingh —Superintendentte l a st eightß a r I;era brieflyrs, sh nwsketched t thhee had prisoner'sbeen sent todurin pg raiosla fflotur felony,ent fo r andi, s had inhumansuffered n anadbuoautt twelveto s w.ifmonths'e._ i Prisoner was committed to gaol six months, with hard labour. E. Harrison, CE., from the Local Government hooks.—The enquiry then terminated; an into the slabes; Board Office, held an inquiry on Wednesday at the Widnes tGhoe lennispoleecntotrßwoialrld, due course, be forwarded t e the I.oe Local Board Office, in reference to a dispute between that Y body and the Newton Building Society. The last-named society had appealed to the Local Government Board against the apportionment upon them as mortgagees in pos- session of certain premises fronting Oakland-street and Bank-street, Widnes. Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, appeared for the appellants, and Mr. R. Oppenheim, St. Helens, for the Local Beard—Amongst those present were Major Cross, chairman of the Board; Messrs. W. 11. Ker- shaw, T. Heyes, T. F. Allen, Thomas Handley, Amos Hanson (land agent), T. Adams, Heaton (contractor, Warrington), and T. Higginson (surveyor to the Board).— Mr. Davies opened the proceedings. He remarked that the matter of the inquiry was not in itself of so much serious importance as that it was the outcome of a series of attempts on the part of • various morgagees in possession, in Widnes (who had had to pay rates for streets long after the same were made, and after the original owners had either left or lost posses- sion), to ascertain how the large sums demanded of them by the Local Board were made up. It was owing to the per- sistence of the Board in refusing to give any information respecting the items composing the aggregate sums demand- ed that the appeal had been rendered necessary. It was quite true that an offer had been made to produce the apportion- ments but these showed only a lump sum and the division thereof, according to the frontages of the various properties, and did not give the particulars required. His objections that day were: first, that certain old materials had not been allowed for, but as this allowance had subsequently been made the inspector would have very little trouble upon that head ; secondly, that certain charges were, he believed, in- cluded which could not be supported—for instance, the one for interest upon the moneys claimed; thirdly, that there bad been excessive expenditure on the work which had been done, as he was prepared to prove by the evidence of Mr. Hanson, land agent and surveyor, of St. Helens, and Mr. Heaton contractor, of Warrington, both of whom would be allowed' to have had considerable experience. He would show by one of the witnesses that instead of the amount charge- able against the Buildino Society being £155 Os. 6d. it ought have been £124 ss. 7d., including the usual 5 per cent., and according to another witness £llB 5e sd. He believed he was correct in saying that the work in question was done in 1879; the apportionment was afterwards duly made this year, and on the 23rd August the petition upon which he appeared that day was addressed to the Local Government Board; and on the 4th September the allowances for the old materials were made.—The Inspector observed that he had to take an equitable view of the subject on the part of the Local Government Board; that he should not enter into any personal matters; but con- fine himself to the particular enquiry before him. It might be convenient for him to briefly state what his course would be. He should first call Mr. Higginson, the surveyor to the Local Board, in order to get from him all the information required to make him thoroughly comprehend what the case was. After that official had been examine& it would be competent for Mr. Davies to ask him any ques- tions he thought proper.—Mr. Davies was quite agreeable to this course being followed.—Mr. Higginson produced the plan and the original estimates for the work, viz., Bank- street £535 and Oakland-street £690. These amounts only included the sums charged for paving, as the sewering had already been done. He proved that the usual notices were given, the tenders were accepted in June, 1878, the work done about April, 1879, and finished in October of the same year. The tenders accepted were Bank-street, £542 18s. and Oakland-street, £6Bl 18s. Bd. The total extras in Oakland- street came to £5 Bs. Id., and in Bank-street to £ll Os. 4d. —ln reply to the Inspector, Mr. Higginson said that four months were allowed for the completion of the work in Bank-street, and six months in Oakland-street, but the con- tractor had to keep the roads in order for a further period of six months. He produced the apportionment.—Mr. Davies was of the opinion that the apportionment proved nothing. What he required to know was whether the sum apportioned in Oakland-street and Bank-street was the amount of the tenders or what other amount.—Mr. Higginson replied that the sum apportioned for Oakland-street was £791 9s. ; and, at the request of the Inspector, he read all the items com- posing the excess over the contractor's tender. They in- cluded £6l for interest, £37 for establishment charges, and £2 138. Bd. for advertising the tenders.—Mr. Davies observed that had the information been given in the large number of similar cases iri which he had some time ago been concerned, or even in this particular one, that inquiry would in all prob- ability, not have taken place. He intended to call Mr. Hanson, who would prove that the work could have been executed for £37 less than the Widnes Local Board had charged. This would clearly show that a very heavy price had been charged, and this was especially the case when the fact was considered that Widnes p)ssessed cheaper facilities for carriage than any other in Lancashire. It would be proved that the small length before the society's property could have been done for 4ii7 less; and in this statement Mr. Hanson would be supported by Mr. Heaton.—Mr. Oppenheim objected to Mr. Hanson being called, on the ground of irrelevancy.—The Inspector said that the duty of the Local Government Board was to only sanction an order for such $ sum as they thought equitable. Mr. Davies and hie clients considered the claim made by the Local Board was not equitable; and that gentleman wished to prove in evidence what his clients believed to be equitable.—Mr. Oppenheim replied that the claim of the Local Board was in accordance with the Act of Parliament —The inspector: If you look at the 268 section, you will see that the Local Government Board have to deal with the equity of the matter.-Mr. uppenhetna was quite winioa to aamit that if the question had been raised as to the amount of the tender being excessive, then Mr. Davies's clients might have called witnesses to prove otherwise.—The Inspector observed that perhaps the Local Board might have reasons for not accepting the lowest tender, and he should not go into that point.—Mr. Davies did not propose to dwell upon the question involved in the old materials, as they had been allowed for. He, however, objected to a bill like £64 being charged for interest, when there ought not to have been a single penny put down under that head. The work had been delayed for three years; and it seemed that his clients had been charged for that period, when they ought not to have been charged for three weeks. That was really one of his points, upon which he thought Mr. Har- rison would have to report.—Mr. Oppenheim: Was there I any unreasonable delay 2—Mr. Higginson: There was no unreasonable delay at all.—The Inspector: The contract was let in the autumn, and not begun until spring.—Mr. Higginson: The winter had been a very bad one, and the work could not be carried on.—Mr. Davies said there was no legal power to charge interest upon money which had been, neglected to be collected. If there was any delay on the part of the contractor, he ought to have been made to pay the penalty, instead of charging the property owners with interest.—The Inspector did not think there was much in the point raised by Mr. Davies. The contractors did not commence their work immediately on taking the contract apparently. The last payment for work actually done was made on the 31stsOctober—about six months from the time when the labour was really commenced; so that the con- tractor did it within the period alloted to him.—Mr. Davies: My third point is the amount expended.—The Inspector: Unless you can show something to the contrary, I shall not value any evidence as to what the work should cost. It was specified; the Board took the ordinary means of obtaining tenders for it. They used their judgment on receiving those tenders, and selected from them; I cannot blame them for that—Mr. Davies: My point is that they might have done it for so much less.—The Inspector: There was a month given for the property owners to examine these matters, and the estimate' and to make objections, and that was the time when they should have done so.—Mr. Davies: If I can prove by competent men from other towns that this labour could have completed for less, is not that sufficient , ground upon which to proceed.—The Inspector: It is notl the ground on which the Local Government Board can exercise a jurisdiction in equity. If there was anything like jobbery about it, that would a different matter; but it is not alleged that there was any jobbery about it. The Board took the ordinary means of ascertaining what was the customary price. There must be great latitude allowed as to tenders. You might call witnesses, but it would merely be as to a question of opinion. As the Board took the best way of ascertaining what was the reasonable cost, I could not alter that.—Mr. Davies: My mouth is, therefore, closed. I thank you for the courtesy with which you have heard my complaint.—The Inspector: You hive appealed to the Local Government Board to decide what equitably you shall pay.—Mr. Davies: We have, and I must now leave the matter with you.—The Inspector: You will see the reason of the course I have adopted.—Mr. Davies : Well, yes I do. Will you allow me to call your attention to a letter written from this office, by Mr. Allen, the clerk to the Local Board, in which he says "the Surveyor has never refused to pro- duce the apportionment sheet, but had merely refused to go , into the question of items; and he begged respectfully to point out that he was not called upon to do so under the provisions of the Public Health Act."—Mr Oppenheim maintained that all necessary information had been offered. —Mr. Davies: That is the third time Mr. Oppenheim has contradicted this statement. The particulars have been re- fused over and over again, and yet Mr. Oppenheim keeps repeating the assertion that people have had this informa- tion. (To one of the witnesses intended to be called :) To whom did you apply for this information 2—The Witness : To Mr. Oppenheim and Mr. Allen too.—The Inspector : First of all, you consider the charges excessive, but you don't say anything about the illegality. That includes the question of interest as well as the doing of the work, Well, I don't see anything as to the charges having been illegally made out. It appears to me that the only question which arises is the one of interest. It is the duty of the surveyor ta make the apportionment upon the charge for the work, and then the owners have a right to appeal.—Mr. Allen: They have a right to see the apportionment sheet, but not every item. We might have all the ratepayers in the town- ship coming up for things of this sort; and they would keep the entire staff doing nothing else but furnishing par- ticulars.—The Inspector: In the first place the owners are entitled to see the plans and the estimate, and from these they can judge what they have to pay, and make any objec- tion they liked which is fair and reasonable. Then when the claim is made upon the apportionment, if the owneer finds that the expense he is put to is considerably aboae what he anticipated from the origin-al estimate, he may— and I should do so myself under such circumstances—exer-i else his right under the 268 section, and appeal to the Loca Government lbard.—Mr. Adam : Let me ask one question 7

AN EARNEST APPEAL is made on behalf of JOHN HARRISON, fcrmerly boatman at Runcorn Ferry, now Permanently disabled by bodily infirmity at the advanced age of 66. During his 45 years' public service as ferryman, he gained the respect of all who knew him by his civility, kind- ness, and steady attention to duty in all weathers, as shown by the fact that not a single accident occurred during his time. Subscriptions receired by G EORGE S. HAZLEITURST, Run- corn, Treasurer; JOHN DAVIES, Widnes, Secretary, or volun- tary holders ot collection books signed by above.

DISTRICT OF WIDNES. THE PUBLIC LIBRARIES' ACTS, 1855-1866-1871-1877. Widnes, Nov. 17th, 1881. (Received November 22, 1880.) To JAMES CROSS, ESQ., Chairman of the Widnes Local Board. Dear Sir,—We, the undersigned Ratepayers of Widnes, humbly ask you to take the necessary steps, as required and statea by you at the General Board Meeting, and as required by Act of Parliament. And we humbly ask you to call a Public Meeting as to the desirability of forming and having a " Free Public Library "in Widnes, and paid for out of a small rate. It is useless in saying anything upon the subject of a free library being wanted in Widnes to you, for there is no one knows better than yourself the requirement and want of chances , in books and reading rooms for working men in their leisure I hours to educate themselves, and to fill their minds with useful knowledge. Also, that business men may lay hold of books which are very often very scarce and very dear, for a small pay- ment. We feel sure if we gain your sympathy in this movement (which we believe we have) we shall also have y..ur valuable help in carrying out the obJect to its fulfillment. We are, dear Sir. Yours respectfully, James Ruddiman, 16, Widnes-road, chem'eal labourer; John Moss, 55, Midwood-street, chemical labourer ; Thomas Prescot. 38, Widnes-road, labourer; Wm. J. Mahon, 9, Saxon- terrace, clerk ; E. Simmonds, collector; H. Beacham, railway inspector; Henry Clat ke, Peel-house-lane, Farnworth ; Thomas Hewitt, 31, Lacey-street; Frank Barton, 5, Midwood-street ; Wm. Pinnington, 10, Widnes-road ; Edward Taylor, 41, West- street ; John Betney, 121, Mersey-road; John Walsh, 1, Carey- street ; Thomas Lancaster, Foster-street ; M. Lancaster, 116, Xent-street ; Thomas Hunt, 70, Appleton-In-Widnes; John W. Holden, 37, Wellington-street . • Samuel Cartwright, Ditton ; Thomas Hall. 24, Mersey-road; J. 0. Rhodes, 26, Mersey-road; Charles Benbow, 78, Mersey-road ' • William Melvin, 42, Mersey-road; William Farmer, 90, Hurst-street; Hugh Brown, licensed victualler; James Birchall, draper; Horatio Syred, pawnbroker; Joseph Stones, Appleton; Joseph Betney, 55, Waterloo-road; Thomas Caldwell, 16, Deacon road ; James Norris, 5, Elliott-street; William Henry Parsons, 33, Chol- mondeley-street ; Alexander Bell, joiner, 12, Midwood-street ; Evan Hughes, joiner, Luntsheath ; James Rimmer, Frederick- street. In accordance with the above requisition, I hereby call a PUBLIC MEETING of the Ratepayers for the district of Widnes, to be held in the VOLUNTEER HALL, WIDNES, on TUESDAY, the 6th day of DECEMBER, 1881, at half-past Seven o'clock in the evening. JAMES CROSS, Chairman, Whines Local Board. Note.—Only persons assessed to, and paying the General District Rate for the township of Widnes, have a right to be present and vote at the above meeting.

MIDDLEMISS, Auctioneer, at the QUERN'S HOTEL, FAWCETT-STREET, SUNDERLAND, OR WEDNESDAY NEXT, the 7th day of DECEMBER, 1881, at Three for Four p.m. (subject to conditions of *ale to be then Produced)—The o.d. established GLASS WORKS, known as The Wearmouth Crown Glass Works, situate at Low Southwick, near Sunderland, in the county of Durham. The manufacturing plant consists of two cones (each with an eight pot furnace and 12 blowing holes), a roiled plate tank with kilns attached, and a newly- erected Siemens gas tank for sheet glass, with necessary pro- ducers, regenerators, tall chimney and appurtenances, large substantial and commodious pot lofts, with storage for 200 pots (165 pots witirstock of -clay being on hand); also extensjag new warehouses, cutting-rooms, sheds, store houses, sW;nl.ll., smiths' and joiners shops, eight coke ovens, convenient and roomy offices (fitted with fire-proof safes), manager's and work- men's dwelling-houses, caretaker's lodge and weighing machine, and all necessary tools, utensils, and appliances for carrying on an extensive business. The property has extensive river front- age, with first-class berths for vessels at the quay, upon which there is a movable steam crane on rails. The site contains about 11 acres of land and 3 acres of foreshore. It is leasehold for 99 years, of which 60 years are unexpired, and is subject to an annual rent cf £325, subject to reduction, as stated in lease. About £B3 per annum is received by the vendors for land let off. The works have good access by river and road, and are in close proximity to a railway goods station, to which at a small Out- lay a siding could be made. The 165 pots and the clay are to be taken by the purchaser at valuation. The stock and book debts may at the option of the purchaser be also taken at a valuation. Immediate possession can be given: The goodwill of the busi- ness, which is the oldest established in the country, will be in- cluded in the sale. The long eepression in the glass trade being now at an end, as is evidenced by the great advance in prices during the last tew Weeks, the present opportunity of acquiring a current going business on most remunerative terms is one rarely to be met with.
